docs.title: 3D computer vision and medical imaging in Python
docs.text:
pardesline loads 43 public 3D and medical imaging datasets in one line (Medical Segmentation Decathlon, TCIA, TotalSegmentator, AMOS, LUNA16, IXI, KITTI, Objaverse, Hugging Face repos), gives you one typed object for point clouds, meshes, volumes and label maps over Open3D, PyVista and SimpleITK, runs 73 algorithms whose defaults are documented and tied to the data, and exposes everything to AI agents through a local MCP server.

pip install "pardesline[all]"

import pardesline as pl

s = pl.load("rire_brain")[0]  # CT + MR T1 of one head, 19 MB, licence printed
moved = s.ct.align(s.mr_t1)  # rigid registration, SimpleITK, catalog defaults
moved.save("mr_on_ct.nii.gz")  # + a sidecar with frame, licence, every parameter
moved.to_pyvista().plot()  # or .to_sitk(), .to_open3d()

  • Datasets in one line

    43 manifests over S3, Zenodo, TCIA, OpenNeuro and the Hugging Face Hub. Lazy, verified, cached; licence and citation attached; archives read by HTTP Range.

    Datasets catalog

  • Algorithms with defaults that work

    Registration, reconstruction, segmentation, LiDAR, SDF, mesh and volume processing. Every default has a written reason and a validation regime.

    Why our defaults work

  • Models

    PointNet, DINOv3 features, 3D JEPA, VAE anomaly detection, nnU-Net preparation as reference scripts; one-line pretrained access on the roadmap.

    Models

  • For AI agents

    pardesline mcp exposes datasets, algorithms and twenty expert guides as MCP tools for Claude, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Codex.

    MCP server

docs.title: Measured, not claimed
docs.text:
• The README demo (RIRE CT/MR registration) runs cold in 21 s on a laptop: 7.6 s download, 8.8 s registration.
  • On the Stanford bunny with a 35° offset, 70 % overlap and 0.5 % noise, textbook Open3D ICP ends 32.0° off with a 0.98 fitness; target.align(moving) ends 0.14° off. The experiment, the numbers.
  • 466 tests on Linux, macOS and Windows, Python 3.10 to 3.13.

Apache-2.0. Built on Open3D, PyVista, VTK, SimpleITK, NumPy, SciPy and the MCP Python SDK. Datasets keep their own licences; every manifest prints them.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Package defaults against upstream defaults, same inputs, same metrics, numbers generated by the scripts in benchmarks/ and committed with the command that produced them. Nothing in this page is typed by hand. Run python benchmarks/run_all.py to regenerate benchmarks/results.md; the raw per-trial numbers are in benchmarks/results/*.json.

What is compared and why it is fair:

  • Registration: the moving cloud is a rotated (35°), partial (70 % overlap) and noisy (0.5 % of the diagonal) copy of the target, a different noise draw per trial. Open3D's ICP is called the way its tutorial calls it (identity start, point-to-point, threshold 0.02); Open3D's global registration uses the tutorial's voxel_size = 0.05; pardesline uses target.align(moving) with the catalog defaults. The rotation error is measured against the known transform.
  • Reconstruction: a noisy partial scan with a hole; Open3D's create_from_point_cloud_poisson(depth=8) versus points.to_mesh() (depth 9, density-trimmed); Chamfer distance to the original mesh and the fraction of reconstructed surface farther than 2 mm from it (the balloon over the hole).

The upstream calls are the documented, tutorial-level calls, which is what a practitioner copies first. An expert can of course tune Open3D to the same result: the point of the package is that the tuning is written down and applied by default.

pardesline 0.2.0, Python 3.11.14, Windows AMD64, CPU only.

docs.title: Rigid point-cloud registration on the Stanford bunny (35 deg, 70 % overlap, 0.5 % noise)
docs.text:
python benchmarks/registration_bunny.py --trials 5

Contender Rotation error, median (deg) Rotation error, worst (deg) NN RMSE, median (m) Time, median (s) open3d_icp_tutorial 32.50 32.98 0.0071 0.2 open3d_ransac_tutorial 134.50 173.21 0.0079 0.2 pardesline 0.11 0.24 0.0014 5.2

docs.title: Poisson surface reconstruction on a partial, noisy bunny scan
docs.text:
python benchmarks/reconstruction_bunny.py --trials 3

Contender Chamfer, median (mm) Surface farther than 2 mm from truth, median Time, median (s) open3d_default 0.80 3.4 % 1.7 pardesline 1.14 0.8 % 6.9

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
• Registration: the tutorial ICP call stays near its 32° start (a local optimiser from a wrong pose); the tutorial RANSAC call fails worse because its fixed voxel_size = 0.05 is a third of the bunny, so there are almost no features to match. The package's defaults derive the voxel from the bounding box and land at 0.11° median, 0.24° worst over five noise draws, at the cost of 5 s instead of 0.2 s.
  • Reconstruction: this one is a trade-off, not a win on every metric. The density-trimmed surface has four times less area far from the truth (0.8 % vs 3.4 %: the balloon over the hole is gone) but a higher Chamfer distance (1.14 mm vs 0.80 mm), because the symmetric Chamfer also measures truth-to-reconstruction, and a trimmed hole is "missing surface" where the untrimmed one offers a wrong but nearby guess. Which is better depends on what you do next: for metrology and printing, no invented surface; for rendering, the closed guess may look better. Both settings are one argument away (density_quantile).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The bunny is a public stand-in for industrial scans; the characteristics (partial overlap, noise, unknown pose) are representative, the material is not.
  • RANSAC is randomised: expect a few hundredths of a degree of spread between runs on the registration median, more on the worst case.
  • No benchmark yet for volume registration or segmentation defaults: the RIRE and MSD examples show single runs with their numbers, and the benchmarks tracking issue lists what comes next.

docs.title: What pardesline gives you, call by call
docs.text:
pl.load(path) A local file as a typed Object: PointCloud, Mesh, Volume, LabelMap, Transform, Image. Volumes get their frame (LPS, mm, affine) from the header; glTF is Y-up metres by specification; formats that carry no unit stay unknown until you say. pl.load(dataset) A Dataset from one of the 43 bundled manifests (pardesline datasets), from hf://org/name[/folder], s3://bucket/prefix, tcia://Collection, from your own manifest file, or from a folder via pl.scan. Files are fetched on first access (per file from the Hub or a bucket, member by member out of remote archives, series by series from TCIA, SHA-512-verified downloads), cached. pl.load("sweep.bin", layout=...) A raw .npy / .npz / .bin array as a PointCloud or a grid, through a declared layout (dtype, shape, columns, key). Never guessed; materialised once as PLY / MetaImage so every algorithm runs on it. ds.export(folder) A standard copy of any dataset: PLY / MetaImage / NIfTI files, one .pardesline.json sidecar each (frame, units, labels, licence, provenance) and a local manifest. obj.run("module.method", **params) Any algorithm; the result is a new Object that keeps the frame and licence and records the step. Aliases: downsample, remove_outliers, normals, poisson, ball_pivoting, decimate, smooth, to_points, icp, ransac, register, segment. Conversions named after the job Volume.segment() -> LabelMap; LabelMap.to_mesh(label) exact boundary in world coordinates; Volume.to_mesh(isovalue); Mesh.to_points(); PointCloud.to_mesh() (Poisson, lossy); PointCloud.align(moving), Volume.align(moving); clean(). pl.run(module, method, input, **params) The same without the object wrapper. Returns output path, sidecar JSON, log and timing. pl.catalog() Every module, method and parameter with type, default, range, choices and description. pl.describe("point_cloud_reconstruction.poisson"). obj.to_open3d() / to_pyvista() / to_sitk() / to_numpy() Hand the result to the library you already use. pl.o3d, pl.pv, pl.sitk are the real libraries when installed. pardesline CLI pardesline list, pardesline describe ..., pardesline run module.method in.ply -o out.ply --voxel_size 0.02, pardesline datasets, pardesline fetch amos22 --take 2, pardesline export msd_task02_heart ./heart --take 2. pardesline.medical Volume I/O (NIfTI, NRRD, MHA, VTI, DICOM series), rigid / affine / B-spline / demons registration, thresholding, watershed, connected components. pardesline.cloud The hosted platform: upload, share in one line, run on GPU, open the browser viewers. Optional, needs an account.

Every algorithm is also a plain command with the same contract the platform uses:

python -m pardesline.ops.point_cloud_processing.voxel_downsample --input scan.ply --output small.ply --voxel_size 0.02

Parameters are checked before anything runs — unknown names, wrong types, out-of-range values and missing second inputs fail with a message that lists what is accepted:

ParameterError: point_cloud_processing.voxel_downsample: unknown parameter(s) voxel.
Did you mean: voxel -> voxel_size?. Accepted: voxel_size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Clean a LiDAR sweep and cluster the objects

sweep = pl.load("sweep.las").with_frame("sensor", "m")
objects = sweep.run("ground_removal").run("object_clustering", eps=0.7, min_points=10)
objects.to_open3d()

Register two CT volumes and check the result

ct_day0 = pl.load("day0.nii")  # LPS, mm, affine from the header
ct_day7 = pl.load("day7.nii")
reg = ct_day0.align(ct_day7, metric="mattes_mutual_information", num_iterations=300)
print(reg.transform["rotation_deg"], reg.transform["translation_mm"])
diff = ct_day0.run("difference_analysis", moving=reg)

Segmentation to a printable surface

mask = pl.load("ct.mha").segment(lower=200, upper=600)
bone = mask.to_mesh(label=1).decimate(target_reduction=0.8)
bone.save("bone.stl")  # + bone.stl.pardesline.json: LPS mm, licence, every step

Follow a long run

res = pl.run(
    "simpleitk_registration",
    "bspline",
    "a.mha",
    moving="b.mha",
    on_progress=lambda pct: print(f"{pct}%"),
    on_log=print,
    timeout=1800,
)

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog and the project uses Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: 0.3.0 — 2026-10-17
docs.text: The "reference repository" release: a documentation site, every default documented with its reason, thirteen executed examples, benchmarks, a contributor funnel and release automation. The package API is unchanged; two bugs found on the way are fixed.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• examples/: thirteen runnable examples, one folder each, titled " on ", with the images and numbers they produce and a README per example; examples/real_cases/ for industrial data that cannot be redistributed.
  • Remote archives up to 64 MB (PARDESLINE_WHOLE_ARCHIVE_MB) are downloaded once and indexed locally instead of one Range request per member: the first pl.load("msd_task04_hippocampus") goes from 194 s to a few seconds.
  • Documentation site at https://pardesline.github.io/pardesline/ (MkDocs Material, versioned with mike): one page per dataset (43) and per algorithm family (19) generated from the manifests and the catalog, model pages, the twenty skills as guides, 18 how-to pages titled as the questions people search for, "Why our defaults work", comparison with Open3D / PyVista / SimpleITK / trimesh / MONAI / TorchIO / Hugging Face datasets, FAQ, API reference from the docstrings, llms.txt and llms-full.txt.
  • docs/_gen/datasets_table.py generates the README dataset table from the manifests; the generated pages carry the date of the source's last commit.
  • Every catalog parameter carries rationale (why the default, when to change it) and every method validated_on (src/pardesline/catalog/data/_defaults.json); pl.describe() prints them; tests/test_catalog.py enforces full coverage.
  • benchmarks/: package defaults vs upstream defaults on the Stanford bunny (registration, Poisson reconstruction), tables generated into benchmarks/results.md.
  • tests/test_docs_snippets.py executes the code blocks of the README, the tutorial and the how-to pages (network marker).
  • Docstrings on every public function and class (31 added).
  • CI: type-check job (mypy), coverage uploaded to Codecov, native matrix on Python 3.10 and 3.13, a job that executes the README demo and the documented code blocks against the live datasets, a nightly workflow that installs from PyPI on three OSes and runs the demo, OpenSSF Scorecard, Dependabot (GitHub Actions only), pre-commit config, .zenodo.json for a DOI per release, docs/assets/make_social_preview.py.
  • Release automation: Release Please opens the release pull request from the conventional commits (version bump in _version.py, CITATION.cff and the two plugin manifests, CHANGELOG section); merging it creates the tag and the GitHub release, then dispatches the PyPI upload (Trusted Publishing) and the versioned documentation.
  • Contributor funnel: issue forms (bug, feature, dataset request, algorithm or model request, real case), pull request template, CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, SECURITY.md, SUPPORT.md, CODEOWNERS, .all-contributorsrc, templates/new_dataset, templates/new_algorithm, templates/new_model, templates/new_pipeline with tests, docs/seo/issues-to-create.md (tracking issues, 16 good first issues, 11 help wanted) and docs/seo/apply_github.py to apply labels, metadata and issues through the API.
  • docs/showcase/: the ten pipeline posters with, for each, the snippet, the expert skill and the MCP tool; posters.gif (carousel), mosaic.jpg, social-preview.png for the repository card; CITATION.cff.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• README rewritten as a front page: poster carousel, the promise in three lines, install, an executed 30-second demo (CT/MR registration on RIRE), generated datasets table, algorithms and models tables, "Defaults that work on real data" side by side with the tutorial defaults, comparison table, gallery, MCP, roadmap (model registry first), community, citation.
  • [local] accepts Open3D 0.20, which ships Python 3.13 wheels: pip install "pardesline[all]" now works on 3.10-3.13 (the native test suite passes on 3.13 with 0.20).
  • PyPI metadata: description, 26 keywords, classifiers and project URLs unified on the documentation site.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• .nii.gz files are accepted by every module that accepts .nii (Volume.segment() on a Decathlon volume raised "does not accept '.gz' files").
  • Archive members whose names would escape the dataset cache (../evil.bin) are ignored at index time and refused by fetch.
  • Docs deployment: mike aliases are copies instead of symbolic links, which the GitHub Pages builder rejects; the old hand-written docs/index.html landing page is removed now that Pages serves the gh-pages branch.

docs.title: 0.2.0 — 2026-10-14
docs.text: First stable release of the open package: everything below is on top of 0.2.0a1.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Eleven expert skills with reference scripts, served by the MCP server (list_skills, get_skill, pardesline://skill/{name}) and shipped in the wheel: 3-D representations, point-cloud registration (RANSAC + FPFH + ICP, CPD), multimodal rigid registration (SimpleITK Mattes MI), atlas label transfer, PointNet segmentation, DINOv3 dense features (Gram anchoring, frozen backbone + Faster R-CNN), JEPA pretraining (3-D ViT reference), VAE anomaly detection, Gaussian splatting (points -> 3DGS PLY), medical segmentation models (nnU-Net export) and 3-D evaluation metrics. The NumPy / Open3D / SimpleITK scripts run on the bundled datasets; the PyTorch ones are reference implementations.
  • Local MCP server (pardesline mcp, extra [mcp]): twelve tools (datasets, samples, scan / confirm, export, catalog, run, describe_object, to_mesh), three resources and a start_here prompt over stdio or streamable HTTP, for Claude, Gemini, Cursor, Codex and any MCP client, without an account. Questions come back as JSON for the agent to relay; the repo ships a .mcp.json and the plugin declares the server. New skill mcp-server.
  • Medical 3D datasets, one line each. 27 new manifests: the ten Medical Segmentation Decathlon tasks, TotalSegmentator CT (117 structures) and MRI (56), LUNA16, IXI, VerSe 2019, SPIDER, CHAOS (DICOM), four TCIA collections (Pancreas-CT, LIDC-IDRI, NSCLC-Radiomics, Prostate-3T), OpenNeuro ds000228, KiTS23, AbdomenAtlas Mini and CT-RATE (gated), the BiomedSegFM 3-D validation set, MedShapeNet (106 101 STL shapes) and the C3VD endoscopy Gaussian splats - 43 manifests in all, each listed and sampled live.
  • New sources: s3 (public bucket, ListObjectsV2, pl.load("s3://...")), tcia (NBIA REST API, one DICOM series per entry, pl.load("tcia://Collection/CT")), urllist (a text index of URLs); archive sources may span several archives (urls).
  • DICOM series as folder entries (fetched whole), MetaImage .raw siblings fetched with their header, repeated pattern placeholders ({id}/anat/{id}_T1w.nii.gz) matched as backreferences.
  • Hugging Face datasets, for real. pl.load("hf://org/name[/sub/folder]") loads a bundled manifest or, for any other repo, lists the folder, drafts a manifest and asks what it cannot establish (licence from the Hub card, units, labels, array layouts) - the same four asking modes as a private folder. Listings go per folder (source.paths), are cached on disk per commit and capped (source.max_files), with a clear message instead of an HTTP 429.
  • Remote archives read by HTTP Range (source.scheme: "archive"): zip (incl. zip64) and uncompressed tar on S3 / Zenodo are indexed for a few KB and read member by member; whole download with checksum when the server ignores ranges.
  • Raw arrays through a layout: .npy / .npz / .bin roles declare layout (dtype, shape, columns, key, spacing); pl.load("sweep.bin", layout=...), RawArray.as_points() / as_volume(); decoded once into PLY / MetaImage so the 73 algorithms run unchanged; wrong layouts fail loudly.
  • Nine manifests: msd_task02_heart, amos22, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, hf_openmind, hf_nsclc_radiomics, hf_objaverse_glb_shard, hf_3d_arena, hf_uniocc_carla_mini, hf_kitti360_gs_subset, each checked against the live source.
  • Dataset.export(folder): a standard copy (PLY / MetaImage / NIfTI, one sidecar per file, a local manifest) of any dataset or subset.
  • CLI: pardesline datasets, describe <dataset>, fetch, export.
  • https files accept an upstream md5 and an archive_root; pattern placeholders other than {id} join into the sample id and become fields (ds.filter(split="Tr")).

docs.title: 0.2.0a1 — 2026-10-10
docs.text: First open-source release of the package. Licence: Apache-2.0.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Local execution of the 73 algorithms that power the PardesLine platform (19 modules: point clouds, meshes, surface reconstruction, registration, deformable registration, segmentation, SDF, LiDAR, stereo, collision, PyVista analysis and volume processing, SimpleITK registration and segmentation). Every algorithm runs on your machine with pl.run(module, method, input, **params) or as a CLI module.
  • Typed catalog (pl.catalog) generated from the platform's module manifests: 371 parameters with type, default, range, choices and description. Parameters are validated and coerced before a run.
  • pl.Object: a local file wrapped with its kind (point cloud, mesh, volume, transform, image), its sidecar metadata (registration transforms) and the provenance of every run that produced it.
  • pl.load(path) for local files; obj.run(...) and obj.methods().
  • pardesline CLI: list, describe, run, plus the cloud commands.

  • pardesline.medical: the SimpleITK service (volume I/O, DICOM series, rigid / affine / B-spline / demons registration, segmentation).

  • Object model: PointCloud, Mesh, Volume, LabelMap, Transform, Image with frame (axes, units, affine, source), labels, license and provenance; with_frame / with_labels / with_license; save() writes a .pardesline.json sidecar that load() reads back. Volume headers give LPS/mm and the affine; glTF is Y-up/m by specification; other formats stay unknown until declared - never guessed.

  • Conversions: Volume.segment() -> LabelMap; LabelMap.to_mesh(label) exact isosurface in world coordinates (in-process, direction cosines applied); Volume.to_mesh(isovalue); Mesh.to_points(); PointCloud.to_mesh(); align() and clean() on clouds and volumes.
  • Datasets: manifest schema (source, licence, citation, roles, samples, questions); Dataset / Sample with lazy fetch, split() by group, filter, take, sample; sources local, https (SHA-512, mirrors, tar/zip archives, cache), hf:// ([hf] extra) and Open3D demo data.
  • Bundled manifests: rire_brain, popi_lung_4dct, liver_tumor_patient01, visible_human_head_mri, open3d_bunny, open3d_armadillo, open3d_icp_demo.

  • pl.scan(folder) drafts a manifest for a private folder and lists its open questions; pl.load(folder) raises NeedsConfirmation until they are answered (in the call, in the saved draft, interactively, or assume=True).

  • Skills for AI agents under skills/ (eight Claude Code skills) with a plugin manifest, so /plugin marketplace add pardesline/pardesline teaches an agent the package; tests/test_skills.py keeps them consistent with the catalog, the datasets and the public API.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: title: pardesline vs Open3D, PyVista, SimpleITK, trimesh, MONAI, TorchIO and Hugging Face datasets description: Where pardesline sits next to the 3D and medical imaging libraries it builds on: dataset access, standardization, manifests, high-level API, data-tied defaults, pretrained models, MCP. Facts with sources, not marketing.

docs.title: Comparison with other libraries
docs.text: pardesline is the dataset layer and the domain-vocabulary API on top of these libraries. It imports Open3D, PyVista, VTK and SimpleITK, runs their algorithms, and hands you their objects (to_open3d(), to_pyvista(), to_sitk()). Nothing here is a criticism of them: without them there would be nothing to wrap. Each cell links to the documentation it was checked against (October 2026); corrections are welcome as issues.

docs.title: Algorithms, defaults and models
docs.text:

docs.title: Which one should you use?
docs.text:
• You work on one library's objects and know its parameters: use it directly. pardesline will not get in the way, it hands you those objects.
  • You need a dataset, in a format you can compute on, with its licence: pardesline, then whichever library you like.
  • You need MONAI or TorchIO transforms and training loops on medical volumes: use them; pardesline can feed them (ds.export(folder) writes NIfTI-compatible MetaImage files, prepare_nnunet_dataset.py writes the nnU-Net layout) and will load their model outputs back as label maps.
  • You need registration, reconstruction or segmentation that works on first call on data that is not the tutorial's: pardesline's defaults, with the reasons written down.
  • You are building an agent that must browse datasets and run pipelines: pardesline's MCP server.

docs.title: Contributing to pardesline
docs.text: Thank you for considering a contribution. The easiest and most useful ones are a dataset manifest, an algorithm, a model manifest and an example; each has a template and a checklist below. The rules exist to keep the package trustworthy for people who run it on data that matters.

docs.title: Ten-minute setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/pardesline/pardesline
cd pardesline
python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ".[all,dev]"                            # Python 3.10-3.13 (Open3D 0.20) or 3.10-3.12 (0.19)
pre-commit install                                     # ruff on every commit (optional, CI runs it anyway)
pytest -q -m "not local and not medical"               # core tests, about a minute
pytest -q                                              # everything, about ten minutes
mkdocs serve                                           # docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000 (pip install mkdocs-material "mkdocstrings[python]" mkdocs-gen-files)

ruff check . and ruff format . must pass; ruff format also formats the Python blocks inside Markdown files.

docs.title: Pull request checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] One change per pull request, with a test.
  • [ ] ruff check ., ruff format --check ., pytest -q -m "not local and not medical" green locally.
  • [ ] No data in the repository: tests generate their inputs, examples download through pl.load.
  • [ ] No silent guessing: when a format does not carry units, a frame or a label meaning, the code raises or asks.
  • [ ] Every new parameter is in the catalog JSON with name, type, default, min, max, description, and in src/pardesline/catalog/data/_defaults.json with the reason for its default and the data it was validated on (tests/test_catalog.py enforces both).
  • [ ] CLI contracts never change silently: every op under pardesline.ops is callable as python -m pardesline.ops.<module>.<script> --input … --output …; renaming or removing a flag is a breaking change with a CHANGELOG entry.
  • [ ] A line in CHANGELOG.md under Unreleased.
  • [ ] Commit messages: imperative, prefixed feat:, fix:, docs:, ci:, tests:, release:, body says what changed and what was verified.

docs.title: Adding a dataset
docs.text:
Copy templates/new_dataset/ and follow its README. In short:

  1. Probe the source before writing anything: Hugging Face tree (HfApi().list_repo_tree, scoped to a sub-folder, 1–2 s between calls), a zip or tar on S3 / Zenodo (RemoteZip / RemoteTar index it by HTTP Range), a TCIA collection (getSeries), an S3 bucket, a URL index. Record the licence exactly as the source states it, with the date you checked.
  2. Write the manifest src/pardesline/data/manifests/<name>.json: source (scheme and location), roles with type, pattern ({id} and other placeholders), frame, units, labels, layout for raw arrays, modality; license (spdx, commercial, redistribution, requires_agreement, note, source_url); citation, homepage, pairing, size_mb, tags. Never embed data; never guess what the files do not say.
  3. Verify offline: pytest -q tests/test_manifest.py tests/test_skills.py.
  4. Verify live: python -c "import pardesline as pl; ds = pl.load('<name>'); print(len(ds.ids)); print(ds[0].describe())" and fetch one small role. Compare the sample count with the source's own count.
  5. Wire it in: the table in docs/datasets.md and the datasets-and-manifests skill, docs/_gen/datasets_table.py picks it up for the README, the docs page is generated at build time. Add the name prefix to tests/test_skills.py if it is new.

What is not accepted: mirrored data, loaders that bypass a gate or a data-use agreement, licences copied from memory.

docs.title: Adding an algorithm
docs.text:
Copy templates/new_algorithm/. In short:

  1. Script src/pardesline/ops/<module>/<name>.py: argparse with --input, --output (and --moving for two-input methods), typed flags for every parameter, exit 0 on success, logs through loguru, a JSON next to the output when the method returns numbers (transforms, metrics).
  2. Catalog entry in src/pardesline/catalog/data/<module>.json: the method with id, name, script, output_extension and every parameter (name, type, default, min, max, options, description, advanced).
  3. Defaults rationale in _defaults.json: validated_on for the method and one sentence per parameter saying why the default is what it is and when to change it. Run the method on a bundled dataset and write what you measured; "generated test data" is an acceptable regime when that is the truth.
  4. Tests: a smoke test in tests/test_ops_smoke.py on generated data; tests/test_catalog.py checks the catalog and the script agree.
  5. High-level call when it fits the object model (align, segment, to_mesh, clean…): src/pardesline/object/__init__.py, with a docstring.
  6. Docs: the algorithm page is generated; add a how-to page under docs/how-to/ if the method answers a question people search for, and an example under examples/ if it runs on a bundled dataset.

docs.title: Adding a model manifest
docs.text:
The model registry (one-line access to pretrained models, the same pattern as datasets) is on the roadmap; model manifests can be contributed now so the runner has something to load when it lands. Copy templates/new_model/: a manifest.json (source, weights URI, licence, input type, task, memory and GPU needs, provenance, citation), a loader stub that says what it would download and how it would be called, and a docs page under docs/models/. List it on the Models wanted issue.

Reference scripts that read a pardesline dataset and run a model today (as the PointNet, JEPA, VAE and DINOv3 scripts do) go under the matching skill's scripts/ folder with a --smoke mode and are documented in the skill.

docs.title: Adding an example
docs.text:
Copy templates/new_pipeline/: one folder under examples/, a run.py that loads a bundled dataset, runs one algorithm or model, writes one image and a JSON summary, and a README.md with the dataset, the licence, the runtime and what the defaults handled. Title it <algorithm or model> on <dataset>, run it, commit the image and the summary (large outputs are ignored by .gitignore), add a row to examples/README.md and a card to the README gallery.

Real industrial or medical cases go to examples/real_cases/ with the data or a loader for it, de-identified by you, under a licence that allows redistribution.

docs.title: Adding a skill (expert guide)
docs.text: skills/<name>/SKILL.md with front matter (name, description between 200 and 1 500 characters), the structure of the existing skills (idea, pipeline, parameters by name, metrics, failure modes, datasets to practise on), optional scripts/. tests/test_skills.py checks that every module.method, pl.<name> and dataset name you cite exists. The page under docs/guides/ or docs/models/ is generated.

docs.title: Reporting a bug
docs.text: Open an issue with the template: the snippet or command, the full log, pardesline version, and the versions of Open3D, PyVista and SimpleITK if relevant. Security issues: see SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Release process (maintainers)
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the CI locally in a clean venv (ruff, core tests on the newest Python).
  2. Bump src/pardesline/_version.py, .claude-plugin/plugin.json, .claude-plugin/marketplace.json; date the CHANGELOG section and its compare links; update the README status line.
  3. Commit release: X.Y.Z, tag vX.Y.Z, push both.
  4. Publish a GitHub release from the tag: the publish.yml workflow uploads to PyPI through Trusted Publishing and the docs.yml workflow deploys the versioned documentation.
  5. Verify pip install pardesline==X.Y.Z in a fresh venv.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: By contributing you agree that your contribution is licensed under the Apache License 2.0, like the rest of the project. Datasets you describe keep their own licences, which your manifest must state as the source states them.

docs.title: Datasets and manifests
docs.text:
pl.load never knows a dataset; it knows a manifest: where the files come from (with checksums or a Hub revision), under which licence, how files group into samples, and what each file cannot say by itself (frame, units, label meanings, array layout). Forty-three manifests ship with the package; pl.datasets() / pardesline datasets list them, pl.describe(name) prints one. Every public source below was listed and one file fetched from it on 2026-10-13/14; the licence column is what the source states.

Medical volumes: CT, MRI, PET, ultrasound (NIfTI, MetaImage, npz)

Dataset What Source Licence msd_task01_braintumour ... msd_task10_colon the ten Medical Segmentation Decathlon tasks (2 633 CT/MRI with labels: brain tumour, heart, liver, hippocampus, prostate, lung, pancreas, hepatic vessels, spleen, colon) one tar per task on S3, read by Range CC-BY-SA-4.0 amos22 600 abdominal CT/MRI, 15 organs zip64 on Zenodo, read by Range (24 GB) CC-BY-SA-4.0 totalsegmentator_ct 1 228 CTs, 117 structures as one mask role each (s.liver, s.vertebrae_l3...) zip on Zenodo, read by Range (24 GB) CC-BY-4.0 totalsegmentator_mri 298 MRIs, 56 structures zip on Zenodo, read by Range CC-BY-NC-SA-2.0 luna16 888 thorax CTs for nodule detection (MetaImage + raw) ten zips on Zenodo, read by Range CC-BY-4.0 ixi_brain_mri ~600 healthy brains, T1 / T2 / PD / MRA four tars at Imperial College, read by Range CC-BY-SA-3.0 verse19_spine 160 spine CTs, 28-class vertebra masks, centroids three zips on S3, read by Range CC-BY-SA-4.0 spider_lumbar_mri 447 lumbar MRIs, vertebra / disc / canal masks two zips on Zenodo, read by Range CC-BY-4.0 hf_openmind OpenMind head MRI, one OpenNeuro study at a time (114k images in all) hf://MIC-DKFZ/OpenMind CC-BY-4.0 hf_nsclc_radiomics 422 lung CTs with tumour and organ masks (TCIA, NIfTI) hf://farrell236/NSCLC-Radiomics-NIFTI CC-BY-3.0 hf_kits23 489 kidney-tumour CTs, kidney / tumour / cyst hf://neheller/KiTS-Challenge-Imaging CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 hf_abdomenatlas_mini abdominal CTs with nine organ masks (first 100 of 5 195) hf://AbdomenAtlas/AbdomenAtlas1.0Mini, gated CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 hf_ct_rate_valid chest CTs paired with radiology reports (first 20 of 50 188) hf://ibrahimhamamci/CT-RATE, gated CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 hf_biomedsegfm_3d_val 2 144 CT / MRI / PET / 3-D ultrasound / microscopy volumes as npz hf://junma/CVPR-BiomedSegFM CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 openneuro_ds000228 T1w MRI of 155 children and adults; any OpenNeuro dataset via s3://openneuro.org/dsXXXXXX public S3 bucket PDDL / CC0 rire_brain, popi_lung_4dct, liver_tumor_patient01, visible_human_head_mri the SimpleITK notebook excerpts https + SHA-512 research use, terms to confirm

DICOM series

Dataset What Source Licence tcia_pancreas_ct 82 abdominal CTs (NIH) TCIA, NBIA API CC-BY-3.0 tcia_lidc_idri 1 018 thorax CTs + DICOM SEG TCIA, NBIA API CC-BY-3.0 tcia_nsclc_radiomics_dicom 422 planning CTs + RTSTRUCT + SEG TCIA, NBIA API CC-BY-3.0 tcia_prostate_3t 64 T2 prostate MRIs TCIA, NBIA API CC-BY-3.0 chaos_abdomen 20 CT + 20 MR (T1 in/out-phase, T2 SPIR) as DICOM series zip on Zenodo, read by Range CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0

Any of the 156 public TCIA collections: pl.load("tcia://Collection[/CT,MR]").

Anatomical meshes, splats and point clouds

Dataset What Source Licence medshapenet 106 101 anatomical and instrument shapes as STL (ds.filter(structure="liver")) public URL index CC-BY-4.0, per source c3vd_endoscopy_splats ten colonoscopy scenes as Gaussian splats + point clouds zip on Zenodo, read by Range CC-BY-4.0 (C3VD NC) hf_3d_arena 29 image-to-3D generators x 100 images, meshes and splats hf://3d-arena/3d-arena MIT hf_objaverse_glb_shard 5 000 glTF objects (one shard) hf://allenai/objaverse ODC-By, per-object CC open3d_bunny, open3d_armadillo, open3d_icp_demo Open3D demo data open3d.data terms to confirm

Driving and LiDAR

Dataset What Source Licence kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001 108 Velodyne sweeps + stereo images zip on S3, read by Range CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0 hf_kitti360_gs_subset 16 KITTI-360 chunks: points + Gaussian-splat arrays hf://GaussianWorld/... CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0 hf_uniocc_carla_mini LiDAR, cameras and occupancy grids (CARLA) hf://tasl-lab/uniocc MIT

Access is lazy by design. Indexing the MSD heart tar costs 32 KB (61 headers), the KITTI zip 157 KB, the 24 GB AMOS zip64 145 KB and the 145k-entry TotalSegmentator zip 14 MB; a case then costs its own size. Hub manifests scope their listing to the folders they need and a listing is capped at 20 000 files: listing OpenMind whole (266 721 files) takes 15 minutes and is rate-limited for anonymous clients. Gated repositories (AbdomenAtlas, CT-RATE) need your own Hub token after you accept their terms; restricted TCIA collections answer 401 and are left to the NBIA Data Retriever. The package never scripts past a click-through.

ds = pl.load("popi_lung_4dct")  # six breathing phases of one thorax CT + a mask
ds.describe()  # licence, citation, roles, samples
phase0 = ds["phase_00"]
phase0.mask.labels  # {1: 'body', 2: 'lungs'}
lungs = phase0.mask.to_mesh(label=2)  # exact surface, LPS mm
moved = phase0.ct.align(ds["phase_50"].ct)

train, test = ds.split(by="patient", fractions=(0.8, 0.2), seed=0)  # leakage-free

Your own folder. pl.scan drafts a manifest (samples, roles, what the headers say) and lists the questions it will not answer for you:

pl.load("/data/study_A")
# NeedsConfirmation: study_a: 4 question(s) before this folder can be loaded:
#   - license: Who owns this data and under which terms may it be used?
#   - roles.mesh.units: p01/la.stl: the format carries no unit. mm, m, ...?
#   - roles.mask.labels: p01/seg.nii.gz looks like a label map. What does each value mean?
#   ...
# Draft saved: /data/study_A/pardesline.manifest.json

ds = pl.load(
    "/data/study_A",
    license="internal, no redistribution",
    units={"mesh": "mm"},
    labels={"mask": {1: "left_atrium"}},
)

Or edit the saved draft, or interactive=True to answer in the terminal, or assume=True to proceed with unknowns (and warnings). Licence terms of public datasets that could not be confirmed are marked TO CONFIRM in the manifest and in ds.license.describe().

Any Hugging Face repo, public bucket or TCIA collection. pl.load("hf://org/name/sub/folder"), pl.load("s3://bucket/prefix") and pl.load("tcia://Collection/CT") use the bundled manifest when there is one, otherwise list the source, draft a manifest and ask the same questions (licence from the Hub card or the archive's policy, units, labels, and the layout of raw arrays). When nothing is left to ask, the dataset loads directly:

pl.load("hf://acme/scans/raw")
# NeedsConfirmation: hf_acme_scans: 1 question(s) ...
#   - roles.scan.layout: raw/p01/scan.bin is a raw array. What is in it? ...
ds = pl.load(
    "hf://acme/scans/raw",
    types={"scan": "points"},
    layout={"scan": {"dtype": "float32", "shape": "(N,4)", "columns": ["x", "y", "z", "i"]}},
    units={"scan": "m"},
    frame={"scan": "sensor"},
)

Sources: local folders; https files with SHA-512 or md5 (and tar/zip downloads); hf repos through huggingface_hub (pip install "pardesline[hf]", your own token for gated data and for higher rate limits); archive: one or several remote zips or tars read member by member with HTTP Range requests (zip64 included, index cached; one verified download when the server ignores ranges); s3: a public bucket listed anonymously; tcia: a collection of The Cancer Imaging Archive through the NBIA API, one DICOM series per entry; urllist: a text index with one download URL per line; Open3D demo data. A DICOM series is a folder entry: fetching it brings every file; a MetaImage header brings its .raw.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: title: Examples gallery — 3D algorithms and models on public datasets description: Twelve executed examples, each a self-contained script on a bundled dataset with its image and numbers committed: registration, ICP comparison, label map to mesh, Poisson, threshold segmentation, LiDAR clustering, atlas transfer, Gaussian splats, metrics, PointNet, JEPA, VAE, DINOv2.

docs.title: Examples gallery
docs.text:
Each example is one folder under examples/ with a self-contained run.py that downloads what it needs through pl.load(...), runs, prints a JSON summary and writes its images next to itself. Every image and number here was produced by the script beside it on 2026-10-16.

pip install "pardesline[all]"      # PyTorch examples: pip install torch (CPU is enough)
python examples/<folder>/run.py

docs.title: Real cases
docs.text: examples/real_cases/ is where runs on data that looks like production data go (industrial scans, de-identified medical volumes, field LiDAR), with the template and the review rules. The README's "Validated on real cases" table only lists folders that exist there or in examples/.

docs.title: Writing one
docs.text: Copy templates/new_pipeline/: a run.py that loads a bundled dataset, runs one algorithm or model, writes one image and a JSON summary, and a README stating the dataset, the licence, the runtime and what the defaults handled.

docs.title: Which datasets are not supported, and why?
docs.text: BraTS is distributed through Synapse under a data-use agreement; ModelNet, ShapeNet and ScanNet require registration before download. pardesline never mirrors data and never bypasses a gate, so these are not bundled. A manifest that fetches them with the user's own credentials after they accept the terms is welcome: see Datasets wanted. Gated Hugging Face repos (AbdomenAtlas, CT-RATE) work once you have accepted the terms and run huggingface-cli login.

docs.title: Does pardesline redistribute datasets?
docs.text: No. Every loader fetches from the owner's server (S3, Zenodo, TCIA, OpenNeuro, the Hub, university servers). The manifest records the licence as stated by the source and the loader warns when the terms are not a standard licence. Mirroring permissive datasets on a pardesline Hugging Face organisation is on the roadmap and will only cover licences that allow it.

docs.title: Why does it print "licence unknown - check the terms"?
docs.text: Because the source states terms outside a standard licence (the RIRE and SimpleITK notebook excerpts, the Open3D demo data). The manifest's note quotes them; ds.describe() prints the note. The package will not guess a licence for you.

docs.title: Python 3.13?
docs.text: The core package runs on 3.10 to 3.13. The native extras depend on Open3D wheels: 0.20 (September 2026) has them for 3.13, 0.19 stops at 3.12. pardesline 0.2.0 on PyPI pins Open3D below 0.20; main accepts 0.20 and the native test suite passes on 3.13 with it. Until 0.3.0 is released, use Python 3.12 or install from main.

docs.title: GPU?
docs.text: Nothing in the package needs one. The classical algorithms run on CPU through Open3D, VTK and SimpleITK. The PyTorch reference scripts use CUDA when available and run on CPU at the sizes the examples use.

docs.title: Does it ship pretrained models?
docs.text: Not yet. Today the deep-learning content is expert guides with reference scripts (PointNet, DINOv3 features, 3D JEPA, VAE anomaly detection, nnU-Net preparation) that read any pardesline dataset. One-line pretrained model access through a model registry is the top roadmap item; the Models pages keep their URLs for it.

docs.title: What is the cloud client?
docs.text: pardesline.cloud is the optional client of the hosted PardesLine platform (sharing, GPU jobs, viewers). It is in the package because the same object model is used on both sides, it is off unless you call its functions, and this documentation covers the local, Apache-2.0 part.

docs.title: Can I use it offline?
docs.text: Yes, once the data is cached: pl.load reads the on-disk index and files; pardesline fetch <dataset> downloads a dataset ahead of time; ds.export(folder) writes standard files you can carry anywhere.

docs.title: How do I load DICOM, and what about identifiers?
docs.text: A DICOM series folder loads as one Volume (pl.load("series_folder/"), or a tcia:// collection). pardesline reads pixel data and geometry and does not de-identify: do that before the data reaches any tool, with the DICOM PS3.15 basic profile or your institution's process. Contributions of real cases must be de-identified by the contributor.

docs.title: How is this different from MONAI or TorchIO?
docs.text: They are training frameworks for medical volumes with excellent transforms. pardesline is the layer before and around them: datasets with licences, one object for points, meshes and volumes, classical algorithms with documented defaults, and an MCP server. See the comparison; ds.export() and prepare_nnunet_dataset.py hand data to them.

docs.title: Where do outputs go?
docs.text: Algorithm outputs go to a temporary folder unless you set pl.set_output_dir(...) or pass output=; obj.save(path) writes where you say, with a .pardesline.json sidecar next to it. Datasets are cached under ~/.cache/pardesline/datasets/ (PARDESLINE_CACHE or pl.set_cache_dir() to move it).

docs.title: How do I cite it?
docs.text: CITATION.cff at the repository root (the "Cite this repository" button on GitHub), or the BibTeX block in the README. Cite the datasets you use as well: ds.citation returns the reference each owner asks for.

docs.title: How do I report a bug or a security issue?
docs.text: Bugs: an issue with the snippet, the full log and pardesline version. Security: GitHub's private vulnerability reporting on the repository, as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: The MCP server for AI agents
docs.text:
pardesline mcp exposes the datasets, the object model and the 73 algorithms to any Model Context Protocol client, on the user's machine, without an account. Twelve tools (list_datasets, describe_dataset, list_samples, load_sample, scan_dataset, confirm_dataset, export_dataset, list_methods, describe_method, run_method, describe_object, to_mesh), three resources and a start_here prompt. Questions the package will not guess (licence, units, array layout) come back as JSON for the agent to relay to the human.

pip install "pardesline[mcp]"
pardesline mcp                                            # stdio
pardesline mcp --transport streamable-http --port 8765    # http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp
Client Configuration Claude Code claude mcp add pardesline -- pardesline mcp (the repo ships a .mcp.json) Claude Desktop, Cursor "mcpServers": {"pardesline": {"command": "pardesline", "args": ["mcp"]}} Gemini CLI gemini extensions install https://github.com/pardesline/pardesline (the repo ships a gemini-extension.json), or the same block in ~/.gemini/settings.json Codex CLI [mcp_servers.pardesline] command = "pardesline" args = ["mcp"] in ~/.codex/config.toml

If pardesline is not on your PATH, the command is python -m pardesline.mcp_server.

Without installing first. uv runs the package with every backend in a cached environment (about a minute the first time, then instant):

{"mcpServers": {"pardesline": {"command": "uvx", "args": ["--with", "pardesline[all]", "pardesline", "mcp"]}}}

With Docker. Open3D, VTK and SimpleITK come preinstalled; mount a folder at /data for the agent to scan or export into:

docker build -t pardesline-mcp https://github.com/pardesline/pardesline.git

{"mcpServers": {"pardesline": {"command": "docker", "args": ["run", "-i", "--rm", "-v", "pardesline-cache:/home/app/.cache/pardesline", "pardesline-mcp"]}}}

Registries. Every release is published to the official MCP Registry as io.github.pardesline/pardesline, from server.json at the repository root.

The skills/ folder holds twenty skills, grounded in the code and checked by the test suite (every module, method, parameter and dataset they mention must exist). Nine teach the package: using-pardesline (start here), catalog-and-run, object-model, datasets-and-manifests, scanning-private-folders, medical-volumes, cloud-client, mcp-server, contributing-algorithms. Eleven are expert guides with reference scripts for the domains the package serves, written for engineers who build the pipelines, and served to any MCP client through list_skills / get_skill:

Skill What it carries Runnable script 3d-representations points vs meshes vs voxels vs splats: memory, architectures, the conversion matrix and its pitfalls - point-cloud-registration RANSAC + FPFH + ICP, every parameter from one voxel size, metrics that lie, CPD registration_eval.py (pose error on a known transform) multimodal-rigid-registration CT/MR with Mattes MI in SimpleITK: initialiser, optimizer scales, pyramid, validation by TRE rigid_ct_mr.py (RIRE pair, metric trace, checkerboard) atlas-label-transfer labelled atlas -> unlabelled scan: registration, nearest-structure labels, per-label surfaces and volumes atlas_label_transfer.py (99 % label agreement on a synthetic scan) pointnet-segmentation PointNet / PointNet++ step by step, data contract, training recipe make_point_dataset.py (label maps -> labelled clouds), pointnet_seg.py (PyTorch) dinov3-dense-features Gram anchoring, frozen backbones, ViTDet pyramid + Faster R-CNN, medical transfer limits dinov3_features.py, dinov3_faster_rcnn.py jepa-pretraining latent prediction instead of reconstruction, 3-D tokenisation, masking, collapse diagnostics jepa3d_pretrain.py (3-D ViT, EMA target, block masks) vae-anomaly-detection normal-only training, residual maps, thresholds, honest limits vae_anomaly.py (train / score / AUROC) gaussian-splatting the primitive, the five-step initialisation, PLY layout, training, medical uses points_to_gaussians.py (any cloud -> 3DGS PLY) medical-segmentation-models nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, transformers, preprocessing, inference, evaluation prepare_nnunet_dataset.py (any dataset -> nnU-Net raw) evaluation-metrics-3d Dice / HD95 / NSD, chamfer / F-score, TRE, folding, AP, AUROC, PSNR, and how to report them metrics3d.py

Install them as a plugin (it also registers the MCP server):

/plugin marketplace add pardesline/pardesline
/plugin install pardesline@pardesline

docs.title: One package, three ways to run the same code
docs.text:
Mode What runs where Needs Install Local the 73 algorithms, the object model, the datasets and the MCP server on your machine; Open3D, SimpleITK and PyVista installed next to the package no account, no network except the dataset downloads you ask for pip install "pardesline[all]" Cloud the same 73 algorithms on the hosted GPU platform, plus sharing, browser viewers, image-to-3D a PardesLine account (pl.login()) pip install pardesline Mixed your pipeline written once; each call runs locally when the library is installed, remotely otherwise both either

The algorithm names, the parameters and the object model are identical in the three modes: scan.downsample(voxel_size=0.02) is the same line on a laptop without a GPU and on the platform.

docs.title: Open3D, SimpleITK and PyVista: direct access, or through the cloud
docs.text:
The native libraries are not hidden behind the package; they are part of it.

import pardesline as pl

scan = pl.load("scan.ply")  # a typed Object with frame, units, licence, provenance
pcd = scan.to_open3d()  # open3d.geometry.PointCloud (or TriangleMesh)
poly = scan.to_pyvista()  # pyvista.PolyData
img = pl.load("ct.mha").to_sitk()  # SimpleITK.Image - DICOM folders accepted
arr = scan.to_numpy()  # points (N, 3), vertices, or voxels (z, y, x)

pl.o3d, pl.pv, pl.sitk, pl.np  # the real libraries, when they are installed
  • With [local] / [medical] installed, pl.o3d is open3d, pl.sitk is SimpleITK, pl.pv is pyvista: write ordinary Open3D or SimpleITK code on the objects pardesline loaded, and hand the results back (os.fspath(obj) is the file path, so every library reader accepts an Object).
  • Without them, after pl.login(), the same four names become the cloud mirrors of the 0.1 client: the call is recorded and executed on the platform, the result comes back when you ask for it (.numpy(), .to_file()). No Open3D, VTK or ITK to install, no 3D environment to set up - the use case pardesline-use-cases/01 runs a full registration + label transfer + Poisson pipeline that way.
  • Either way the object keeps its frame, units, labels and licence, and records every step it went through (obj.provenance).

docs.title: Cloud (optional)
docs.text:
The hosted platform adds sharing, GPU methods (image → 3D, 2D AI), browser viewers and a node editor. The 0.1.x client is unchanged, under pardesline.cloud and at the top level; pl.o3d / pl.pv / pl.sitk become its server-side mirrors when the libraries are not installed locally (see One package, three ways to run the same code):

pl.login()  # email + one-time code
remote = pl.upload(surface)  # an Object or a path
pl.share(remote, to="colleague@lab.org")
remote.view()  # link to the 3D viewer

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text: pardesline mcp turns the package into a local Model Context Protocol server: an agent can list and describe datasets, fetch one sample, run any catalog method with validated parameters, convert objects, export standard files and read the twenty expert guides. Nothing leaves the machine; there is no account.

docs.title: Setup
Tools
docs.text:
Tool What it does list_datasets(tag, scheme, medical_only) the 43 bundled manifests with title, licence, tags describe_dataset(ref, count_samples) roles, frames, units, labels, licence, citation of a bundled name, an hf:// / tcia:// / s3:// URI, a manifest path or a folder list_samples(ref, limit, offset, **fields) sample ids and fields, paged load_sample(ref, sample, role, standard) fetches one role: path, kind, frame, units, labels, licence, provenance, the methods that accept it, and standard_path (PLY / MetaImage) for raw arrays and DICOM folders scan_dataset(ref) drafts a manifest for a folder or a Hub repo and returns the questions confirm_dataset(ref, answers, save_to) answers the questions, saves the manifest export_dataset(ref, folder, take, overwrite) standard files + sidecars + manifest list_methods(extension, module) the catalog, filtered by file type describe_method(method) parameters with type, default, range, description and rationale run_method(method, input, moving, output, params) runs one method; returns the output path and the recorded step describe_object(path) kind, frame, units, labels, sidecar of any file to_mesh(path, label, isovalue) label map or volume to a surface list_skills(), get_skill(name, file) the twenty expert guides and their scripts

Resources: pardesline://datasets, pardesline://manifest/{name}, pardesline://catalog, pardesline://skills, pardesline://skill/{name}. Prompt: start_here.

docs.title: What an agent does with it
docs.text:
1. list_datasets(tag="ct") → picks msd_task09_spleen; describe_dataset tells it the mask has label 1 = spleen under CC-BY-SA 4.0.
  2. load_sample("msd_task09_spleen", 0, "ct") fetches one 30 MB volume out of the 1.6 GB tar and says which methods accept it.
  3. get_skill("medical-volumes") before touching HU windows; describe_method("simpleitk_segmentation.manual_threshold") for the parameters and why they are what they are.
  4. run_method(...), to_mesh(...), export_dataset(...): files on disk with sidecars, paths returned.

Questions the package will not guess (licence, units, label names, array layout) come back as structured JSON ({"error": "NeedsConfirmation", "questions": [...]}) for the agent to relay to the human, then confirm_dataset. Errors are returned as JSON too; the server never dies on a bad call. Logs go to stderr, never to the protocol channel.

docs.title: Contract and tests
docs.text:
The full tool contract, the error shapes and the client details are in MCP reference. tests/test_mcp_server.py exercises every tool in-process and runs a stdio round trip with the official MCP client, which is what every external client does.

The server is Apache-2.0 like the rest of the package; MCP registries can list it from the repository's .mcp.json.

docs.title: Collision Detection & Measurement
docs.text:
collision_detection: Detect and measure collisions between 3D geometries using SDF-based penetration analysis. Computes penetration depth, collision region, and bounding box intersection.

Methods sdf_collision, penetration_depth Input files .ply, .obj, .stl, .off Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats, hf_objaverse_glb_shard CLI pardesline run collision_detection.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Collision detection between 3D objects can be performed using Signed Distance Fields (SDF). Given a static mesh \(S\) and a moving mesh \(M\), we sample points on \(M\) and compute their signed distance to \(S\):

\[ d(p) = \text{SDF}_S(p), \quad p \in M \]

Points where \(d(p) < 0\) lie inside the static mesh, indicating collision. The penetration depth is:

\[ \delta = \max_{p \in M} |\min(d(p), 0)| \]

This approach is robust for arbitrary mesh geometries and provides continuous penetration measurements.

docs.title: sdf_collision
docs.text:
Samples points uniformly on the input mesh surface, then creates a synthetic obstacle (sphere) and computes the SDF of the input points against the obstacle.

Penetrating points satisfy \(\text{SDF}(p) < 0\). The collision region is visualized by coloring points by their signed distance: red (deep penetration) to blue (no contact).

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("collision_detection.sdf_collision")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.collision_detection.sdf_collision --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated meshes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it obstacle_radius float 0.5 0.1 to 5.0 Radius of the synthetic obstacle sphere. 0.5 in file units: a sphere half the size of a unit object, the demo obstacle. penetration_ratio float 0.3 0.05 to 0.8 Fraction of obstacle radius for penetration overlap. 0.3: the obstacle is placed so that 30 % of its radius overlaps the part, enough to show a clear collision patch. num_samples int 50000 5000 to 200000 Number of surface sample points for SDF evaluation. 50 000 surface samples give a dense signed-distance map on the part in under a second. obstacle_resolution (advanced) int 50 4 to 200 Sphere tessellation resolution for the synthetic obstacle mesh. 50 tessellation steps make the sphere smooth enough that its SDF has no facet artefacts. obstacle_viz_points (advanced) int 5000 100 to 100000 Points sampled on the obstacle for visualization. 5 000 points draw the obstacle without hiding the part. colormap (advanced) string coolwarm Matplotlib colormap used to color points by signed distance. coolwarm is diverging around zero distance: red inside the obstacle, blue outside.

docs.title: penetration_depth
docs.text:
Computes the maximum penetration depth between the input geometry and a synthetic obstacle:

\[\delta = |\min_i \text{SDF}(p_i)|\]

Also computes the bounding box of the collision region and outputs a combined point cloud showing the penetration zone with color-coded depth.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("collision_detection.penetration_depth")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.collision_detection.penetration_depth --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated meshes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it obstacle_radius float 0.5 0.1 to 5.0 Radius of the synthetic obstacle sphere. 0.5 in file units, the demo obstacle. overlap_distance float 0.15 0.01 to 2.0 Distance the obstacle overlaps with the input geometry. 0.15 in file units: the obstacle overlaps the part by 15 % of a unit object. num_samples (advanced) int 50000 5000 to 200000 Number of surface sample points for SDF evaluation. 50 000 surface samples. obstacle_resolution (advanced) int 50 4 to 200 Sphere tessellation resolution for the synthetic obstacle mesh. 50 tessellation steps make the sphere smooth enough that its SDF has no facet artefacts. colormap (advanced) string hot Matplotlib colormap used to color penetrating points by depth. hot maps zero depth to black and the deepest penetration to white.

docs.title: Deformable Registration
docs.text:
deformable_registration: Non-rigid point cloud alignment using Coherent Point Drift (CPD) and Gaussian deformation fields. Handles elastic deformations between shapes.

Methods cpd_deformable, gaussian_deformation Input files .ply, .pcd, .txt, .xyz Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats CLI pardesline run deformable_registration.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Deformable registration finds a non-rigid transformation that aligns a source shape to a target. CPD models source points as GMM centroids and fits them via EM optimization.

The displacement function is:

\[ \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} w_m \phi(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}_m\|) \]

where \(\phi\) is a Gaussian kernel and \(w_m\) are optimized coefficients.

docs.title: cpd_deformable
docs.text:
CPD treats alignment as probability density estimation. The E-step computes correspondence probabilities, the M-step updates the transformation with regularization: $\(E(W) = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_n \|T(y_n) - x_n\|^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2} \text{tr}(W^T G W)\)$

import pardesline as pl

fixed, moving = pl.load("fixed.ply"), pl.load("moving.ply")
result = fixed.run("deformable_registration.cpd_deformable", moving=moving)  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.deformable_registration.cpd_deformable --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py; the point-cloud-registration skill documents its use after a rigid stage

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it max_iterations int 100 10 to 500 Maximum EM iterations. 100 EM iterations: CPD converges in 30-80 on organ-sized clouds; the tolerance below usually stops it first. tolerance float 0.001 0.0001 to 0.01 Convergence tolerance. 1e-3 relative change of the objective: tighter costs iterations without visible change in the displacement field. beta (advanced) float 100.0 0.1 to 200.0 CPD Gaussian-kernel width (smoothness). 100 is pycpd's default Gaussian kernel width in file units, i.e. a very smooth, almost global deformation for unit-scale clouds; lower it to about the size of the structures you expect to move independently (10-20 mm for organs). lambda_val (advanced) float 2.0 0.1 to 20.0 CPD regularization weight. 2.0 regularisation weight: the pycpd default, balancing fit against smoothness; raise it when the field folds. w (advanced) float 0.0 0.0 to 0.99 Outlier/noise weight. 0 assumes no outliers; set 0.1-0.3 when the fixed cloud has clutter the moving cloud should not reach. low_rank (advanced) bool false Use low-rank Gaussian-kernel acceleration. Off below about 10k points; on above, where the full kernel matrix no longer fits in memory. num_eig (advanced) int 100 10 to 500 Eigenvectors when low_rank=True. 100 eigenvectors keep the low-rank approximation close to the full kernel at a fraction of the cost.

docs.title: gaussian_deformation
docs.text:
A localized Gaussian deformation: $\(\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p}) = d_{\max} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\)$

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("deformable_registration.gaussian_deformation")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.deformable_registration.gaussian_deformation --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it displacement float 0.02 0.001 to 0.1 Maximum displacement at pressure center. 0.02 in file units: a visible but plausible dent on a unit-scale object, used to synthesise test cases for non-rigid registration. radius float 0.1 0.01 to 0.5 Radius of influence. 0.1 in file units: the dent spans 10 % of a unit object. sigma_factor (advanced) float 0.5 0.05 to 1.0 Gaussian falloff sigma as a fraction of radius. 0.5: the Gaussian falls to about 13 % at the radius, so the dent fades smoothly instead of leaving a crease.

docs.title: Features Extraction
docs.text:
features_extraction: Extract geometric features from point clouds: normals, curvature, and FPFH descriptors for registration and analysis.

Methods normal_estimation, fpfh_features, curvature_estimation Input files .ply, .pcd, .txt, .xyz Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats CLI pardesline run features_extraction.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Geometric feature extraction computes descriptors that characterize the local or global shape of a point cloud.

Normal estimation fits a local tangent plane to neighbors. Curvature is estimated from eigenvalues of the local covariance matrix. FPFH descriptors encode angular relationships between normals.

docs.title: normal_estimation
docs.text:
The normal \(\vec{n}_i\) is the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{C}_i\). Normals are oriented consistently using tangent plane propagation.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("features_extraction.normal_estimation")  # catalog defaults
# same thing, domain vocabulary: `points.normals()`
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.features_extraction.normal_estimation --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: Stanford bunny through the registration pipeline; generated clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it radius float 0.05 0.005 to 0.5 Search radius for normal estimation. 0.05 in file units: about 5x the spacing of a centimetre-resolution scan; the covariance needs 10-30 points inside the radius. max_nn int 30 10 to 100 Maximum nearest neighbors. 30 neighbours cap the cost and keep normals local at edges. fast_normal_computation (advanced) bool true Use the faster (less accurate) covariance eigen solver in estimate_normals. On: Open3D's closed-form eigen solver is accurate to visual precision and several times faster than the iterative one. orient_k (advanced) int 0 0 to 100 k neighbors for consistent tangent-plane orientation (0 = auto min(max_nn,15)). 0 lets the script choose min(max_nn, 15) for the orientation propagation: small enough to stay consistent across thin parts.

docs.title: fpfh_features
docs.text:
Fast Point Feature Histograms encode angular relationships between normals into a 33-dimensional descriptor using three angular features \((\alpha, \phi, \theta)\).

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("features_extraction.fpfh_features")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.features_extraction.fpfh_features --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: Stanford bunny and Open3D fragments through registration.ransac_global; generated clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it voxel_size float 0.005 0.001 to 0.05 Voxel size for downsampling before feature computation. 0.005 in file units (5 mm on a metre object) keeps enough points for descriptive histograms; the registration pipeline derives it from the bounding box instead. normal_radius_factor (advanced) float 2.0 1.0 to 10.0 Normal search radius as a multiple of voxel_size. 2x the voxel for normals. normal_max_nn (advanced) int 30 10 to 200 Maximum nearest neighbors for normal estimation. 30 neighbours cap the normal-estimation cost on dense clouds while keeping the covariance stable. feature_radius_factor (advanced) float 5.0 1.0 to 20.0 FPFH search radius as a multiple of voxel_size. 5x the voxel: the Open3D-recommended FPFH support. feature_max_nn (advanced) int 100 10 to 500 Maximum nearest neighbors for FPFH feature computation. 100 neighbours bound the histogram cost.

docs.title: curvature_estimation
docs.text:
Curvature \(\kappa_i = \frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_0 + \lambda_1 + \lambda_2}\). Near 0 = flat, near \(1/3\) = high curvature.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("features_extraction.curvature_estimation")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.features_extraction.curvature_estimation --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it radius float 0.05 0.005 to 0.5 Search radius for curvature computation. 0.05 in file units for the covariance neighbourhood, as for normals. max_nn int 30 10 to 100 Maximum nearest neighbors. 30 neighbours cap the cost and keep the estimate local at edges. normalize_percentile (advanced) float 99 50 to 100 Percentile of curvature used as the color-normalization ceiling. Colour scale capped at the 99th percentile so a few extreme points (edges, noise) do not flatten the map.

docs.title: LiDAR-Camera Fusion
docs.text:
lidar_camera_fusion: Sensor fusion operations: distance-based colorization, region-of-interest extraction, and multi-resolution analysis for combined LiDAR and camera processing.

Methods intensity_colorization, roi_extraction, multi_resolution Input files .ply, .pcd, .txt, .xyz, .las Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats CLI pardesline run lidar_camera_fusion.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
LiDAR-Camera fusion combines 3D point cloud data with 2D imagery. A 3D point \(P = (X,Y,Z)\) projects to pixel \((u,v)\) via:

\[ \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} K [R|t] \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \]

docs.title: intensity_colorization
docs.text:
Points colored by distance from origin using a selected colormap.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("lidar_camera_fusion.intensity_colorization")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.lidar_camera_fusion.intensity_colorization --input ... --output ....

docs.title: LiDAR Scene Analysis
docs.text:
lidar_scene_detection: Analyze LiDAR-style point clouds: height-based colorization, ground plane removal, and object clustering for autonomous driving and robotics applications.

Methods height_colorization, ground_removal, object_clustering Input files .ply, .pcd, .txt, .xyz, .las Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats Example Ground removal and clustering on KITTI CLI pardesline run lidar_scene_detection.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensors produce dense 3D point clouds of the environment. Processing these point clouds is fundamental to autonomous driving, robotics, and mapping.

Key operations include: - Height colorization: Mapping the Z-coordinate to color for visual analysis - Ground removal: Fitting a plane to the ground surface and removing it - Object clustering: Grouping non-ground points into individual objects

Ground removal typically uses RANSAC to fit a plane \(ax + by + cz + d = 0\) where the normal is approximately vertical (\(c \approx 1\)). Non-ground points are then clustered using DBSCAN to identify individual objects.

docs.title: height_colorization
docs.text:
Points are colored based on their Z-coordinate (height) using a gradient: $\(c_i = \text{colormap}\left(\frac{z_i - z_{\min}}{z_{\max} - z_{\min}}\right)\)$

This reveals terrain structure, building heights, and vegetation layers in the scene.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("lidar_scene_detection.height_colorization")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.lidar_scene_detection.height_colorization --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: KITTI sweeps (examples/kitti_lidar_ground_and_objects); generated clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it colormap int 0 0 to 3 Colormap: 0=height gradient, 1=viridis, 2=plasma, 3=turbo 0 (height gradient) maps the sensor z axis directly to colour, which is how LiDAR engineers read a sweep.

docs.title: ground_removal
docs.text:
RANSAC fits a ground plane and removes points within a threshold: 1. Fit plane \(ax + by + cz + d = 0\) using RANSAC 2. Compute distance \(d_i = |ax_i + by_i + cz_i + d| / \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}\) 3. Remove points where \(d_i < \epsilon\) (ground points)

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("lidar_scene_detection.ground_removal")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.lidar_scene_detection.ground_removal --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: KITTI Velodyne HDL-64E sweeps, sensor frame, metres (examples/kitti_lidar_ground_and_objects)

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it distance_threshold float 0.3 0.01 to 2.0 Distance threshold for ground plane inliers. 0.3 m: a road is not flat over a 100 m sweep (camber, slope, curb), so a 30 cm band keeps the whole surface as ground while a car's lowest points (sills at 0.4-0.5 m) stay out; lower to 0.1 m for indoor floors. ransac_n (advanced) int 3 3 to 10 Points sampled per RANSAC iteration. 3 points define the plane. num_iterations (advanced) int 1000 100 to 10000 RANSAC iterations. 1 000 iterations are plenty when the ground holds 30-50 % of a sweep's points.

docs.title: object_clustering
docs.text:
After ground removal, non-ground points are clustered using DBSCAN: 1. Remove ground plane 2. Apply DBSCAN with parameters \((\epsilon, n_{\min})\) 3. Each cluster represents a potential object 4. Filter clusters by minimum size

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("lidar_scene_detection.object_clustering")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.lidar_scene_detection.object_clustering --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: KITTI sweeps: 35 476 points clustered into cars, poles, walls after ground removal (examples/kitti_lidar_ground_and_objects)

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it ground_threshold float 0.3 0.01 to 2.0 Distance threshold for ground removal before clustering. 0.3 m, as in ground_removal: the band that follows a real road's camber and slope. cluster_eps float 0.5 0.1 to 5.0 DBSCAN epsilon for object clustering. 0.5 m: the HDL-64E spacing between rings reaches 0.3-0.5 m at 30 m, so a smaller epsilon splits one car into ring-stripes; a larger one merges parked cars. min_cluster_points int 10 3 to 100 Minimum points to form a cluster. 10 points keep ring fragments and speckle out while a pedestrian at 20 m (about 15-30 points) still clusters. ransac_n (advanced) int 3 3 to 10 Points sampled per RANSAC iteration. 3 points define the ground plane. num_iterations (advanced) int 1000 100 to 10000 Ground-plane RANSAC iterations. 1 000 ground-plane iterations. print_progress (advanced) bool false Print DBSCAN progress. Off: terminal output only.
