docs.title: Signed Distance Fields
docs.text:
sdf: Compute and visualize Signed Distance Fields from meshes. Foundation for implicit surface representations, marching cubes reconstruction, and neural SDFs.

Methods compute_sdf, occupancy_reconstruction, sdf_voxel_visualization Input files .ply, .obj, .stl, .off Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats, hf_objaverse_glb_shard CLI pardesline run sdf.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A Signed Distance Field (SDF) is a scalar function \(f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) that returns the signed distance from any point \(x\) to the closest surface point:

\[ f(x) = \text{sign}(x) \cdot \min_{y \in S} \|x - y\| \]

where \(f(x) < 0\) inside the surface, \(f(x) > 0\) outside, and \(f(x) = 0\) on the surface \(S\) itself. The zero level-set \(\{x : f(x) = 0\}\) implicitly defines the surface.

SDFs have several key properties: - The gradient \(\nabla f(x)\) points in the direction of steepest distance increase - \(\|\nabla f(x)\| = 1\) almost everywhere (Eikonal equation) - Boolean operations become simple min/max on SDF values:

\[ \text{Union:} \min(f_A, f_B), \quad \text{Intersection:} \max(f_A, f_B), \quad \text{Difference:} \max(f_A, -f_B) \]

docs.title: compute_sdf
docs.text:
1. SDF Computation The SDF is computed using Open3D's RaycastingScene which casts rays to determine signed distance. Query points are placed on a regular 3D grid covering the mesh bounding box with padding.

For a grid with voxel size \(v\) and padding \(p\), the query points are: $\(Q = \{(x_0 + iv, y_0 + jv, z_0 + kv) : 0 \leq i,j,k < N\}\)$

where \((x_0, y_0, z_0)\) is the padded minimum bound.

2. Marching Cubes The surface is reconstructed at the zero-level set \(\{x : f(x) = 0\}\) using the Marching Cubes algorithm (Lorensen & Cline, 1987). Each voxel cube is classified by the signs of its 8 corner SDF values, producing 256 possible configurations mapped to triangle meshes via a lookup table.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("sdf.compute_sdf")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.sdf.compute_sdf --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated meshes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it voxel_size float 0.01 0.002 to 0.05 Voxel size for the SDF grid. Smaller = more detail but slower. 0.01 in file units for a 100-voxel grid on a unit object; the SDF cost grows with the cube of the resolution. padding int 5 1 to 20 Number of padding voxels around the bounding box. 5 voxels of margin so the zero level set is closed inside the grid. level (advanced) float 0.0 -0.05 to 0.05 Iso-level for surface extraction. 0.0 is the surface itself (zero signed distance); offset it to inflate or shrink the mesh. mc_step_size (advanced) int 1 1 to 5 Marching-cubes voxel step (coarser = faster). 1 samples every voxel; a larger step is a quick coarse preview. mc_method (advanced) enum lewiner lewiner, lorensen Marching-cubes algorithm variant. Lewiner marching cubes resolves the ambiguous cases that the original Lorensen tables get wrong on thin structures. mc_gradient_direction (advanced) enum descent descent, ascent Surface-interior interpretation for normals. descent orients normals so that the inside is negative distance, which is the convention of the SDF grid. mc_allow_degenerate (advanced) bool true Allow degenerate output triangles. On, matching scikit-image: degenerate triangles are removed later by the mesh cleaning step rather than by rejecting the surface.

docs.title: occupancy_reconstruction
docs.text:
Occupancy testing determines whether query points lie inside or outside a watertight mesh. The occupancy function \(o: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \{0, 1\}\) is: $\(o(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \text{ is inside } S \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

The boundary is extracted using marching cubes at iso-value 0.5.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("sdf.occupancy_reconstruction")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.sdf.occupancy_reconstruction --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated meshes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it voxel_size float 0.01 0.002 to 0.05 Voxel size for the occupancy grid. Same grid as compute_sdf for comparable results. padding int 5 1 to 20 Number of padding voxels around the bounding box. 5 voxels of margin around the bounding box. level (advanced) float 0.5 0.1 to 0.9 Iso-value for occupancy boundary. 0.5 is the half-occupancy boundary of a binary occupancy grid. mc_step_size (advanced) int 1 1 to 5 Marching-cubes voxel step (coarser = faster). 1 samples every voxel. mc_method (advanced) enum lewiner lewiner, lorensen Marching-cubes algorithm variant. Lewiner resolves ambiguous cube cases. mc_gradient_direction (advanced) enum descent descent, ascent Surface-interior interpretation for normals. descent keeps normals pointing outward for occupancy grids. mc_allow_degenerate (advanced) bool true Allow degenerate output triangles. On, matching scikit-image.

docs.title: sdf_voxel_visualization
docs.text:
1. Signed Distance Function The SDF is sampled on a regular 3D grid of resolution \(N^3\). For each voxel center \(x_i\), the signed distance is computed: $\(d_i = f(x_i) = \text{sign}(x_i) \cdot \min_{y \in S} \|x_i - y\|\)$

2. Distance Clamping SDF values are clamped to a user-defined range \([d_{\min}, d_{\max}]\) to focus on the near-surface region: $\(\hat{d}_i = \text{clamp}(d_i, d_{\min}, d_{\max})\)$

This truncation is the basis for Truncated SDFs (TSDFs), widely used in real-time 3D reconstruction (KinectFusion, Curless & Levoy 1996).

3. Colormap Encoding The clamped distances are normalized to \([0, 1]\) and mapped to a diverging colormap (coolwarm): - Blue (\(d < 0\)): interior of the surface - White (\(d \approx 0\)): on or near the surface - Red (\(d > 0\)): exterior of the surface

4. Connection with Collision Detection The SDF provides constant-time collision queries: a point \(x\) collides with the surface if \(f(x) \leq 0\). The penetration depth is \(|f(x)|\) and the normal direction is \(\nabla f(x)\).

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("sdf.sdf_voxel_visualization")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.sdf.sdf_voxel_visualization --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated meshes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it resolution int 32 8 to 128 Grid resolution per axis. Higher = more detail. Total voxels = resolution^3. 32 voxels per axis (32 768 cells) renders in a second and still shows the shape of the field; it is a visualisation, not the SDF you compute with. min_clamp float -0.1 -1.0 to 0.0 Minimum SDF clamp value (interior threshold). -0.1 clamps the interior so colours stay readable near the surface instead of saturating at the object centre. max_clamp float 0.1 0.0 to 1.0 Maximum SDF clamp value (exterior threshold). 0.1 clamps the exterior for the same reason. padding_factor (advanced) float 0.15 0.0 to 1.0 Bbox padding as a fraction of the max extent. 15 % of the extent as margin shows the field decaying outside the object. colormap (advanced) string coolwarm Matplotlib diverging colormap (coolwarm, bwr, seismic, RdBu). coolwarm is diverging around zero, which is what a signed field needs: blue inside, red outside.

docs.title: SimpleITK Registration
docs.text:
simpleitk_registration: Medical image registration using SimpleITK. Rigid, affine, B-spline FFD, and demons deformable registration for CT/MR and other medical volumes.

Methods rigid, advanced_rigid, affine, bspline, demons, difference_analysis Input files .vti, .mha, .nrrd, .nii, .dcm (and .nii.gz) Two inputs input is the fixed reference, moving (Moving Volume) is transformed Bundled datasets to try rire_brain, liver_tumor_patient01, visible_human_head_mri, spider_lumbar_mri, msd_task04_hippocampus, msd_task09_spleen Example SimpleITK rigid registration on RIRE CLI pardesline run simpleitk_registration.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Medical image registration seeks a spatial transformation \(T: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) that aligns a moving image \(I_M\) to a fixed image \(I_F\). The optimal transformation minimizes a similarity metric:

\[ T^* = \arg\min_{T} \mathcal{S}(I_F, I_M \circ T) + \lambda \mathcal{R}(T) \]

where \(\mathcal{S}\) is the similarity metric (e.g., Mutual Information for multi-modal, Mean Squared Error for mono-modal), \(\mathcal{R}(T)\) is a regularization term enforcing transformation smoothness, and \(\lambda\) controls the trade-off.

SimpleITK implements a multi-resolution optimization framework with configurable metrics, interpolators, and optimizers for both rigid and deformable registration.

docs.title: rigid
docs.text:
1. Rigid Transformation Model A rigid transformation has 6 degrees of freedom — 3 rotation angles \((\theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z)\) and 3 translations \((t_x, t_y, t_z)\): $\(T_{\text{rigid}}(\mathbf{x}) = R \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}\)$ where \(R \in SO(3)\) is the rotation matrix and \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) is the translation vector.

2. Mattes Mutual Information For multi-modal registration (CT-MR), Mutual Information measures the statistical dependency between the two images: $\(MI(I_F, I_M) = H(I_F) + H(I_M) - H(I_F, I_M)\)$ where \(H\) denotes Shannon entropy and \(H(I_F, I_M)\) is the joint entropy. Mattes' implementation uses a stochastic sampling strategy with 50 histogram bins.

3. Multi-Resolution Framework The optimization proceeds from coarse to fine resolution, avoiding local minima. At each level, the optimizer refines the parameters from the previous scale.

import pardesline as pl

fixed, moving = pl.load("fixed.nii.gz"), pl.load("moving.nii.gz")
result = fixed.run("simpleitk_registration.rigid", moving=moving)  # catalog defaults
# same thing, domain vocabulary: `fixed.align(moving)` on a `Volume`
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_registration.rigid_registration --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: RIRE CT / MR-T1 brain pair: 0.65 x 0.65 x 4 mm CT vs 1.25 x 1.25 x 4 mm MR, 40 mm initial offset, registered in 8.8 s (examples/register_ct_mr_rire, the README demo); the multimodal-rigid-registration skill reports 3.9 deg / 1 mm-class agreement with the RIRE truth

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it learning_rate float 1.0 0.1 to 5.0 Gradient descent learning rate. 1.0 with optimizer scales from physical shift: each step moves the image by about one unit of the scaled parameters, fast on the coarse levels and still stable because the scales normalise rotations and translations. num_iterations int 100 10 to 500 Maximum number of optimizer iterations. 100 per level: Mattes MI on 1 % sampling plateaus within 50-80 iterations on head and abdomen volumes; the convergence window stops it earlier. sampling_percentage float 0.01 0.005 to 0.5 Metric sampling percentage (0.01 = 1%). 1 % of the voxels is enough for the MI estimate on 256^3 volumes and makes each iteration cheap; raise to 5-15 % on small fields of view or very noisy images. initializer (advanced) enum GEOMETRY GEOMETRY, MOMENTS Centered-initializer mode (geometric center vs center-of-mass). GEOMETRY aligns the geometric centres of the two volumes, which works when both scans cover the same anatomy; MOMENTS (intensity centre of mass) is better when one field of view is much larger than the other. metric (advanced) enum mattes_mutual_information mattes_mutual_information, mean_squares, correlation, joint_histogram_mi Similarity metric. Mattes mutual information is the only one of the four that works across modalities (CT vs MR): it assumes a statistical dependence, not a linear intensity relation. number_of_histogram_bins (advanced) int 50 10 to 256 Mattes MI histogram bins. 50 bins: 32-64 is the sweet spot for the Parzen-window joint histogram, fewer is blurry, more is noisy. sampling_strategy (advanced) enum RANDOM NONE, REGULAR, RANDOM Metric sampling strategy. RANDOM adds a little stochasticity that helps the optimizer leave shallow local minima; REGULAR aliases with voxel grids. interpolator (advanced) enum LINEAR LINEAR, NEAREST, BSPLINE Resampling interpolator during optimization. LINEAR during optimisation is the standard trade-off; B-spline is slower and only pays off for the final resampling. convergence_minimum_value (advanced) float 1e-06 1e-08 to 0.001 Gradient-descent convergence threshold. 1e-6 on the metric change over the window. convergence_window_size (advanced) int 10 3 to 50 Gradient-descent convergence window. 10 iterations smooth the stochastic metric before the convergence test. shrink_factors (advanced) list 4,2,1 Multi-resolution shrink factors per level (comma-separated). 4,2,1: three resolution levels give the capture range to recover a 40 mm offset at the coarse level and sub-voxel precision at the fine one. smoothing_sigmas (advanced) list 2,1,0 Gaussian smoothing sigma per level (comma-separated). 2,1,0 mm match the shrink factors so each level sees a properly band-limited image. smoothing_sigmas_in_physical_units (advanced) bool true Interpret sigmas in mm vs voxels. On: sigmas in millimetres so anisotropic voxels (4 mm slices) are smoothed consistently. optimizer_scales_from_physical_shift (advanced) bool true Auto-estimate per-parameter optimizer scales. On: rotations in radians and translations in millimetres have different sensitivities; the physical-shift scales equalise them, which is the single setting that makes a fixed learning rate work across datasets.

docs.title: advanced_rigid
docs.text:
1. Two-Stage Composite Approach From the reference implementation (modulesReg.py::registration_advanced), this method uses a two-stage approach: first, a geometry-based initial transform centers the images, then a second optimized Euler3D transform is applied. The final result is a CompositeTransform combining both stages.

2. Conservative Parameters Compared to basic rigid registration: - Learning rate: 0.2 (vs 1.0) for more stable convergence - Sampling: 15% (vs 1%) for better metric estimation - Iterations: 200 (vs 100) for thorough optimization

3. Advantages The two-stage approach prevents the optimizer from getting stuck in local minima near the initial position, and the higher sampling percentage produces smoother metric landscapes.

import pardesline as pl

fixed, moving = pl.load("fixed.nii.gz"), pl.load("moving.nii.gz")
result = fixed.run("simpleitk_registration.advanced_rigid", moving=moving)  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_registration.advanced_rigid_registration --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: RIRE CT / MR pair with the exhaustive rotation pre-search (multimodal-rigid-registration skill); generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it learning_rate float 0.2 0.05 to 2.0 Gradient descent learning rate (lower = more stable). 0.2 is lower than the plain rigid method because the exhaustive phase already lands near the optimum; smaller steps then avoid overshooting. num_iterations int 200 50 to 500 Maximum optimizer iterations per stage. 200 per stage: the second stage starts close and the window stops it early. sampling_percentage float 0.15 0.01 to 0.5 Metric sampling percentage (0.15 = 15%). 15 % of the voxels: the exhaustive search compares many poses and needs a less noisy metric than gradient descent does. exhaustive_steps_per_axis (advanced) int 12 4 to 24 Rotation-search steps per axis (phase 1). 12 steps per axis over the rotation range sample every 15 degrees, enough to land inside the capture range of the gradient stage. metric (advanced) enum mattes_mutual_information mattes_mutual_information, mean_squares, correlation, joint_histogram_mi Similarity metric. Mattes MI for cross-modality. number_of_histogram_bins (advanced) int 50 10 to 256 Mattes MI histogram bins. 50 bins: 32-64 is the sweet spot for the Parzen-window joint histogram, fewer is blurry, more is noisy. sampling_strategy (advanced) enum RANDOM NONE, REGULAR, RANDOM Metric sampling strategy. RANDOM sampling adds a little stochasticity that helps the optimizer leave shallow local minima; REGULAR aliases with voxel grids. interpolator (advanced) enum LINEAR LINEAR, NEAREST, BSPLINE Resampling interpolator during optimization. LINEAR interpolation during optimisation is the standard trade-off between speed and smoothness of the metric. convergence_minimum_value (advanced) float 1e-06 1e-08 to 0.001 Gradient-descent convergence threshold. 1e-6 on the metric change over the window stops the optimizer once improvements are below noise. convergence_window_size (advanced) int 10 3 to 50 Gradient-descent convergence window. 10 iterations smooth the stochastic metric before the convergence test. shrink_factors (advanced) list 4,2,1 Multi-resolution shrink factors per level (comma-separated). 4,2,1: three resolution levels give the capture range for large offsets at the coarse level and sub-voxel precision at the fine one. smoothing_sigmas (advanced) list 2,1,0 Gaussian smoothing sigma per level (comma-separated). 2,1,0 mm match the shrink factors so each level sees a properly band-limited image. smoothing_sigmas_in_physical_units (advanced) bool true Interpret sigmas in mm vs voxels. On: sigmas in millimetres so anisotropic voxels (4 mm slices) are smoothed consistently. optimizer_scales_from_physical_shift (advanced) bool true Auto-estimate per-parameter optimizer scales. On: rotations in radians and translations in millimetres have different sensitivities; physical-shift scales equalise them so one learning rate works across datasets.

docs.title: affine
docs.text:
1. Affine Transformation Model An affine transformation has 12 DOF — rotation, translation, scaling, and shearing: $\(T_{\text{affine}}(\mathbf{x}) = A \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}\)$ where \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}\) is a general invertible matrix (not restricted to \(SO(3)\)).

2. Degrees of Freedom Compared to rigid (6 DOF), affine adds: - 3 scaling parameters: \(s_x, s_y, s_z\) - 3 shearing parameters: \(k_{xy}, k_{xz}, k_{yz}\)

This allows compensating for scanner calibration differences, growth between acquisitions, and anisotropic scaling.

import pardesline as pl

fixed, moving = pl.load("fixed.nii.gz"), pl.load("moving.nii.gz")
result = fixed.run("simpleitk_registration.affine", moving=moving)  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_registration.affine_registration --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py; same stack as rigid, which ran on the RIRE pair

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it learning_rate float 1.0 0.1 to 5.0 Gradient descent learning rate. 1.0 with physical-shift scales, as for rigid. num_iterations int 100 10 to 500 Maximum number of optimizer iterations. 100 per level. sampling_percentage float 0.01 0.005 to 0.5 Metric sampling percentage (0.01 = 1%). 1 % of the voxels is enough for the mutual-information estimate on 256^3 volumes and keeps each iteration cheap. initializer (advanced) enum GEOMETRY GEOMETRY, MOMENTS Centered-initializer mode (geometric center vs center-of-mass). GEOMETRY aligns the geometric centres before the first iteration; MOMENTS (intensity centre of mass) when one field of view is much larger than the other. metric (advanced) enum mattes_mutual_information mattes_mutual_information, mean_squares, correlation, joint_histogram_mi Similarity metric. Mattes MI for cross-modality; mean squares is faster for same-modality follow-ups. number_of_histogram_bins (advanced) int 50 10 to 256 Mattes MI histogram bins. 50 bins: 32-64 is the sweet spot for the Parzen-window joint histogram, fewer is blurry, more is noisy. sampling_strategy (advanced) enum RANDOM NONE, REGULAR, RANDOM Metric sampling strategy. RANDOM sampling adds a little stochasticity that helps the optimizer leave shallow local minima; REGULAR aliases with voxel grids. interpolator (advanced) enum LINEAR LINEAR, NEAREST, BSPLINE Resampling interpolator during optimization. LINEAR interpolation during optimisation is the standard trade-off between speed and smoothness of the metric. convergence_minimum_value (advanced) float 1e-06 1e-08 to 0.001 Gradient-descent convergence threshold. 1e-6 on the metric change over the window stops the optimizer once improvements are below noise. convergence_window_size (advanced) int 10 3 to 50 Gradient-descent convergence window. 10 iterations smooth the stochastic metric before the convergence test. shrink_factors (advanced) list 4,2,1 Multi-resolution shrink factors per level (comma-separated). 4,2,1: three resolution levels give the capture range for large offsets at the coarse level and sub-voxel precision at the fine one. smoothing_sigmas (advanced) list 2,1,0 Gaussian smoothing sigma per level (comma-separated). 2,1,0 mm match the shrink factors so each level sees a properly band-limited image. smoothing_sigmas_in_physical_units (advanced) bool true Interpret sigmas in mm vs voxels. On: sigmas in millimetres so anisotropic voxels (4 mm slices) are smoothed consistently. optimizer_scales_from_physical_shift (advanced) bool true Auto-estimate per-parameter optimizer scales. On: the 12 affine parameters mix scale, shear and translation, so scale normalisation matters even more than for rigid.

docs.title: bspline
docs.text:
1. Free-Form Deformation The displacement field is parameterized by a regular grid of \(n_x \times n_y \times n_z\) control points \(\{\phi_{i,j,k}\}\). The deformation at any point \(\mathbf{x}\) is interpolated using cubic B-spline basis functions: $\(T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \sum_{l=0}^{3} \sum_{m=0}^{3} \sum_{n=0}^{3} B_l(u) B_m(v) B_n(w) \, \phi_{i+l, j+m, k+n}\)$ where \((u, v, w)\) are the local coordinates within the control point cell.

2. Multi-Scale Refinement Registration proceeds from coarse grids (large grid_spacing) to fine grids, progressively capturing finer deformations. The LBFGSB optimizer handles the large number of parameters efficiently.

3. Regularization The bending energy of the B-spline ensures smooth deformations: $\(\mathcal{R}_{\text{bend}} = \int \left\| \nabla^2 T(\mathbf{x}) \right\|^2 d\mathbf{x}\)$

import pardesline as pl

fixed, moving = pl.load("fixed.nii.gz"), pl.load("moving.nii.gz")
result = fixed.run("simpleitk_registration.bspline", moving=moving)  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_registration.bspline_registration --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: POPI 4D-CT breathing phases (medical-volumes skill); generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it grid_spacing float 50.0 10.0 to 100.0 Control point grid spacing in mm. 50 mm control-point spacing captures organ-scale motion (breathing, bowel) without fitting noise; 20-30 mm for finer local deformation. num_iterations int 100 20 to 300 LBFGSB optimizer iterations. 100 LBFGSB iterations: the deformable metric improves quickly then flattens. bspline_order (advanced) int 3 1 to 3 B-spline basis order. 3 (cubic) is the standard smooth basis. mesh_coarsening_factor (advanced) int 4 1 to 8 Extra coarsening divisor applied to the control-point mesh. 4 starts the multi-resolution schedule with a coarser control mesh so large motion is recovered first. sampling_percentage (advanced) float 0.01 0.005 to 0.5 Fraction of voxels sampled by the metric. 1 % of the voxels for the metric. interpolator (advanced) enum LINEAR LINEAR, NEAREST, BSPLINE Resampling interpolator. LINEAR interpolation during optimisation is the standard trade-off between speed and smoothness of the metric. gradient_convergence_tolerance (advanced) float 1e-05 1e-07 to 0.001 LBFGSB gradient convergence tolerance. 1e-5 is the LBFGSB default. max_number_of_corrections (advanced) int 5 1 to 20 LBFGSB stored corrections (memory). 5 stored corrections is the LBFGSB default memory. cost_function_convergence_factor (advanced) float 10000000.0 10.0 to 1000000000000.0 LBFGSB cost-function convergence factor. 1e7 is the LBFGSB default (moderate accuracy). scale_factors (advanced) list 1,2,4 B-spline multi-resolution scale factors (comma-separated). 1,2,4 refine the control mesh across three levels.

docs.title: demons
docs.text:
1. Optical Flow Formulation Demons registration computes a dense displacement field \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})\) by iteratively solving an optical flow equation. The update step for the displacement at each voxel is: $\(\Delta \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) = rac{(I_M(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{u}) - I_F(\mathbf{x})) abla I_F(\mathbf{x})}{\| abla I_F(\mathbf{x})\|^2 + (I_M - I_F)^2}\)$

2. Symmetric Forces The symmetric variant uses gradients from both images for improved convergence: $\(\Delta \mathbf{u} = rac{(I_M - I_F)( abla I_F + abla I_M)}{\| abla I_F + abla I_M\|^2 + (I_M - I_F)^2}\)$

3. Gaussian Smoothing After each iteration, the displacement field is convolved with a Gaussian kernel of standard deviation \(\sigma\) (standard_deviations parameter) to enforce diffeomorphic-like smoothness.

import pardesline as pl

fixed, moving = pl.load("fixed.nii.gz"), pl.load("moving.nii.gz")
result = fixed.run("simpleitk_registration.demons", moving=moving)  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_registration.demons_registration --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py; same-modality use only (the metric is intensity difference)

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it num_iterations int 20 5 to 100 Number of demons iterations. 20 demons iterations are enough for small same-modality deformations; the method is for follow-up scans, not CT-to-MR. standard_deviations float 2.0 0.5 to 5.0 Displacement field smoothing sigma. 2.0 voxels of Gaussian smoothing of the displacement field keep it regular (no folding) at the cost of fine detail. smooth_displacement_field (advanced) bool true Smooth the total displacement field each iteration. On: smoothing the total field each iteration is what keeps demons from producing a torn deformation.

docs.title: difference_analysis
docs.text:
1. Registration Quality Assessment After registration, the absolute difference image \(D = |I_F - I_M^{\text{reg}}|\) reveals regions of misalignment. Low values indicate good alignment; high values indicate residual error.

2. Thresholding Binary thresholding on the difference image extracts voxels with significant misalignment: $\(M(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \tau_L \leq D(\mathbf{x}) \leq \tau_U \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

3. Statistics Mean, max, and standard deviation of the difference image quantify overall registration accuracy. The percentage of high-difference voxels provides a single summary metric.

import pardesline as pl

fixed, moving = pl.load("fixed.nii.gz"), pl.load("moving.nii.gz")
result = fixed.run("simpleitk_registration.difference_analysis", moving=moving)  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_registration.difference_analysis --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it lower_threshold float 50.0 0.0 to 500.0 Lower threshold for highlighting high-difference regions. 50 intensity units: below that, differences are noise and interpolation. upper_threshold float 400.0 100.0 to 3000.0 Upper threshold for difference analysis. 400: above that, differences are bone or air boundaries that any residual misalignment produces; the band in between highlights soft-tissue change.

docs.title: SimpleITK Segmentation
docs.text:
simpleitk_segmentation: Medical image segmentation using SimpleITK. Automatic thresholding, region growing, watershed, and connected components for organ/tissue segmentation.

Methods otsu_threshold, manual_threshold, connected_components, watershed Input files .vti, .mha, .nrrd, .nii (and .nii.gz) Bundled datasets to try rire_brain, liver_tumor_patient01, visible_human_head_mri, spider_lumbar_mri, msd_task04_hippocampus, msd_task09_spleen Example Threshold segmentation on MSD spleen CLI pardesline run simpleitk_segmentation.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Segmentation partitions a medical image \(I: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) into disjoint regions \(\{R_1, R_2, \ldots, R_k\}\) such that \(\bigcup_{i} R_i = \Omega\) and \(R_i \cap R_j = \emptyset\) for \(i \neq j\).

Each region corresponds to an anatomical structure (organ, bone, lesion). The segmentation can be expressed as a labeling function:

\[ L(\mathbf{x}) = \arg\max_{c \in \{1, \ldots, k\}} P(c \mid I(\mathbf{x})) \]

SimpleITK provides methods ranging from global thresholding (Otsu) to topological segmentation (watershed), each suited to different imaging scenarios.

docs.title: otsu_threshold
docs.text:
1. Between-Class Variance Maximization Otsu's method finds the optimal threshold \(t^*\) that maximizes the between-class variance \(\sigma_B^2(t)\) for a bimodal intensity histogram: $\(t^* = \arg\max_t \sigma_B^2(t) = \arg\max_t \, \omega_0(t) \omega_1(t) [\mu_0(t) - \mu_1(t)]^2\)$ where \(\omega_0, \omega_1\) are the class probabilities and \(\mu_0, \mu_1\) are the class means for intensities below and above threshold \(t\).

2. Segmentation The binary output is: $\(L(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I(\mathbf{x}) > t^* \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.vti")
result = obj.run("simpleitk_segmentation.otsu_threshold")  # catalog defaults
# same thing, domain vocabulary: `volume.segment()`
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_segmentation.otsu_threshold --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: MSD spleen CT through Volume.segment() (examples/spleen_ct_threshold_segmentation uses the manual window); generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it number_of_histogram_bins (advanced) int 128 16 to 512 Histogram bins for the Otsu criterion. 128 bins resolve the bimodal histogram of CT (air/tissue) or MR (background/foreground) without the noise of 512. inside_value (advanced) int 1 0 to 255 Foreground label. 1: the foreground label, so the result is a LabelMap with label 1. outside_value (advanced) int 0 0 to 255 Background label. 0 is the background label, so the result is a label map with a single foreground label.

docs.title: manual_threshold
docs.text:
1. Range Thresholding A simple but effective segmentation using user-specified intensity bounds \([l, u]\): $\(L(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } l \leq I(\mathbf{x}) \leq u \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

2. Hounsfield Units For CT images, intensities are calibrated in Hounsfield Units (HU): - Air: \(-1000\) HU - Water: \(0\) HU - Soft tissue: \(+40\) to \(+80\) HU - Bone: \(+300\) to \(+3000\) HU

This allows reproducible thresholds across scanners.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.vti")
result = obj.run("simpleitk_segmentation.manual_threshold")  # catalog defaults
# same thing, domain vocabulary: `volume.segment(lower=..., upper=...)`
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_segmentation.manual_threshold --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: MSD spleen CT, 30-200 HU soft-tissue window (examples/spleen_ct_threshold_segmentation); generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it lower float 100.0 -1000.0 to 3000.0 Lower intensity threshold. 100 HU is the placeholder bone/contrast threshold on CT; Volume.segment(lower, upper) takes the window you mean (30-200 HU soft tissue, 300+ bone). upper float 1000.0 -1000.0 to 3000.0 Upper intensity threshold. 1000 HU caps the window below metal and dense bone. inside_value (advanced) int 1 0 to 255 Foreground label. 1: foreground label. outside_value (advanced) int 0 0 to 255 Background label. 0 is the background label, so the result is a label map with a single foreground label.

docs.title: connected_components
docs.text:
1. Labeling Algorithm After binary thresholding, connected component analysis assigns a unique label \(l_i\) to each maximal connected region. Two voxels are connected if they share a face (6-connectivity) or edge (26-connectivity).

2. Size Filtering Small components (noise) are removed by discarding regions with fewer than min_size voxels: $\(R_i' = \begin{cases} R_i & \text{if } |R_i| \geq n_{\min} \\ \emptyset & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$ where \(|R_i|\) denotes the voxel count of region \(R_i\).

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.vti")
result = obj.run("simpleitk_segmentation.connected_components")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_segmentation.connected_components --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: MSD spleen CT after thresholding (examples/spleen_ct_threshold_segmentation, min_size 1000); generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it threshold float 100.0 -1000.0 to 3000.0 Intensity threshold before labeling. 100 intensity units binarises before labelling; on a LabelMap input use 0.5. min_size int 15 1 to 1000 Minimum object size in voxels. 15 voxels removes speckle components; raise to the hundreds or thousands to keep only organs. upper_threshold (advanced) float 255.0 -1000.0 to 3000.0 Upper bound for binarization. 255 is the upper bound for 8-bit inputs; raise it for HU. fully_connected (advanced) bool false 26-connectivity (True) vs 6-connectivity (False). Off (6-connectivity): diagonal-only contacts do not join two structures, which keeps touching organs apart. inside_value (advanced) int 1 0 to 255 Foreground label. 1: foreground label. outside_value (advanced) int 0 0 to 255 Background label. 0 is the background label, so the result is a label map with a single foreground label.

docs.title: watershed
docs.text:
1. Distance Transform From a binary mask \(B\), the Euclidean distance transform computes: $\(D(\mathbf{x}) = \min_{\mathbf{y} \in \partial B} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|_2\)$ Local maxima of \(D\) serve as seed points for the watershed.

2. Watershed Algorithm The watershed treats \(-D(\mathbf{x})\) as a topographic surface. Starting from seed points (local minima of \(-D\)), regions are grown by immersion — flooding the surface from each seed and building dams where floods from different seeds meet.

3. Pipeline The full pipeline is: 1. Binary threshold: \(B = \{\mathbf{x} : I(\mathbf{x}) > t\}\) 2. Morphological opening: remove small noise 3. Distance transform: \(D(\mathbf{x})\) 4. Seed generation: local maxima of \(D\) with radius \(r\) 5. Watershed: flood from seeds to produce labels

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.vti")
result = obj.run("simpleitk_segmentation.watershed")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .vti. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.simpleitk_segmentation.watershed --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated volumes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it threshold float 100.0 -1000.0 to 3000.0 Initial binary threshold. 100 intensity units for the initial binarisation. seed_radius float 10.0 1.0 to 50.0 Seed generation radius in mm. 10 mm: markers are placed where the distance map exceeds this radius, so only objects at least 2 cm across become basins. min_object_size int 15 1 to 1000 Minimum object size after watershed. 15 voxels drops speckle basins. upper_threshold (advanced) float 255.0 -1000.0 to 3000.0 Upper bound for initial binarization. 255 for 8-bit inputs. opening_radius (advanced) list 10,10,10 BinaryOpening radius per axis (comma-separated). 10,10,10 voxels of binary opening detach thin bridges between objects before the distance map. closing_radius (advanced) list 10,10,10 BinaryClosing radius per axis (comma-separated). 10,10,10 voxels of closing fill small holes inside objects. distance_inside_is_positive (advanced) bool false SignedMaurerDistanceMap insideIsPositive. Off: SimpleITK's convention, inside is negative. distance_squared (advanced) bool false SignedMaurerDistanceMap squaredDistance. Off: true Euclidean distance in mm. mark_watershed_line (advanced) bool true Draw watershed dam lines between basins. On: dam lines between basins are drawn, which shows where touching objects were split. inside_value (advanced) int 1 0 to 255 Foreground label. 1: foreground label. outside_value (advanced) int 0 0 to 255 Background label. 0 is the background label, so the result is a label map with a single foreground label.

docs.title: Stereo & Depth Estimation
docs.text:
stereo_3d_reconstruction: Depth-based point cloud analysis: colorize by depth, filter by depth range. Foundation for stereo vision and 3D reconstruction from camera images.

Methods depth_colorization, depth_filter Input files .ply, .pcd, .txt, .xyz Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats CLI pardesline run stereo_3d_reconstruction.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Stereo vision reconstructs 3D structure from camera views. The fundamental relationship between depth \(Z\), disparity \(d\), focal length \(f\), and baseline \(B\) is:

\[ Z = \frac{f \cdot B}{d} \]

A 3D point \(\mathbf{X} = (X, Y, Z)^T\) in world coordinates projects to pixel \((u, v)\) via the camera intrinsic matrix \(K\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} K \mathbf{X}, \quad K = \begin{pmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \]

For point cloud analysis, depth-based operations include colorization by Euclidean distance and depth-range filtering for region-of-interest extraction.

docs.title: depth_colorization
docs.text:
1. Distance Computation For each point \(p_i\) in the cloud, the Euclidean distance from the origin (camera center) is computed: $\(d_i = \|p_i - \mathbf{o}\|_2 = \sqrt{x_i^2 + y_i^2 + z_i^2}\)$

2. Normalization and Colormap Distances are normalized to \([0, 1]\) and mapped through a perceptually uniform colormap (jet, viridis, plasma, or turbo): $\(c_i = \text{colormap}\left(\frac{d_i - d_{\min}}{d_{\max} - d_{\min}}\right)\)$

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("stereo_3d_reconstruction.depth_colorization")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.stereo_3d_reconstruction.depth_colorization --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated depth clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it colormap int 0 0 to 3 Colormap: 0=jet, 1=viridis, 2=plasma, 3=turbo 0 (jet) is what stereo and depth tooling has used for decades, so the colours are readable at a glance; the others are perceptually uniform alternatives.

docs.title: depth_filter
docs.text:
1. Percentile-Based Filtering Instead of absolute depth thresholds, the filter uses percentiles of the distance distribution for robustness across different scales: $\(P_{\text{keep}} = \{p_i : q_{\min} \leq d_i \leq q_{\max}\}\)$ where \(q_{\min}, q_{\max}\) are the min_depth and max_depth percentiles of \(\{d_i\}\).

2. Application Useful for removing background points (far range) or ground plane (near range) in LiDAR and depth camera data.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("stereo_3d_reconstruction.depth_filter")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.stereo_3d_reconstruction.depth_filter --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated depth clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it min_depth float 0.1 0.0 to 1.0 Lower depth percentile (0-1 fraction). Dropping the nearest 10 % removes the lens-edge and occlusion artefacts stereo matching produces close to the camera. max_depth float 0.9 0.0 to 1.0 Upper depth percentile (0-1 fraction). Dropping the farthest 10 % removes the sky and the far-range noise where disparity is below one pixel.

docs.title: Voxelization & Volume
docs.text:
voxel_to_mesh: Convert meshes and point clouds to voxel grids. Perform volumetric operations like binary erosion and marching cubes reconstruction.

Methods voxelization, binary_erosion Input files .ply, .obj, .stl, .off Bundled datasets to try open3d_bunny, open3d_icp_demo, kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001, medshapenet, c3vd_endoscopy_splats, hf_objaverse_glb_shard CLI pardesline run voxel_to_mesh.<method> input.ext [--param value]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Voxelization discretizes a 3D space into a regular grid of cubic cells (voxels). Each voxel stores a scalar value (occupancy, SDF, density). The inverse process extracts a surface mesh from this volumetric representation.

Marching Cubes is the standard iso-surface extraction algorithm. For each cube in the voxel grid, it classifies vertices as inside or outside the iso-surface based on their scalar values relative to an iso-value \(\tau\).

Binary erosion shrinks a solid by removing boundary voxels using a structuring element.

docs.title: voxelization
docs.text:
Voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a 3D occupancy grid. Open3D creates a VoxelGrid by testing which voxels intersect the mesh surface. The voxel size \(v\) controls the resolution of the grid.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("voxel_to_mesh.voxelization")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.voxel_to_mesh.voxelization --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated meshes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it voxel_size float 0.01 0.002 to 0.05 Size of each voxel cube. Smaller = more detail. 0.01 in file units gives a 100-voxel grid across a unit-sized object: coarse enough to run in a second, fine enough to see shape; the range (0.002-0.05) assumes objects around a metre, so scale it for millimetre data.

docs.title: binary_erosion
docs.text:
Binary erosion shrinks a solid by removing boundary voxels. For a volume \(V\) and structuring element \(B\): $\(V \ominus B = \{x : B_x \subseteq V\}\)$ The eroded volume is then reconstructed back to a mesh using marching cubes at iso-value 0.5.

import pardesline as pl

obj = pl.load("input.ply")
result = obj.run("voxel_to_mesh.binary_erosion")  # catalog defaults
result.provenance[-1]  # the step, every parameter used, duration, version

Output: .ply. Script: python -m pardesline.ops.voxel_to_mesh.binary_erosion --input ... --output ....

Defaults validated on: generated meshes in tests/test_ops_smoke.py

Parameter Type Default Range What it does Why this default, when to change it voxel_size float 0.01 0.002 to 0.05 Voxel size for the occupancy grid. Same grid as voxelization so the two can be compared on the same object. erosion_iterations int 1 1 to 5 Number of erosion iterations. 1 iteration removes one voxel layer: the thinnest shell, which is what you want to strip surface noise without eating thin parts. erosion_connectivity (advanced) int 1 1 to 3 Connectivity of the 3D structuring element (1=faces, 2=+edges, 3=+corners). 1 (faces only) is the most conservative structuring element: each iteration removes the least material. iso_level (advanced) float 0.5 0.0 to 1.0 Marching-cubes iso-surface level. 0.5 is the half-occupancy surface of a binary grid: the boundary between inside and outside voxels. padding_voxels (advanced) int 5 0 to 50 Padding added around the bounding box, expressed in voxels. 5 voxels of margin keep marching cubes from clipping the surface at the grid border.

docs.title: Why ICP fails on real scans, and what we set by default
docs.text:
Upstream libraries give you the method with the defaults of the paper or the tutorial. Those defaults are tuned for the tutorial's data. Real scans are partial, noisy, anisotropic and at a scale the tutorial never saw. This page is the written proof behind the one-liners: for each algorithm family, the failure on textbook defaults, the parameters that matter, what pardesline sets, the data it was validated on, and when you should override.

Every number here is reproducible from the committed examples (examples/<name>/result.json) and every parameter is in the catalog with the same rationale (pl.describe("module.method"), the algorithm pages). Where a claim is only backed by generated test data, it says so.

docs.title: Registration of point clouds (registration)
docs.text:
The failure. Open3D's registration_icp(source, target, 0.02, identity, PointToPoint()), the call from the tutorial, on the Stanford bunny against a copy rotated by 35°, trimmed to 70 % overlap and jittered by 0.5 % of the diagonal: it stops 32.0° off and reports a fitness of 0.98. Two things went wrong at once: ICP is a local optimiser whose basin is a few degrees wide, so a 35° start converges to the nearest wrong minimum; and the threshold 0.02 (in file units, here metres on a 15 cm object) is so wide that almost every point finds a "correspondence", which is why the fitness looks excellent.

What pardesline sets (target.align(moving) = registration.ransac_icp_pipeline):

Parameter Value Why voxel_size 0 → 1.3 % of the bounding-box diagonal every other distance is a multiple of it; the pipeline scales itself to a 15 cm part and a 15 m facade; the same code runs in mm and in m normal_radius_factor, fpfh_radius_factor 2×, 5× the voxel normals need a neighbourhood slightly larger than a cell; FPFH needs about five cells of support to be descriptive and still local on partial views distance_threshold_factor 1.5× the voxel (RANSAC) tolerant to scanner noise, still rejects outliers mutual_filter on both directions of the feature match must agree: the setting that most reduces false correspondences on symmetric parts ransac_n, edge_length_threshold 3, 0.9 the minimum sample for a rigid transform; triplets whose pairwise distances disagree by more than 10 % are pruned before the expensive inlier count icp_threshold_factor 0.4× the voxel the final ICP is tight so the 30 % of points without a counterpart cannot pull it icp_estimation_method point-to-plane (point-to-point fallback without normals) converges in far fewer iterations and does not fight the surface

Validated on: the bunny experiment (examples/icp_registration_bunny): 0.14° residual, inlier RMSE 0.9 mm against a 1.4 mm noise floor; the bunny atlas transfer (examples/atlas_label_transfer_bunny): 99.4 % label agreement, 0.06° pose error; the Open3D indoor fragments (open3d_icp_demo). The ultrasound and CBCT cases of the point-cloud registration guide are the founder's production experience and are not reproducible here: the honest claim is "the same settings, on public data with the same characteristics".

When to override

  • RANSAC fitness below 0.3 and ICP does nothing: the features are meaningless because the voxel is wrong for the data. Pass voxel_size explicitly, 2–5× the point spacing. Check units first (obj.frame): mm read as m makes every radius wrong.
  • Symmetric objects (cylinders, vertebral bodies, single teeth): the global stage converges to a mirrored pose. ransac_n=4, a prior pose, or more context in the scan.
  • Flat scenes (floors, walls): point-to-plane slides. icp_estimation_method="point_to_point", or constrain the degrees of freedom.
  • Different devices with unknown scale: ransac_with_scaling=True once, then fix the scale.

Judge by inlier RMSE and the pose error on the overlapping region, not by fitness alone: fitness counts source points within the threshold and caps at the overlap ratio.

docs.title: Surface reconstruction (point_cloud_reconstruction)
docs.text:
The failure. Poisson reconstruction at Open3D's depth=8 with no density trimming on a partial scan: the surface balloons over holes and the back of the object becomes a smooth bubble that looks plausible and is wrong. At depth=11 on 20k points it fits the noise and takes minutes.

What pardesline sets (points.to_mesh() = point_cloud_reconstruction.poisson): depth=9 (512 cells across the bounding cube: organ- and part-level detail on 20k–200k points), scale=1.1 (Kazhdan's reference), density_quantile=0.01 (the 1 % of vertices with the least sample support are removed, which is exactly where Poisson balloons), normals estimated at normal_radius=0.1 with normal_orient_k=15 when the cloud has none. The result is a clean, density-trimmed surface, not a closed one, and the sidecar says so.

Validated on: the bunny, 20 000 Poisson-disk points after outlier removal (examples/poisson_reconstruction_bunny); generated clouds in tests/test_ops_smoke.py.

When to override: very partial scans, density_quantile=0.05–0.1; dense metrology scans (millions of points), depth=10–11; thin structures (vessels, wires), ball pivoting with radius_factor=1.5–2 instead of Poisson.

docs.title: Downsampling and cleaning (point_cloud_processing)
docs.text:
The failure. voxel_size=0.05 from the tutorial on a dental scan in millimetres keeps one point per 5 cm, i.e. one point. statistical_outlier_removal with std_ratio=1.0 removes the thin parts of a scan along with the noise.

What pardesline sets: voxel_downsample has an absolute voxel_size=0.02 in file units because a downsample is a measurement choice (2 cm on a room, 0.5 mm on a tooth): the registration and feature pipelines derive their own voxel from the bounding box instead. points.clean() uses nb_neighbors=20, std_ratio=2.0: 20 neighbours give a stable mean distance per point; two standard deviations drop the flying pixels of scanners and keep edges and thin parts.

Validated on: the bunny with 0.5 % Gaussian noise (both bunny examples); KITTI sweeps; generated clouds.

When to override: depth cameras indoors, std_ratio=1.0; clean CAD-derived clouds, std_ratio=3.0; always set voxel_size in the units of your file.

docs.title: LiDAR scenes (lidar_scene_detection)
docs.text:
The failure. A ground plane fitted with a 1 cm RANSAC threshold on a 100 m sweep: the road is not flat (camber, slope, curbs), so half the road survives as "objects" and the clustering explodes. DBSCAN with eps=0.02 on an HDL-64E sweep: the ring spacing reaches 0.3–0.5 m at 30 m, so every car becomes thirty stripes.

What pardesline sets (lidar_scene_detection.object_clustering): ground_threshold=0.3 m (a band that follows a real road while car sills at 0.4–0.5 m stay out), cluster_eps=0.5 m (bridges the ring spacing at 30 m without merging parked cars), min_cluster_points=10 (a pedestrian at 20 m still clusters, ring fragments do not).

Validated on: KITTI drive 2011_09_26_0001, Velodyne HDL-64E in the sensor frame (examples/kitti_lidar_ground_and_objects): 35 476 points after ground removal clustered into cars, poles and walls.

When to override: 16-beam sensors, cluster_eps=0.8–1.0; indoor robots, ground_threshold=0.05–0.1; the sweep must be in metres, which the manifest layout guarantees for KITTI (frame sensor, units m).

docs.title: Rigid registration of volumes (simpleitk_registration)
docs.text:
The failure. SimpleITK's ImageRegistrationMethod with mean squares between a CT and a T1 MRI: bone is bright in one and dark in the other, so the metric is minimised by a wrong pose. With GradientDescent(learningRate=1.0) and no optimizer scales, one radian of rotation and one millimetre of translation are treated as the same step, so the rotation explodes on the first iteration. Without multi-resolution, a 40 mm initial offset is outside the capture range.

What pardesline sets (fixed.align(moving) = simpleitk_registration.rigid): Mattes mutual information with 50 bins (works across modalities), sampling_percentage=0.01 RANDOM (cheap and slightly stochastic, which helps leave shallow minima), initializer=GEOMETRY (centres aligned before the first iteration), shrink_factors=4,2,1 with smoothing_sigmas=2,1,0 mm (capture range at the coarse level, sub-voxel precision at the fine one; sigmas in physical units so 4 mm slices are handled), optimizer_scales_from_physical_shift=True (the setting that makes learning_rate=1.0 work on any dataset), 100 iterations per level with a 10-iteration convergence window.

Validated on: RIRE training_001, CT 0.65×0.65×4 mm against MR 1.25×1.25×4 mm, 40 mm initial offset, registered in 8.8 s (examples/register_ct_mr_rire, the README demo). The CT/MR registration guide traces the metric per iteration and compares with a hand-written SimpleITK stack.

When to override: initial misalignment above 30° or different patient positions, simpleitk_registration.advanced_rigid (exhaustive rotation search first); same modality follow-ups, metric="mean_squares" is faster; small fields of view, sampling_percentage=0.05–0.15; scanner calibration differences, affine.

docs.title: Threshold segmentation of volumes (simpleitk_segmentation)
docs.text:
The failure. Otsu on a whole CT splits air from everything else, not the organ from its neighbours. A fixed threshold=100 on an 8-bit windowed image and on a 16-bit HU image mean different things. Connected components with fully_connected=True (26-connectivity) joins two organs that touch at a corner.

What pardesline sets: volume.segment() without bounds is Otsu with 128 bins (resolves the bimodal CT and MR histograms); volume.segment(lower, upper) takes the window you mean in intensity units (30–200 HU soft tissue, 300+ bone); connected_components uses 6-connectivity so diagonal contacts do not merge structures, and min_size=15 voxels drops speckle.

Validated on: MSD spleen, soft-tissue window then components of at least 1 000 voxels against the expert label (examples/spleen_ct_threshold_segmentation). The example shows the honest result: a threshold finds soft tissue, not the spleen. That is the baseline a learned model has to beat, which is why the models section exists.

When to override: MR has no absolute scale, so pass bounds from the volume's percentiles, not HU; contrast-enhanced CT, raise the upper bound; for organs, go to medical segmentation models.

docs.title: Mesh processing (pyvista_mesh_processing, mesh_processing)
docs.text:
The failure. Laplacian smoothing for 100 iterations on a marching-cubes organ surface shrinks it by a visible fraction of a millimetre and rounds every edge; quadric decimation to a fixed triangle count on a mesh with open boundaries pulls the rim inward.

What pardesline sets: mesh.smooth() is Taubin smoothing (pass_band=0.1, 20 iterations): a low-pass filter that removes the voxel staircase and keeps the volume, so it can run longer than Laplacian smoothing without shrinkage; mesh.decimate() removes 50 % of the triangles, which on marching-cubes output is the redundant co-planar half; mesh.clean() merges exact duplicates only (tolerance=0), which is safe on any mesh.

Validated on: MSD hippocampus label surfaces (examples/hippocampus_mask_to_mesh); generated meshes.

When to override: volume measurements, decimate(volume_preservation=True); CAD parts with sharp edges, smooth(feature_smoothing=True); closing scan seams, clean(tolerance=<spacing>).

docs.title: What is not covered yet
docs.text: Deformable registration (cpd_deformable, bspline, demons), SDF and voxel operations, stereo depth and the PyVista analysis filters are validated on generated data only (tests/test_ops_smoke.py) and their rationale lines say so. The benchmarks page regenerates the numbers above from scripts; real industrial and medical cases go to examples/real_cases with the data or a loader for it.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The top-level namespace is the public API; everything below is reachable as pardesline.<name>.

Data load, scan, datasets, Dataset, Sample, Manifest, Layout, License, cache settings Objects Object, PointCloud, Mesh, Volume, LabelMap, RawArray, Transform, Image, Frame Catalog catalog, modules, describe, Catalog, Module, Method, Parameter Runner run, RunResult, output directory MCP server build_server, the impl_* functions behind each tool

PardesLine — 3D vision and medical imaging, locally or in the cloud.

import pardesline as pl

scan = pl.load("scan.ply")                       # a local point cloud (Object)
surface = scan.downsample(voxel_size=0.01).poisson(depth=9)
surface.save("surface.ply")                      # + surface.ply.pardesline.json (frame, licence…)

ds = pl.load("rire_brain")                       # a dataset: manifest + fetched-on-access files
s = ds[0]; s.roles                               # ['ct', 'mr_t1']
moved = s.ct.align(s.mr_t1)                      # rigid registration, transform in moved.transform

ds = pl.load("/data/study_A", license="internal", units={"mesh": "mm"})   # your own folder

pl.run("simpleitk_registration", "rigid", "ct.mha", moving="mr.mha")
pl.catalog().describe("point_cloud_reconstruction.poisson")

Everything under pl.run / pl.load executes on this machine. The cloud client (pl.login, pl.upload, pl.share, hosted compute, viewers) lives in pardesline.cloud and stays reachable from the top level.

load(ref: str | PathLike, *, manifest: str | PathLike | None = None, assume: bool = False, interactive: bool = False, save_draft: bool = True, layout: Layout | dict[str, Any] | None = None, kind: str | None = None, **answers: Any) -> Object | Dataset

Open a file as an :class:Object or a dataset as a :class:Dataset.

A raw array file (.npy, .npz, .bin) needs layout= (dtype, shape, columns / key) and takes kind= ("points", "volume", "labels"); with a layout and no kind, a (N,k) shape is points and a (a,b,c) shape is a grid.

For a folder without a confirmed manifest - or a Hub repo without a bundled one - pl.scan drafts a manifest. docs.title: pardesline.catalog
docs.text:
The typed catalog of modules, methods and parameters.

The catalog is generated from the same manifests that drive the PardesLine platform (catalog/data/<module>.json). It is the single source of truth for what an algorithm is called, which file types it accepts, which flags it takes, their defaults and their ranges. Nothing here imports a native library.

>>> import pardesline as pl
>>> cat = pl.catalog()
>>> m = cat.method("point_cloud_processing", "voxel_downsample")
>>> m.validate({"voxel_size": 0.05})
{'voxel_size': '0.05'}

docs.title: pardesline.data.manifest.SourceSpec
docs.text:
Bases: _Model

Where the files come from.

  • local: root folder (absolute, or relative to the manifest file).
  • https: files with checksums, optional mirrors.
  • hf: repo_id on the Hugging Face Hub; paths restricts the listing to sub-folders (a 100k-file repo is never listed whole); max_files caps what one listing may return.
  • open3d: a class of open3d.data.
  • archive: one remote url (or several urls that form one dataset) of zip or uncompressed tar read with HTTP Range requests: the index costs a few KB, a member costs its own size, the archive is never downloaded whole when the server supports ranges. prefix restricts the listing to members under it.
  • s3: a public bucket listed with ListObjectsV2 (bucket, endpoint, prefix); relative paths are the keys under prefix.
  • tcia: a public collection of The Cancer Imaging Archive through the NBIA REST API (collection, optional modalities); one entry per DICOM series as <PatientID>/<Modality>/<SeriesInstanceUID>/.

docs.title: pardesline.mcp_server
docs.text:
pardesline mcp: the package as a Model Context Protocol server.

Any MCP client - Claude Desktop and Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex, a LangChain or OpenAI Agents tool loop - gets the 43 bundled datasets, any hf:// / s3:// / tcia:// source, private folders through pl.scan, the typed object model and the 73 catalog algorithms, on the user's machine, without a PardesLine account. Nothing leaves the machine except the downloads the user asks for.

Run it with pardesline mcp (stdio, the default every client speaks) or pardesline mcp --transport streamable-http --port 8765. Needs pip install "pardesline[mcp]".

Design rules for tools: - every result is plain JSON (paths as strings), small enough for a context window (lists are paged with limit / offset); - blocking work (downloads, algorithms) runs in a worker thread so the server keeps answering; - the package's own rules hold: nothing is guessed, a question is returned as data for the agent to relay to the human (scan_dataset -> confirm_dataset), gated sources explain what the human must do.

docs.title: pardesline.object.arrays
docs.text:
Raw arrays (.npy, .npz, .bin) read through a declared layout.

A raw array says nothing about what its numbers mean: KITTI's .bin is float32 (N,4) x, y, z, reflectance; a KITTI-360 chunk is coord.npy (N,3); an occupancy grid is (L,W,H) class ids. The layout comes from the manifest (or from the caller); nothing here guesses it. Decoded data is materialised in a standard file (PLY for points, MetaImage for grids) so the catalog ops - which read files - run unchanged.

docs.title: pardesline.runner
docs.text:
Run one algorithm from the catalog as a subprocess, on this machine.

Each op is an argparse script (python -m pardesline.ops.<module>.<script> --input ... --output ... [--flag value ...]). Running it in a child process keeps the exact contract the platform uses and isolates native-library crashes from the caller.

What a run produced.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run(module: str, method: str | None = None, input: str | PathLike | None = None, /, output: str | PathLike | None = None, *, moving: str | PathLike | None = None, params: dict[str, Any] | None = None, timeout: float = DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, python: str | None = None, on_log: Callable[[str], None] | None = None, on_progress: Callable[[int], None] | None = None, cwd: str | PathLike | None = None, **kwargs: Any) -> RunResult

Run one algorithm on a local file and return a :class:RunResult.

run("point_cloud_processing", "voxel_downsample", "scan.ply", voxel_size=0.05) or run("point_cloud_processing.voxel_downsample", "scan.ply", ...).

Parameters go as keyword arguments (or in params); they are validated against the catalog before anything runs. The first three arguments are positional-only, so a parameter that happens to be called method or input can still be passed by keyword. Two-input methods (registration) take the moving file through moving. The result is written to output or to :func:output_dir. Raises :class:ParameterError or :class:RunError.

docs.title: Datasets catalog
docs.text:
Every dataset below loads with one call and comes back as typed objects (volumes, label maps, meshes, point clouds, splats, images) that know their frame, units, labels, licence and citation. Files are fetched on access, verified, cached; archives are read by HTTP Range so one sample costs one sample. pl.datasets() lists the names, pl.describe(name) prints a manifest.

import pardesline as pl

print(pl.datasets())                      # 43 names
print(pl.datasets(tag="ct"))             # by tag
ds = pl.load("msd_task09_spleen")        # lazy: nothing downloaded yet
ct = ds.filter(split="Tr")[0].ct          # one 30 MB volume out of a 1.6 GB tar

Not bundled, and why: BraTS (Synapse data-use agreement), ModelNet, ShapeNet and ScanNet (registration-gated downloads). They are tracked on the Datasets wanted issue; a manifest that fetches with the user's own credentials is welcome.

docs.title: Any source, not only the bundled ones
docs.text:
URI What happens pl.load("hf://org/repo") the Hub tree is listed, a manifest is drafted, you confirm units / labels / licence once, it is saved pl.load("tcia://Collection") a public TCIA collection through the NBIA API, DICOM series as folders pl.load("s3://openneuro.org/ds000228") an OpenNeuro dataset from the public bucket pl.load("https://.../archive.zip") a remote zip or tar read by HTTP Range pl.scan("/data/study") your folder: a draft manifest and the questions the files cannot answer

See How to standardize a folder of medical images and the manifest schema.

docs.title: AMOS 22: abdominal multi-organ segmentation, 600 CT and MRI with 15 organ labels
docs.text:
pl.load("amos22") loads this dataset. The AMOS benchmark (Ji et al., NeurIPS 2022): 500 CT and 100 MRI scans with 15 abdominal organs annotated; 240 training, 120 validation and 240 test images. docs.title: Standardized layout
docs.text:
Files are fetched on first access into the dataset cache and stay in their original format; ds.export(folder) writes every sample as standard files (PLY for points and meshes, MetaImage for volumes and label maps) with a .pardesline.json sidecar carrying frame, units, labels, licence and provenance, plus a manifest for the folder. Label maps become exact surfaces with to_mesh(label=k), DICOM series become one volume, raw arrays are decoded through the layout above.

ds = pl.load("totalsegmentator_mri").take(2)
ds.export("./standardized")        # PLY / MetaImage + sidecars + manifest.json

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: title: Concepts — dataset, manifest, object, catalog description: The four ideas behind pardesline: a dataset is a manifest plus a source; an object is a file with frame, units, labels, licence and provenance; the catalog validates every algorithm parameter; standardization is explicit, never guessed.

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
A Dataset is a manifest plus a source. pl.load(name_or_uri) returns one; nothing is downloaded until a sample's role is accessed. Samples are grouped by what the manifest says pairs files (patient, frame, folder); ds.filter(split="Tr"), ds.take(n), ds.sample(n, seed), ds.split(by="patient") never mix patients across splits. ds[0] or ds["case_001"] is a Sample; sample.role_name is an Object.

ds = pl.load("totalsegmentator_ct")
s = ds.take(1)[0]
s.roles  # ['ct', 'liver', 'spleen', 'kidney_left', ...]  (118 roles)
s.liver  # LabelMap, fetched now (one 50 MB member out of a 23 GB zip)
ds.citation  # what the data owner asks you to cite

docs.title: Manifest
docs.text:
A JSON document (pydantic model pardesline.Manifest) that says everything the files cannot say by themselves:

Field What it holds Example source scheme and location: https files with checksums, hf repo + paths, archive url(s) read by HTTP Range, s3 bucket, tcia collection, urllist index, open3d, local {"scheme": "archive", "url": "https://.../Task04_Hippocampus.tar", "prefix": "Task04_Hippocampus"} roles one entry per file kind in a sample: type (volume, labels, mesh, points, splat, image, transform, array), pattern with placeholders, frame, units, labels, layout for raw arrays, modality "mask": {"type": "labels", "pattern": "Task04_Hippocampus/labelsTr/{id}.nii.gz", "labels": {"1": "anterior", "2": "posterior"}} license spdx, commercial, redistribution, requires_agreement, note, source_url {"spdx": "CC-BY-SA-4.0", "commercial": true, "redistribution": "allowed"} citation, homepage, pairing, size_mb, tags provenance and discovery samples explicit list when patterns cannot derive it the four SimpleITK excerpts questions non-empty on a draft: what a human must confirm scan output

The 43 bundled manifests live in src/pardesline/data/manifests/; pl.describe(name) prints one; pl.Manifest.load(path) reads yours. A manifest never embeds data and never guesses: a .bin without a layout, a label map without labels, a mesh without units are questions, not defaults.

docs.title: Object
docs.text:
Every file becomes one of PointCloud, Mesh, Volume, LabelMap, Transform, Image, RawArray (subclasses of pardesline.Object), carrying:

  • frame (axes convention: LPS, RAS, sensor, Y-up; the affine for volumes) and units (mm, m);
  • labels for label maps and the layout for raw arrays;
  • license and provenance: the dataset, sample and role it came from, then every step applied;
  • conversions named after the job: volume.segment(), mask.to_mesh(label), volume.to_mesh(isovalue), mesh.to_points(), points.to_mesh(), points.align(moving), volume.align(moving), clean(), decimate(), smooth(), downsample(), normals();
  • the libraries themselves: to_open3d(), to_pyvista(), to_sitk(), to_numpy();
  • save(path) writes the file and a .pardesline.json sidecar; load of such a file reads the sidecar back.

Conversions are exact when they can be (a label boundary, a DICOM series to a volume) and say so when they are not (Poisson reconstruction is lossy and parametric; the sidecar records depth and density_quantile).

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text:
pl.catalog() is the typed list of 19 modules, 73 methods and 371 parameters (src/pardesline/catalog/data/*.json): name, type, default, range, options, description, and since 0.3 the rationale for each default and the data it was validated on (_defaults.json). pl.run("module.method", file, **params) validates before anything runs: unknown names, wrong types and out-of-range values raise ParameterError with the accepted list. obj.run(...) does the same and records the step. pl.describe("module.method") prints all of it.

Every method is a script under pardesline.ops with an argparse CLI (python -m pardesline.ops.registration.ransac_icp_pipeline --input ... --moving ... --output ...), kept byte-identical to the PardesLine platform so results match between the laptop and the hosted version.

docs.title: Standardization
docs.text:
What "standardized" means here, concretely:

  • Typed roles: a file is a volume, a label map, a mesh, a point cloud, a splat, an image or a raw array, and the type decides the conversions and the algorithms.
  • Frame and units are known before you compute: LPS millimetres for medical volumes (from the header), the sensor frame in metres for KITTI sweeps (from the manifest), Y-up metres for the bunny.
  • Labels have names; layouts turn headerless arrays into point clouds.
  • Standard files on export: PLY for points, meshes and splats; MetaImage for volumes and label maps; sidecars next to each; a manifest for the folder (ds.export(folder)).
  • Patient-level splits (ds.split(by="patient")) and licence on every object.

What it does not do: resample to a common spacing, reorient to a canonical axis order, normalise intensities. Those are algorithm choices (see pyvista_volume_processing, simpleitk_registration) and the medical-volumes guide explains when to make them.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: ds.license / obj.license is a License with spdx, commercial, redistribution, requires_agreement, note. Gated sources (AbdomenAtlas, CT-RATE) need your own Hub token after accepting the terms; non-commercial sources are flagged; sources without a standard licence print a warning and the owner's terms. Nothing is mirrored by pardesline: every loader fetches from the owner.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: pardesline mcp serves the same datasets, objects and catalog as tools for AI agents, plus the twenty expert guides. See MCP server.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install pardesline                 # core: catalog, object model, datasets, CLI; no native libraries
pip install "pardesline[local]"        # + Open3D, PyVista, SciPy, scikit-image, pycpd: points, meshes, LiDAR, SDF
pip install "pardesline[medical]"      # + SimpleITK: volumes, DICOM series, registration, segmentation
pip install "pardesline[hf]"           # + huggingface_hub: datasets on the Hub
pip install "pardesline[mcp]"          # + mcp: the local server for AI agents
pip install "pardesline[all]"          # everything above

Linux x86_64 / aarch64 macOS arm64 Windows x86_64 Core (pardesline) 3.10 – 3.13 3.10 – 3.13 3.10 – 3.13 [local], [all] 3.10 – 3.13 3.10 – 3.13 3.10 – 3.13

The native extras depend on Open3D wheels: Open3D 0.20 (September 2026) covers Python 3.10 to 3.13, 0.19 covers 3.10 to 3.12. pardesline 0.2.0 on PyPI pins Open3D below 0.20, so on Python 3.13 use a 3.12 interpreter or install from main until 0.3.0 ships:

pip install "pardesline[all] @ git+https://github.com/pardesline/pardesline"

conda create -n pl python=3.12

docs.title: Where files go
docs.text:
• Datasets: ~/.cache/pardesline/datasets/<name>/ (pl.set_cache_dir(...) or PARDESLINE_CACHE to move it).
  • Outputs of algorithms: a temporary folder unless pl.set_output_dir(...) or output= is given; obj.save(path) writes where you say.
  • Logs: stderr through loguru; PARDESLINE_LOG=DEBUG for the HTTP Range and archive details.

docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix MissingDependency: SimpleITK the [medical] extra is not installed pip install "pardesline[medical]" No matching distribution found for open3d Python version without an Open3D wheel use 3.10 – 3.13 with Open3D 0.20, or 3.10 – 3.12 with 0.19 ImportError: libGL.so.1 on a headless Linux box Open3D / VTK need the GL runtime apt-get install libgl1 libegl1 libglib2.0-0 libgomp1 libxrender1 libsm6 PyVista renders nothing in CI or over SSH no display PYVISTA_OFF_SCREEN=true, use Plotter(off_screen=True) and screenshot() HTTP 429 from the Hugging Face Hub when listing a large repo anonymous rate limit huggingface-cli login; the bundled manifests scope their listings to sub-folders HTTP 429 from Zenodo too many small Range requests the archive source already groups contiguous members and retries with backoff; wait a minute licence unknown - check the terms warning the source states terms outside a standard licence read ds.describe(); the warning is the point: nothing is guessed does not accept '.gz' files pardesline 0.2.0 checked only the last suffix fixed on main (.nii.gz accepted wherever .nii is); until 0.3.0, decompress or install from main

Still stuck: GitHub Discussions, or open an issue with the output of pardesline version and the full log.

docs.title: 5-minute tutorial
docs.text: Everything below ran on 2026-10-16 with pip install "pardesline[all]". The first run downloads 19 MB (RIRE) and 28 MB (hippocampus).

docs.title: 1. A dataset, and what it knows about itself
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

ds = pl.load("msd_task04_hippocampus")  # nothing is downloaded yet
print(ds.describe())

msd_task04_hippocampus  -  Medical Segmentation Decathlon, Task04 Hippocampus
  ...
  licence: CC-BY-SA-4.0 (CC-BY-SA 4.0 as stated in the archive's dataset.json ...)
  cite:    Antonelli M., Reinke A., Bakas S., et al. The Medical Segmentation Decathlon. Nat Commun 13:4128, 2022. ...
  samples: pattern-derived, paired by id
  roles:
    mri          volume     MR image (NIfTI, LPS mm from the header); split Tr = labelled, Ts = test
    mask         labels     Label map (training cases only)  [labels 1=anterior, 2=posterior]

The roles come from the manifest, so you know before downloading anything that mask is a label map with two named labels, in the frame and units of the NIfTI header, under CC-BY-SA 4.0.

docs.title: 2. One sample, one object
docs.text:
case = ds.filter(split="Tr")[0]  # the first labelled case
mri, mask = case.mri, case.mask  # fetched now: two files out of the 28 MB tar
print(mask.info())  # {'size': (35, 51, 35), 'spacing': (1.0, 1.0, 1.0), ...}
print(mask.labels)  # {1: 'anterior', 2: 'posterior'}

mri is a Volume, mask a LabelMap. Both know their frame (LPS millimetres), their licence and where they came from (obj.provenance).

docs.title: 3. A label becomes a surface
docs.text:
anterior = mask.to_mesh(label=1)  # exact boundary of label 1, world coordinates
anterior = anterior.smooth()  # Taubin smoothing, catalog defaults (20 iterations, pass band 0.1)
anterior.save("anterior.stl")  # + anterior.stl.pardesline.json: frame, licence, both steps

Open the sidecar: it records to_mesh(label=1) then pyvista_mesh_processing.pv_smooth_taubin with every parameter, the duration and the package version. Hand the surface to the library you prefer:

anterior.to_pyvista().plot()  # PyVista
o3d_mesh = anterior.to_open3d()  # Open3D TriangleMesh

docs.title: 4. Registration, across modalities
docs.text:
s = pl.load("rire_brain")[0]  # CT + MR T1 of one head; the licence line is printed
moved = s.ct.align(s.mr_t1)  # simpleitk_registration.rigid, Mattes mutual information
print(moved.transform["sub_transforms"][0]["rotation_deg"])  # [0.34, -0.35, -4.38]
print(moved.provenance[-1]["params"])  # {} = every catalog default was used

moved is the MR resampled on the CT grid. print(pl.describe("simpleitk_registration.rigid")) lists the fourteen parameters with their ranges and the reason for each default; pass any of them to align.

docs.title: 5. Your own files and folders
docs.text:
ct = pl.load("scan.nii.gz")  # a Volume; frame from the header
pts = pl.load("sweep.bin", layout=dict(dtype="float32", shape="(N,4)", columns=["x", "y", "z", "i"]))
ds = pl.scan("/data/my_study")  # drafts a manifest, asks what it cannot know

pl.scan raises NeedsConfirmation with the questions (units? label names? licence?) and the draft path; answer them once (pl.load(draft, units="mm", ...)) and the manifest is saved for next time. See Standardize a folder of medical images.
