docs.title: Rules the package enforces (do not fight them, explain them)
docs.text:
• Never guess silently. A format that carries no unit or axis convention (PLY, STL, OBJ, PCD, VTK grids) gives obj.units is None. Declare with obj.with_frame("Z-up", "mm") or a manifest. Volumes read LPS/mm from their header; glTF is Y-up/m by specification.
  • Parameters are validated before anything runs against the catalog (type, range, choices, unknown names with a "did you mean"). Read the error: it lists what is accepted.
  • Two-input methods need moving= (registration). Without it the call raises instead of self-aligning a synthetic copy.
  • A folder needs a confirmed manifest. pl.load(folder) raises NeedsConfirmation listing licence / units / labels questions; answer them in the call, in the saved draft, interactively, or pass assume=True.
  • Licences travel with the data. ds.license.describe(); bundled public datasets whose terms are not established say TO CONFIRM.

docs.title: Errors (all derive from pl.PardesLineError, each has .code)
docs.text: ParameterError (bad or unknown parameter), CatalogError (unknown module/method), RunError (script failed: .returncode, .log, .command), MissingDependency (install an extra), ManifestError, FetchError (download or checksum), NeedsConfirmation (.questions, .draft_path). FileNotFoundError for missing inputs.

docs.title: Quick facts
docs.text:
19 modules, 73 methods, 371 parameters (pl.catalog()), 43 bundled datasets (pl.datasets(): 35 medical - DICOM, NIfTI, MetaImage, npz, STL, splats - over https, Hugging Face, remote archives by HTTP Range, S3, TCIA and URL indexes), outputs default to pl.output_dir() (system temp, change with pl.set_output_dir), downloads cache in ~/.cache/pardesline (PARDESLINE_CACHE). pl.o3d, pl.pv, pl.sitk, pl.np are the real libraries when installed, the cloud-executed mirrors otherwise.

Source: skills/using-pardesline/SKILL.md, one of the twenty skills served by pardesline mcp; published on 2026-10-14.

docs.title: Align two scans in python
docs.text: title: How to align two scans in Python (meshes, point clouds, CT and MRI volumes) description: Align two meshes, two point clouds or two volumes in Python with one call that picks the right method for the object type: RANSAC + ICP for geometry, mutual-information rigid registration for volumes, Coherent Point Drift for non-rigid cases; the transform and how to apply it.

docs.title: How to align two scans in Python
docs.text:
align(moving) is defined on every object type and picks the method that fits it:

You have Call Method underneath two point clouds target.align(moving) FPFH + RANSAC, then point-to-plane ICP (registration.ransac_icp_pipeline) two meshes target.to_points().align(moving.to_points()) same, on sampled points two volumes (CT, MR, any modality) fixed.align(moving) SimpleITK rigid, Mattes mutual information (simpleitk_registration.rigid) a scan and an atlas with labels scan.align(atlas) then transfer labels see Label a scan from an atlas organ motion, breathing rigid first, then deformable_registration.cpd_deformable (points) or simpleitk_registration.bspline (volumes) non-rigid 
import pardesline as pl

a = pl.load("scan_a.stl")  # Mesh
b = pl.load("scan_b.stl")
pa, pb = a.to_points(num_points=50000, seed=1), b.to_points(num_points=50000, seed=1)
moved = pa.align(pb)  # pb moved onto pa
T = moved.transform["transformation_matrix"]  # 4x4, apply it to b's vertices to move the mesh

docs.title: Applying the transform to the original mesh
docs.text:
import numpy as np

T = np.asarray(T)
verts = b.to_numpy()
moved_verts = (T[:3, :3] @ verts.T).T + T[:3, 3]

Or let PyVista do it: b.to_pyvista().transform(T, inplace=False).

docs.title: Units first
docs.text: Both inputs must be in the same units and the frame must be known: a.frame, a.units; with_frame("sensor", "mm") to declare them. A millimetre scan against a metre scan "aligns" to nonsense with a plausible-looking fitness.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Fitness caps at the overlap and lies when the threshold is wide; inlier RMSE should approach the noise level; landmarks not used by the algorithm are the real test. Why our defaults work has the numbers for each method.

Related: Register two point clouds with ICP · Register CT and MRI · Fix ICP

docs.title: Convert a dicom series to nifti in python
docs.text: title: How to convert a DICOM series to NIfTI in Python description: Convert a folder of DICOM slices into one NIfTI (or MetaImage) volume in Python with the geometry preserved: pl.load(folder).save("scan.nii.gz"), with SimpleITK underneath and a sidecar recording frame, spacing and provenance.

docs.title: How to convert a DICOM series to NIfTI in Python
docs.text:
A DICOM series is a folder of slices; a NIfTI is one file with the spacing, origin and direction in the header. pardesline reads the series with SimpleITK's series reader (slices ordered by position, geometry from the headers) and writes any volume format you name.

import pardesline as pl

ct = pl.load("/data/patient01/CT")  # a folder of .dcm files -> one Volume
print(ct.info())  # size, spacing, origin, pixel type, modality from the headers
ct.save("patient01_ct.nii.gz")  # NIfTI; .nii, .mha, .nrrd, .vti work the same way

The sidecar patient01_ct.nii.gz.pardesline.json records the source folder, the frame (LPS millimetres, the DICOM convention), the licence if the object has one and the conversion step.

docs.title: From a TCIA collection or a bundled dataset
docs.text:
s = pl.load("tcia_prostate_3t")[0]
s.mr.save(f"{s.id.replace('/', '_')}_t2.nii.gz")

For many series: pl.load("tcia_prostate_3t").take(10).export("./prostate_std") writes MetaImage volumes with sidecars; MetaImage and NIfTI carry the same geometry, and every reader (SimpleITK, ITK, nibabel, MONAI, TorchIO) opens both.

docs.title: Checks worth doing
docs.text:
import SimpleITK as sitk

img = ct.to_sitk()
print(img.GetSpacing(), img.GetDirection())  # anisotropic slices and oblique acquisitions show here
  • Slices with varying spacing or missing instances make the series reader warn; ct.info()["size"] should match the slice count.
  • Multi-frame DICOM (one file with all frames) and enhanced CT/MR are read by the same reader.
  • Orientation: NIfTI stores RAS, DICOM LPS; SimpleITK converts on write and on read, so the Volume.frame stays LPS in pardesline. Do not reorient voxel arrays by hand.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
pardesline reads pixel data and geometry; it does not de-identify. Remove identifiers before the data reaches any tool (DICOM PS3.15 basic profile or your institution's process).

Related: Download a TCIA collection · Guide: medical volumes · Standardize a folder

docs.title: Convert a point cloud to gaussian splats in python
docs.text: title: How to convert a point cloud to Gaussian splats in Python (3DGS PLY) description: Initialise 3D Gaussians from a point cloud or mesh in Python and write a 3DGS-compatible PLY that opens in gsplat, Nerfstudio and the Hugging Face viewers: scale from k-nearest neighbours, identity rotation, SH degree-0 colour; load the bundled splat datasets.

docs.title: How to convert a point cloud to Gaussian splats in Python
docs.text:
A Gaussian splat is a point with a covariance (three log-scales and a quaternion), an opacity and spherical-harmonics colour. The reference script initialises one Gaussian per point, which is the standard starting state of a 3DGS optimisation and already renders as a soft surface.

pip install "pardesline[local]"
python skills/gaussian-splatting/scripts/points_to_gaussians.py cloud.ply splat.ply --k 4
python examples/points_to_gaussians_bunny/run.py           # the bunny: 50 000 Gaussians, 12 MB

In Python, with the script's functions:

import pardesline as pl

points = pl.load("open3d_bunny")[0].mesh.to_points(num_points=50000, seed=1)
# the script reads any point cloud or mesh pardesline opens (raw arrays with --layout)

Per Gaussian: scale = log(mean distance to the k nearest neighbours) on the three axes, rotation = identity quaternion, opacity = logit(0.1), f_dc = (rgb - 0.5) / 0.2820948 with f_rest = 0. The PLY has the 62 floats per vertex the reference implementation expects; --sh-degree 3 adds the higher-order coefficients as zeros.

docs.title: Reading splats back
docs.text:
splat = pl.load("splat.ply")  # a PointCloud: x, y, z are standard properties
centres = splat.to_numpy()

The extra properties (scale_0..2, rot_0..3, opacity, f_dc_*) stay in the file; a splat viewer renders them. Two bundled datasets ship fitted splats: c3vd_endoscopy_splats (colonoscopy scenes) and hf_kitti360_gs_subset (street chunks as .npy arrays with a layout).

docs.title: From here
docs.text:
Optimising the Gaussians against images needs a renderer (gsplat, the reference CUDA code); the guide explains the parameters, the densification schedule and how medical volumes map onto the representation. A first-class Splat kind (render, convert to points, metrics) is on the roadmap.

Related: Guide: Gaussian splatting · 3D representations

docs.title: How to download a medical imaging dataset in Python
docs.text:
Pick a name from the datasets catalog, load it, touch a sample. The licence and the citation come with it; files are verified and cached; archives are read by HTTP Range so one case costs one case.

import pardesline as pl

print([m.name for m in pl.datasets(tag="ct")])  # the CT datasets

ds = pl.load("msd_task09_spleen")  # lazy: the 1.6 GB tar is indexed, not downloaded
print(ds.describe())  # roles, labels, licence CC-BY-SA-4.0, citation
case = ds.filter(split="Tr")[0]  # the first labelled case
ct, mask = case.ct, case.mask  # two files fetched now (about 30 MB)
print(ct.info(), mask.labels)  # {'size': ..., 'spacing': ...}  {1: 'spleen'}

Expected output:

{'size': (512, 512, 55), 'spacing': (0.976, 0.976, 5.0), 'origin': (...), 'pixel_type': '32-bit float', ...} {1: 'spleen'}

docs.title: The whole dataset, or a subset
docs.text:
ds.take(10).fetch_all()  # download the first ten cases now (returns the file count)
ds.sample(20, seed=0).fetch_all()  # a reproducible random subset
pl.load("msd_task09_spleen").fetch_all()  # everything (1.6 GB)

From the command line: pardesline fetch msd_task09_spleen and pardesline export msd_task09_spleen ./out.

docs.title: Where it went
docs.text: ~/.cache/pardesline/datasets/msd_task09_spleen/ keeps the original files and the archive index; pl.set_cache_dir("/data/cache") or PARDESLINE_CACHE=/data/cache moves it. ds.export("./spleen_std") writes standard MetaImage files with sidecars instead.

docs.title: Patient-level splits
docs.text:
train, test = ds.filter(split="Tr").split(by="id", fractions=(0.8, 0.2), seed=0)

split(by=...) groups by a sample field before splitting, so a patient never appears on both sides.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text: Message Meaning Do licence unknown - check the terms the source has no standard licence read the note in ds.describe(); the warning is deliberate requires_agreement / HTTP 401 on a Hub repo gated dataset (AbdomenAtlas, CT-RATE) accept the terms on the Hub, huggingface-cli login, retry HTTP 429 from Zenodo too many requests the loader retries with backoff; wait a minute the first load of an MSD task takes minutes the tar index is built by walking headers cached afterwards; archives below 64 MB are downloaded whole on main

docs.title: Datasets not bundled
docs.text:
BraTS (Synapse DUA), ModelNet, ShapeNet, ScanNet (registration-gated): see the FAQ. Any other public source: Hugging Face repos, TCIA collections, s3://openneuro.org/dsXXXXXX, or a remote zip / tar URL.

Related: Datasets catalog · Concepts: manifest · Standardize your own folder

docs.title: Download a tcia collection in python
docs.text: title: How to download a TCIA collection in Python description: Download DICOM series from The Cancer Imaging Archive in Python without the NBIA Data Retriever: tcia://Collection through the public REST API, series as folders, one volume per series, licence attached.

docs.title: How to download a TCIA collection in Python
docs.text:
The Cancer Imaging Archive serves public collections through the NBIA REST API: getSeries lists the series of a collection, getImage returns one series as a zip of DICOM files. pardesline wraps both as a dataset source: every series is a sample whose role is a DICOM folder that opens as one Volume.

import pardesline as pl

ds = pl.load("tcia_pancreas_ct")  # bundled: Pancreas-CT, 82 CTs, CC-BY-3.0
print(ds.describe())
s = ds[0]
print(s.id, s.fields)  # PatientID / Modality / SeriesInstanceUID, ImageCount, ...
ct = s.ct  # the series zip is fetched and unpacked once (about 100 MB)
print(ct.info())  # one volume, LPS mm from the DICOM headers
ct.save("pancreas_0001.nii.gz")  # NIfTI + sidecar

Four collections ship with a manifest: tcia_pancreas_ct, tcia_lidc_idri, tcia_nsclc_radiomics_dicom, tcia_prostate_3t.

docs.title: Any public collection
docs.text:
ds = pl.load("tcia://Pancreas-CT")  # same as the bundled one
ds = pl.load("tcia://CPTAC-PDA/CT,MR")  # a collection, restricted to the CT and MR modalities

The collection name is the one on cancerimagingarchive.net. Restricted collections answer 401: they need the TCIA Data Retriever and your credentials, which pardesline does not handle. Licences are per collection (most CC BY 3.0 or 4.0, some non-commercial): the drafted manifest asks you to confirm it from the collection page, the bundled ones record it.

docs.title: Segmentations and RT structures
docs.text: LIDC-IDRI and NSCLC-Radiomics also carry DICOM SEG and RTSTRUCT series; they appear as their own samples (Modality field SEG / RTSTRUCT). Converting them to label maps on the CT grid is not built in yet: pydicom-seg and rt-utils do it from the folder s.path("seg") returns.

docs.title: Size and time
docs.text:
describe_dataset and s.fields["ImageCount"] tell you the slice count before downloading. LIDC-IDRI is 122 GB in all; ds.filter(Modality="CT").take(5).fetch_all() gets five CTs.

Related: Convert a DICOM series to NIfTI · Datasets catalog

docs.title: How to extract DINOv3 features from medical images in Python
docs.text:
A frozen DINOv3 (or DINOv2) backbone turns an image into a grid of patch embeddings that already separate tissue, bone, instrument and background without any medical training. The reference script extracts them, colours them by PCA so you can see what the model sees, and saves them for a head.

pip install "pardesline[local]" torch transformers pillow
python skills/dinov3-dense-features/scripts/dinov3_features.py frame.png --out ./feats --model facebook/dinov2-small --size 448
python skills/dinov3-dense-features/scripts/dinov3_features.py ./echo_frames --out ./feats --model facebook/dinov3-vits16-pretrain-lvd1689m

Output per image: <name>.npz with patches (H/p, W/p, d) float16, cls (d,), the grid and the size, and <name>_pca.png. DINOv2 weights download without an agreement; DINOv3 weights are gated: accept the licence on the Hub, then huggingface-cli login. Grayscale images are replicated to three channels; --size is rounded to the patch size (14 for DINOv2, 16 for DINOv3).

The KITTI example runs it on a camera frame read out of the KITTI zip by HTTP Range:

docs.title: From a pardesline dataset
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

frame = next(s for s in pl.load("kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001") if "image_left" in s.roles)
image = frame.image_left  # an Image object: image.path is the PNG

Volumes: extract per slice (vol.to_numpy()[z] to PNG) or use the 3D route (JEPA) when you need volumetric features.

docs.title: A head on top
docs.text: dinov3_faster_rcnn.py puts a Faster R-CNN detection head on the frozen backbone (the echocardiography use case of the DINOv3 guide); a linear or small convolutional head on the patch grid gives a segmentation. Keep the backbone frozen first: it is the point of the method, and it trains in minutes on CPU for small datasets.

docs.title: Coming
docs.text:
One-line model access (pl.load_model("dinov3"), pl.run(model, dataset)) through the model registry; this page's commands keep working.

Related: DINOv3 model page · Models

docs.title: How to fix ICP that does not converge
The symptom
docs.text: registration_icp returns a fitness of 0.9 and the clouds are visibly misaligned; or the fitness is 0.05 and nothing moved; or it converges to a mirrored pose. On the Stanford bunny against a copy rotated 35° with 70 % overlap and 0.5 % noise, the tutorial call ends 32.0° off with a fitness of 0.98 (the experiment).

docs.title: The parameters behind it
docs.text: Parameter (Open3D) What goes wrong What to set init (initial transform) ICP is a local optimiser; its basin is a few degrees and a fraction of the object size. From the identity, a 35° offset converges to the nearest wrong minimum. A global stage first: FPFH features + RANSAC. That is what align() does. max_correspondence_distance Too wide (0.02 m on a 0.15 m bunny): every point finds a partner, fitness looks excellent, the pose is wrong. Too tight: no correspondences, nothing moves. Tie it to the data: 1.5× a voxel of 1.3 % of the bounding-box diagonal for the coarse pass, 0.4× for the fine pass. estimation_method Point-to-point zigzags and stalls on smooth surfaces. Point-to-plane with target normals; point-to-point only when normals are unreliable (sparse LiDAR). units Millimetres read as metres make every distance 1000× too small. obj.frame.units; with_frame("sensor", "mm"). overlap The 30 % of points without a counterpart pull the solution. A tight fine-pass threshold; judge by inlier RMSE on the overlap, not by fitness. symmetry Cylinders, spheres, vertebral bodies have several equally good poses. ransac_n=4, a prior pose, more context in the scan.

docs.title: The one-liner that already handles it
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

target, moving = pl.load("scan_a.ply"), pl.load("scan_b.ply")
aligned = target.align(moving)
print(aligned.transform["ransac_fitness"], aligned.transform["inlier_rmse"])

align = registration.ransac_icp_pipeline: voxel from the bounding box, FPFH at 5× the voxel, RANSAC with the mutual filter at 1.5× the voxel, then point-to-plane ICP at 0.4× the voxel. Every value and its reason: pl.describe("registration.ransac_icp_pipeline").

docs.title: Still off? Walk the diagnostics
docs.text:
1. ransac_fitness below 0.3: the features are meaningless. The voxel is wrong for the data: pass voxel_size = 2–5× the point spacing. Check the units first.
  2. Good RANSAC, bad ICP: the fine threshold is too wide for the noise or the overlap: icp_threshold_factor=0.2–0.3.
  3. Flat scene: point-to-plane slides along planes: icp_estimation_method="point_to_point".
  4. Converges to a mirror: symmetric object; verify with a target registration error on landmarks the algorithm did not see.
  5. Different scale: ransac_with_scaling=True once (photogrammetry vs scanner), then fix the scale and run rigid again.

docs.title: Measuring instead of guessing
docs.text:
The registration_eval.py script applies a known transform with noise and partial overlap to any cloud and prints fitness, inlier RMSE, rotation and translation error, Chamfer and HD95: the way to tune on your data before trusting a number.

Related: Register two point clouds · Why our defaults work · Benchmarks

docs.title: Fix ransac global registration that fails
docs.text: title: How to fix RANSAC global registration that fails (FPFH features, voxel size, mutual filter) description: Why FPFH + RANSAC global registration returns a low fitness or a wrong pose on real scans: voxel size, feature radius, units, symmetry, the mutual filter; what pardesline sets and how to diagnose with ransac_fitness.

docs.title: How to fix RANSAC global registration that fails
The symptom
docs.text: ransac_fitness is 0.05 and the pose is random; or RANSAC takes a minute and returns a pose that ICP then "refines" into a wrong minimum.

docs.title: Causes, in the order to check them
docs.text:
1. Units. A millimetre cloud with a voxel chosen for metres has one point per cell. obj.frame.units, then with_frame(units="mm").
  2. Voxel size. Features are computed on the downsampled cloud. Too small: the FPFH histograms describe noise. Too large: there is nothing left to describe. Rule: 2–5× the point spacing, about 1 % of the bounding-box diagonal. align() picks 1.3 % of the diagonal when voxel_size=0.
  3. Feature radius. FPFH needs about five voxels of support (fpfh_radius_factor=5); normals need two (normal_radius_factor=2). Larger radii blur partial views, smaller ones make every point look the same.
  4. Mutual filter off. Without it, one-directional matches flood RANSAC with false correspondences; mutual_filter=True is the single most effective setting on symmetric or repetitive parts.
  5. Overlap below 30 %. FPFH cannot match what is not there. Crop both clouds to the region that overlaps, or acquire more.
  6. Symmetry. Cylinders, spheres, planes: several poses score the same. ransac_n=4, a prior from the fixture, or landmarks.

docs.title: What pardesline sets
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

coarse = target.run("registration.ransac_global", moving=moving)  # inspect the global stage alone
print(coarse.transform["fitness"], coarse.transform["inlier_rmse"])
print(pl.describe("registration.ransac_global"))  # every parameter with its rationale

voxel_size=0 (auto), normal_radius_factor=2, fpfh_radius_factor=5, distance_threshold_factor=1.5, mutual_filter=True, ransac_n=3, edge_length_threshold=0.9, ransac_max_iteration=100000, ransac_confidence=0.999. The rationale for each is on the registration page.

docs.title: A quick experiment
docs.text:
for v in (0.5, 1, 2, 4):  # multiples of the auto voxel, in file units
    r = target.run("registration.ransac_global", moving=moving, voxel_size=v * 0.013 * diag)
    print(v, r.transform["fitness"], r.transform["inlier_rmse"])

Pick the voxel with the highest fitness at a sane RMSE, then run the full pipeline with it.

Related: Fix ICP that does not converge · Guide: point-cloud registration

docs.title: Label a scan from an atlas in python
docs.text: title: How to label a scan from an atlas in Python (atlas-based segmentation of point clouds and meshes) description: Transfer labels from a labelled atlas to an unlabelled 3D scan in Python: rigid registration with RANSAC + ICP, nearest-structure label transfer, per-label surfaces and volumes, and the agreement measured on a known case; the reference script and the one-liners behind it.

docs.title: How to label a scan from an atlas in Python
docs.text:
Atlas-based labelling: register a labelled reference shape (the atlas) onto a new scan, give each scan point the label of its nearest atlas structure, rebuild per-label surfaces. It works for ultrasound reconstructions, CBCT teeth, bones, LiDAR objects: anything where the anatomy or the part varies little between instances.

import pardesline as pl

scan = pl.load("new_scan.ply")  # unlabelled, the fixed reference
atlas = pl.load("atlas.ply")  # labelled: one label per point, same order as a labels.npy
moved_atlas = scan.align(atlas)  # the atlas in the scan's frame; point order is kept

Labels travel with point order, so after registration the nearest atlas point to each scan point gives the label:

import numpy as np
import open3d as o3d

labels = np.load("labels.npy")  # (N_atlas,) ints
tree = o3d.geometry.KDTreeFlann(moved_atlas.to_open3d())
scan_pts = scan.to_numpy()
scan_labels = np.array([labels[tree.search_knn_vector_3d(p, 1)[1][0]] for p in scan_pts])

Then per structure: pl.load(...) of the filtered points, to_mesh() for a surface, to_pyvista().volume for a volume.

docs.title: The reference script
docs.text:
atlas_label_transfer.py does all of it, with a tolerance on the transfer distance, per-label Poisson surfaces, volumes, and an evaluation against the truth when it is known. The bunny example runs it on a synthetic case: the bunny labelled into head, ears, body and base is the atlas; a rotated, noisy, sub-sampled copy is the scan; the transfer agrees with the truth on 99.4 % of the points with a 0.06° pose error.

python examples/atlas_label_transfer_bunny/run.py
python skills/atlas-label-transfer/scripts/atlas_label_transfer.py --atlas atlas.ply --atlas-labels labels.npy --scan scan.ply --out ./transfer

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
• Registration off: see Fix ICP that does not converge; on a symmetric atlas (a single tooth) add context (the arch).
  • Labels bleed across boundaries: the transfer tolerance is too large for the point spacing; --tolerance in file units, about 2× the spacing.
  • Shape differs (a bigger liver, a missing tooth): rigid cannot follow it; run deformable_registration.cpd_deformable after the rigid stage, then transfer.

Related: Guide: atlas label transfer · Align two scans · Evaluation metrics

docs.title: Load a hugging face 3d dataset in python
docs.text: title: How to load a Hugging Face 3D dataset in Python description: Load any Hugging Face Hub repository of 3D or medical files (NIfTI, PLY, GLB, npz) as typed objects in Python: bundled manifests for KiTS23, OpenMind, Objaverse, 3D Arena, BiomedSegFM, UniOcc, or hf://org/repo with a drafted manifest.

docs.title: How to load a Hugging Face 3D dataset in Python
docs.text: The Hub stores 3D files it cannot open: a repository of NIfTI, PLY or GLB files comes back from datasets.load_dataset as paths at best. pardesline lists the repository tree, groups files into samples with a manifest, and opens them as volumes, meshes, point clouds or label maps.

docs.title: A bundled Hub dataset
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

ds = pl.load("hf_kits23")  # neheller/KiTS-Challenge-Imaging, CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0
print(ds.describe())
case = ds[0]
print(case.roles)  # ['ct', 'mask']
mask = case.mask  # downloaded through huggingface_hub, cached in its cache
print(mask.labels)  # {1: 'kidney', 2: 'tumor', 3: 'cyst'}

Ten Hub datasets ship with a manifest (pl.datasets(scheme="hf")): KiTS23, OpenMind, NSCLC-Radiomics NIfTI, AbdomenAtlas mini, CT-RATE, BiomedSegFM, Objaverse (one shard), 3D Arena, UniOcc, KITTI-360 Gaussian splats.

docs.title: Any repository: hf://
docs.text:
ds = pl.load("hf://farrell236/NSCLC-Radiomics-NIFTI")  # a bundled manifest matches: used as is
ds = pl.load("hf://some-org/some-3d-repo")  # no manifest: the tree is listed and a draft is made

For an unknown repository the second call raises NeedsConfirmation with the questions the files cannot answer (which role is a label map and what its labels mean, the units of a mesh, the licence) and the path of the saved draft. Answer once:

ds = pl.load("hf://some-org/some-3d-repo", license="CC-BY-4.0", units="mm", labels={"mask": {1: "tumor"}})

or assume=True to load with unknowns left unknown (the objects carry None and a warning), or interactive=True to answer in the terminal. The confirmed manifest is saved next to the draft and reused next time. Large repositories: pl.scan("hf://org/repo", max_files=5000) limits the listing, and the bundled manifests scope their paths to sub-folders because listing a 266 721-file repository anonymously takes 15 minutes and ends in HTTP 429.

docs.title: Gated repositories
docs.text: AbdomenAtlas and CT-RATE require accepting the terms on the Hub. Then huggingface-cli login; the manifests mark requires_agreement: true and the loader explains the 401 otherwise.

docs.title: Raw arrays on the Hub
docs.text: BiomedSegFM ships .npz files; UniOcc ships occupancy grids. The manifests carry the layout (key, dtype, shape) that turns them into volumes, and allow_pickle stays off. See raw point clouds with a layout.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
Message Do HTTP 429 while listing log in (huggingface-cli login), or pass paths= in a manifest to scope the listing NeedsConfirmation answer the questions as keyword arguments, or interactive=True the repo has parquet tables, not files that is a datasets-style repo: use datasets.load_dataset; pardesline is for file-based 3D repos

Related: Datasets catalog · Standardize a folder · Contributing a manifest

docs.title: How to load raw .npy and .bin point clouds with a layout
docs.text:
A .bin file is numbers. Only you know that KITTI's are float32 (N, 4) with x, y, z, reflectance in the sensor frame in metres. pardesline refuses to guess and takes a layout:

import pardesline as pl

sweep = pl.load(
    "0000000000.bin",
    layout={"dtype": "float32", "shape": "(N,4)", "columns": ["x", "y", "z", "reflectance"]},
).with_frame("sensor", "m")
print(sweep.kind, sweep.to_numpy().shape)  # pointcloud (N, 3)
sweep.save("sweep.ply")  # PLY with reflectance as a property + sidecar with the layout

A (N,k) shape is points, an (a,b,c) shape is a grid; kind="volume" or kind="labels" forces it. For .npz, key= picks the array; allow_pickle stays off.

occ = pl.load(
    "frame.npz",
    layout={"key": "occ_label", "shape": "(200,200,16)", "spacing": [0.4, 0.4, 0.4]},
    kind="labels",
)
occ = occ.with_labels({0: "free", 1: "car", 2: "pedestrian"})
occ.to_mesh(label=1).save("cars.ply")

docs.title: In a manifest, once for the whole dataset
docs.text:
The bundled KITTI manifest declares the layout on the role, so every sweep opens without arguments:

drive = pl.load("kitti_raw_2011_09_26_drive_0001")
frame = next(s for s in drive if "lidar" in s.roles)
sweep = frame.lidar  # (N, 4) decoded through the manifest layout, sensor frame, metres
objects = sweep.run("lidar_scene_detection.object_clustering")

For your own folder of .bin files, pl.scan(folder) asks for the layout as a question; answer with layout={"lidar": {...}} or edit the manifest.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Point count: len(file) / (4 * 4) must be an integer for float32 (N,4); otherwise the dtype or the column count is wrong.
  • Scale: KITTI ranges reach 80 m; if to_numpy().max() is 80 000 the file is in millimetres.
  • Order: order="F" for Fortran-ordered grids (MATLAB exports).

Related: KITTI raw manifest · UniOcc occupancy grids · Concepts: object

docs.title: Reconstruct a surface from a point cloud in python
docs.text: title: How to reconstruct a surface from a point cloud in Python (Poisson, ball pivoting, alpha shapes) description: Point cloud to mesh in Python: clean the cloud, estimate oriented normals, Poisson reconstruction with density trimming so holes do not balloon, ball pivoting for thin structures, alpha shapes for convex-ish objects; what the defaults do and how to check the result.

docs.title: How to reconstruct a surface from a point cloud in Python
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

mesh = pl.load("open3d_bunny")[0].mesh
points = mesh.to_points(
    num_points=20000, seed=1
).clean()  # Poisson-disk sampling, statistical outlier removal
surface = points.to_mesh()  # Poisson, depth 9, density-trimmed at the 1 % quantile
surface.save("bunny_surface.ply")
print(surface.info(), surface.provenance[-1]["params"])

Your own scan: pl.load("scan.ply").clean().to_mesh(). The output is a clean, density-trimmed surface: Poisson closes the object, and the trimming removes the vertices with the least sample support, which is where it would balloon over holes and the unseen back side. It is lossy and parametric, and the sidecar records depth and density_quantile.

docs.title: Choosing the method
docs.text: Method Call Good for Watch out Poisson points.to_mesh() closed organic objects, scans with noise, 10k–1M points balloons over holes without trimming; needs oriented normals (estimated if missing) Ball pivoting points.run("point_cloud_reconstruction.ball_pivoting") thin structures, uniform sampling, interpolating the points exactly holes where the sampling is sparse; radius_factor relative to the point spacing Alpha shape points.run("point_cloud_reconstruction.alpha_shape", alpha=0.03) convex-ish objects, quick hulls with concavities alpha in file units: larger than the gaps, smaller than the concavities Convex hull points.run("point_cloud_reconstruction.convex_hull") bounding geometry no concavities

docs.title: Parameters that matter
docs.text:
• depth (Poisson): 9 gives 512 cells across the bounding cube; 8 is Open3D's default and blurs small features; 10–11 need hundreds of thousands of points. Benchmark.
  • density_quantile: 0.01 by default; 0.05–0.1 on very partial scans.
  • Normals: estimated at normal_radius=0.1 file units with normal_orient_k=15 when the cloud has none. Scans in millimetres need normal_radius scaled (about 5–10× the point spacing).

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import open3d as o3d

tree = o3d.geometry.KDTreeFlann(points.to_open3d())
d = [np.sqrt(tree.search_knn_vector_3d(p, 1)[2][0]) for p in surface.to_numpy()[::50]]
print("median vertex-to-cloud distance", np.median(d))  # should be at the noise level

A vertex far from any input point is a balloon: raise density_quantile.

Related: point_cloud_reconstruction · Why our defaults work · Guide: 3D representations

docs.title: Register ct and mri of the same patient in python
docs.text: title: How to register CT and MRI of the same patient in Python description: Rigid CT to MRI registration in Python with SimpleITK through one call: mutual information, multi-resolution, physical-shift optimizer scales; the transform in degrees and millimetres, the resampled volume, a checkerboard check, and what to do when it fails.

docs.title: How to register CT and MRI of the same patient in Python
docs.text:
Mean squares fails across modalities (bone is bright in CT and dark in T1); mutual information does not assume an intensity relation. The call below runs SimpleITK's rigid registration with Mattes MI, three resolution levels and optimizer scales from physical shift, which is what makes one learning rate work on any pair.

import pardesline as pl

s = pl.load("rire_brain")[0]  # CT 0.65x0.65x4 mm, MR T1 1.25x1.25x4 mm, 19 MB
moved = s.ct.align(s.mr_t1)  # fixed = CT, moving = MR; 8.8 s on a laptop
t = moved.transform["sub_transforms"][0]
print(t["rotation_deg"], t["translation_mm"])  # [0.34, -0.35, -4.38] [16.2, -33.1, -21.6]
moved.save("mr_on_ct.nii.gz")  # the MR resampled on the CT grid + sidecar

Your own volumes: pl.load("ct.nii.gz").align(pl.load("mr.nii.gz")), or a DICOM folder for either. The registration runs in physical space (origin, spacing, direction from the headers), so different spacings and fields of view need no resampling first.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
import pyvista as pv

ct, mr = s.ct.to_pyvista(), moved.to_pyvista()
p = pv.Plotter()
p.add_mesh(ct.slice("z"), cmap="gray")
p.add_mesh(mr.slice("z"), cmap="magma", opacity=0.5)
p.show()

Or s.ct.run("simpleitk_registration.difference_analysis", moving=moved) for a difference map. The clinical check is a target registration error on landmarks placed in both volumes and not used by the algorithm; RIRE reports about 1 mm for rigid brain CT/MR.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Do metric flat from the first iterations the initial offset is outside the capture range (above ~30° or different patient position) s.ct.run("simpleitk_registration.advanced_rigid", moving=s.mr_t1): exhaustive rotation search first converges, visibly wrong wrong centre initialisation when one field of view is much larger initializer="MOMENTS" noisy metric, jittery result too few samples on a small field of view sampling_percentage=0.05 to 0.15 same modality follow-up MI is overkill metric="mean_squares", faster scanner scale or shear not rigid simpleitk_registration.affine; deformation: bspline, demons

print(pl.describe("simpleitk_registration.rigid")) lists the fourteen parameters, their ranges and the reason for each default.

Related: Guide: multimodal rigid registration (a hand-written SimpleITK stack next to the one-liner, metric traced per iteration) · RIRE dataset · Why our defaults work

docs.title: Register two point clouds with icp in python
docs.text: title: How to register two point clouds with ICP in Python description: Rigid registration of two point clouds in Python with RANSAC on FPFH features followed by point-to-plane ICP, in one call with defaults that scale to the data: target.align(moving), the transform, fitness and RMSE, and how to verify the result.

docs.title: How to register two point clouds with ICP in Python
docs.text:
ICP alone only works from a nearby start. The call below runs global registration (FPFH features + RANSAC) first, then ICP, with every distance derived from the data's own scale.

import pardesline as pl

ds = pl.load("open3d_icp_demo")  # three indoor fragments, sensor frame, metres
pair = ds["pair_0_1"]
aligned = pair.target.align(pair.source)  # registration.ransac_icp_pipeline, catalog defaults
print(aligned.transform["fitness"], aligned.transform["inlier_rmse"])
print(aligned.transform["transformation_matrix"])  # 4x4, source -> target
aligned.save("source_on_target.ply")  # the moved cloud + sidecar with every parameter used

Your own files: pl.load("scan_a.ply").align(pl.load("scan_b.ply")). The result is the moving cloud in the target's frame; .transform holds the matrix, fitness, inlier RMSE and the RANSAC pre-pass numbers.

docs.title: Verify, do not trust fitness alone
docs.text:
• Fitness is the fraction of source points with a correspondence within the threshold: it caps at the overlap ratio and is high for any pose when the threshold is wide.
  • Inlier RMSE should approach the scanner's noise floor (1 mm for a structured-light scanner, 2–3 cm for automotive LiDAR).
  • With a known transform (phantom, synthetic test), the rotation error is arccos((trace(R_est R_true^T) - 1) / 2): the bunny example measures 0.14° against 32.0° for a textbook ICP call.
  • Look at it: aligned.to_pyvista() next to pair.target.to_pyvista() in one plotter.

docs.title: The parameters, when you need them
docs.text:
aligned = pair.target.align(
    pair.source, voxel_size=0.05, icp_threshold_factor=0.3, icp_estimation_method="point_to_point"
)
print(pl.describe("registration.ransac_icp_pipeline"))  # every parameter, range, default and why

voxel_size=0 (the default) picks 1.3 % of the bounding-box diagonal; every other distance is a multiple of it. The reasons are on the registration page and in Why our defaults work.

docs.title: Two stages separately
docs.text:
coarse = pair.target.run("registration.ransac_global", moving=pair.source)  # inspect the global pose
fine = pair.target.run("registration.icp_refinement", moving=coarse)  # then refine

Related: Fix ICP that does not converge · Fix RANSAC that fails · Guide: point-cloud registration

docs.title: Run a pretrained 3d segmentation model on your ct scans
docs.text: title: How to run a pretrained 3D segmentation model on your CT scans (nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator) with pardesline description: Run a pretrained 3D medical segmentation model on your CT scans in Python today: prepare the data in the nnU-Net layout from any pardesline dataset, run nnU-Net or TotalSegmentator, load the predictions back as label maps, measure Dice against the reference; and what the coming model registry changes.

docs.title: How to run a pretrained 3D segmentation model on your CT scans
docs.text:
Status

pardesline does not ship weights or an inference API yet. This page shows the working path today (prepare → run the model's own tool → load the result back) and what one-line model access will replace it with.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the data in the model's layout
docs.text:
pip install "pardesline[medical]"
python skills/medical-segmentation-models/scripts/prepare_nnunet_dataset.py msd_task09_spleen --out ./nnUNet_raw/Dataset509_Spleen --take 20
python skills/medical-segmentation-models/scripts/prepare_nnunet_dataset.py /data/my_cts --image ct --mask seg --out ./nnUNet_raw/Dataset900_Mine

The script writes imagesTr/<case>_0000.nii.gz, labelsTr/<case>.nii.gz and dataset.json (channel names, labels, number of cases) from any pardesline dataset or scanned folder: NIfTI, MetaImage, DICOM series and npz grids are converted with SimpleITK; several binary mask roles are merged into one label map in the order given. Split by patient before exporting (ds.split(by="patient")).

docs.title: 2. Run the model with its own tool
docs.text:
• nnU-Net v2: nnUNetv2_predict -i imagesTs -o preds -d 509 -c 3d_fullres with the trained or downloaded weights.
  • TotalSegmentator (117 structures on CT): TotalSegmentator -i case_0000.nii.gz -o seg_case --ml writes one multi-label NIfTI.

Both read NIfTI in physical coordinates, which is what the preparation step wrote.

docs.title: 3. Load the predictions back and measure
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

pred = pl.load("preds/spleen_10.nii.gz").as_labels({1: "spleen"})
case = pl.load("msd_task09_spleen")["spleen_10"]
surface = pred.to_mesh(label=1).smooth()
surface.save("spleen_10_pred.stl")

python skills/evaluation-metrics-3d/scripts/metrics3d.py --help        # dice, hd95, surface_dice with spacing

The metrics guide explains which numbers mean something; the threshold baseline is the comparison a model report should include.

docs.title: Why models fail on new scanners
docs.text: Spacing and field of view outside the training distribution, contrast phase, cropping, and label-definition mismatches (is the splenic vein spleen?) account for most failures. The medical segmentation models guide lists the checks: resample to the model's spacing, compare intensity histograms, run on a few cases with reference labels first.

docs.title: What changes with the model registry
docs.text:
A model manifest (source, weights URI, licence, input type, task, memory needs, provenance) and pl.load_model("totalsegmentator") / pl.run(model, dataset) will replace steps 1–3 with one call that returns LabelMap objects with the model's label names and provenance. Follow the tracking issue; model manifests can be written now from templates/new_model/.

Related: Models · Segment organs in a CT scan · MSD spleen dataset

docs.title: Segment organs in a ct scan in python
docs.text: title: How to segment organs in a CT scan in Python description: Segment structures in a CT volume in Python: Hounsfield windows with volume.segment(lower, upper), Otsu, connected components and watershed in one call each, the honest limits of thresholds against an expert label, and where learned organ segmentation models come in.

docs.title: How to segment organs in a CT scan in Python
docs.text:
Thresholds segment tissue classes, not organs: bone (300+ HU), soft tissue (30–200 HU), lung (−900 to −500 HU) separate well; the spleen from the liver does not. Start with the threshold, measure it against an expert label, then decide whether a model is needed.

import pardesline as pl

case = pl.load("msd_task09_spleen").filter(split="Tr")[0]
ct = case.ct  # CT in Hounsfield units, LPS mm
soft = ct.segment(lower=30, upper=200)  # LabelMap, label 1 = inside the window
blobs = soft.run("simpleitk_segmentation.connected_components", threshold=0.5, min_size=1000)
surface = blobs.as_labels().to_mesh(isovalue=0.5).smooth()
reference = case.mask.to_mesh(label=1).smooth()  # the expert spleen label

ct.segment() without bounds is Otsu (128 bins). Bone: ct.segment(lower=300, upper=3000). Lungs: ct.segment(lower=-950, upper=-500) then the two largest components.

docs.title: Measure before believing
docs.text:
import numpy as np

pred = blobs.to_numpy() > 0
truth = case.mask.to_numpy() == 1
dice = 2 * (pred & truth).sum() / (pred.sum() + truth.sum())
print(round(float(dice), 3))

The spleen example draws both surfaces: the threshold finds every soft-tissue organ, and the Dice against the spleen label is low. That is the baseline a learned model has to beat, and the number to put in a report before any model is trained. For Dice, HD95 and surface Dice with spacing, use metrics3d.py.

docs.title: Watershed when structures touch
docs.text:
parts = ct.run(
    "simpleitk_segmentation.watershed",
    threshold=30,
    upper_threshold=200,
    seed_radius=15,
    min_object_size=1000,
)

Markers are placed where the distance map exceeds seed_radius mm, so only objects at least twice that size become basins; dam lines are drawn between touching structures.

docs.title: MR, PET, 8-bit images
docs.text: MR has no absolute intensity scale: take bounds from percentiles of the volume (np.percentile(mr.to_numpy(), [60, 99])). PET SUV windows are per study. 8-bit windowed exports (the SimpleITK liver excerpt) need bounds in 0–255.

docs.title: Organs: use a model
docs.text:
Organ-level segmentation on CT is a solved problem for nnU-Net and TotalSegmentator-class models (117 structures). pardesline does not ship weights yet; prepare_nnunet_dataset.py writes any dataset in the nnU-Net layout, the model's output loads back as a LabelMap, and one-line model access is the top roadmap item.

Related: simpleitk_segmentation · Run a pretrained 3D segmentation model · Why our defaults work

docs.title: Standardize a folder of medical images in python
docs.text: title: How to standardize a folder of medical images in Python description: Turn a folder of NIfTI, DICOM, MetaImage, PLY or STL files into a dataset with typed roles, frames, units, label names and a licence in Python: pl.scan drafts a manifest, you confirm what the files cannot say, export writes standard files with sidecars.

docs.title: How to standardize a folder of medical images in Python
docs.text: "Standardize" means: every file typed (volume, label map, mesh, points), its frame and units known, label values named, the licence written down, samples grouped by patient, and standard files on disk with that information next to them. pardesline does it with a manifest that you confirm once.

docs.title: 1. Scan
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

draft = pl.scan("/data/my_study")  # reads headers, groups files by sub-folder and name prefix
print(draft.describe())
for q in draft.questions:
    print(q.field, "->", q.message, "| suggestion:", q.suggestion)

Typical questions: license (none found), roles.seg.labels (a label map with values 1, 2, 3 and no names), roles.scan.units (a mesh without units), pairing (what groups files into a sample: a patient folder, a name prefix). Suggestions come from what was found (a LICENSE file, the distinct label values, the folder layout) and are never applied silently.

docs.title: 2. Confirm, once
docs.text:
ds = pl.load(
    "/data/my_study",
    license="CC-BY-4.0",
    pairing="folder",
    labels={"seg": {1: "liver", 2: "tumor"}},
    units={"scan": "mm"},
)

The confirmed manifest is saved as /data/my_study/.pardesline-manifest.json (or manifest= to put it elsewhere) and pl.load("/data/my_study") uses it from now on. Alternatives: interactive=True asks in the terminal; assume=True loads with unknowns left unknown and warns; pardesline describe /data/my_study prints the draft.

docs.title: 3. Use it like any dataset
docs.text:
s = ds[0]
print(s.roles, s.ct.frame, s.seg.labels)
tumor = s.seg.to_mesh(label=2).smooth()
train, test = ds.split(by="patient", fractions=(0.8, 0.2), seed=0)

docs.title: 4. Export standard files
docs.text:
ds.export("/data/my_study_std")

One folder per sample; volumes and label maps as MetaImage (.mha), points and meshes as PLY, each with a .pardesline.json sidecar (frame, units, labels, licence, provenance) and a manifest.json for the folder. DICOM series become one volume each; .npz / .bin arrays are decoded through their layout.

docs.title: What standardization does not do by itself
docs.text: Resampling to a common spacing, reorienting to a canonical axis order and intensity normalisation change the data; they are explicit steps (pyvista_volume_processing, simpleitk_registration, your training transforms) and the sidecar records them when you run them.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
Situation Do files with identifiers (DICOM names, dates) de-identify before scanning (DICOM PS3.15); pardesline does not de-identify two volumes per patient with the same pattern refine the pattern in the manifest ({patient}/{phase}/ct.nii.gz) or set pairing a .bin or .npy without meaning answer layout={"lidar": {"dtype": "float32", "shape": "(N,4)", "columns": ["x","y","z","i"]}}

Related: Concepts: manifest · Guide: scanning a private folder · DICOM to NIfTI

docs.title: How to turn a segmentation mask into a mesh in Python
docs.text:
A label map's boundary at value k is an exact surface in the volume's world coordinates. Marching cubes on a label map at isovalue 0.5 between k and not-k gives it; the staircase is removed by Taubin smoothing, which keeps the volume; decimation then halves the triangle count without visible change.

import pardesline as pl

case = pl.load("msd_task04_hippocampus").filter(split="Tr")[0]
mask = case.mask  # LabelMap, labels {1: 'anterior', 2: 'posterior'}
anterior = mask.to_mesh(label=1)  # exact boundary, LPS millimetres
anterior = anterior.smooth().decimate()  # Taubin 20 iterations, then 50 % fewer triangles
anterior.save("hippocampus_anterior.stl")  # + .pardesline.json: frame, licence, the three steps

Your own mask: pl.load("seg.nii.gz").as_labels({1: "liver", 2: "tumor"}).to_mesh(label=2). A grey-level volume uses volume.to_mesh(isovalue=300) (bone on CT in Hounsfield units).

docs.title: What the sidecar says
docs.text:
{"step": "to_mesh", "label": 1, "label_name": "anterior", "isovalue": null, ...}
{"module": "pyvista_mesh_processing", "method": "pv_smooth_taubin", "params": {}, ...}
{"module": "pyvista_mesh_processing", "method": "pv_decimate", "params": {}, ...}

Empty params means every catalog default was used; pl.describe("pyvista_mesh_processing.pv_smooth_taubin") says what they are and why.

docs.title: Units and frames
docs.text: The mesh is in the volume's physical frame (LPS millimetres for NIfTI and DICOM through SimpleITK). To compare with a scanner mesh in RAS, flip x and y; obj.frame tells you which one you have. Volumes in millimetres from a mesh: anterior.to_pyvista().volume.

docs.title: Several labels, several meshes
docs.text:
for label, name in mask.labels.items():
    mask.to_mesh(label=label).smooth().save(f"hippocampus_{name}.stl")

TotalSegmentator ships one mask role per structure: s.liver.to_mesh() works without a label argument because the role has a single named label.

docs.title: When it looks wrong
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Do staircase surface no smoothing .smooth(); more iterations (n_iterations=40) for coarse slices small structures shrink Laplacian smoothing use .smooth() (Taubin); avoid pv_smooth_laplacian for thin anatomy holes in the surface the label touches the volume border pad the volume, or accept an open surface wrong size voxel indices instead of world coordinates to_mesh always uses world coordinates; check mask.info()["spacing"]

Related: Hippocampus example · Mesh processing · Guide: medical volumes

docs.text: title: Pretrained 3D and medical imaging models in Python: what pardesline ships and what is coming description: Reference implementations and expert guides for DINOv3 features, 3D JEPA pretraining, PointNet segmentation, VAE anomaly detection, nnU-Net preparation and 3D metrics; one-line pretrained model access is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Deep learning in pardesline today is reference implementations and expert guides that read any pardesline dataset: no weights are shipped and there is no inference API yet. Each page below documents the scripts, the example that ran them on a bundled dataset, and the recipe at full scale.

Coming: one-line model access

Models will get the same treatment as datasets: a model manifest (source, weights URI, licence, input type, task, memory and GPU needs, provenance) and a single loader / runner API that looks the same whatever the source (Hugging Face Hub, torch.hub, vendor repositories): pl.load_model("dinov3") then pl.run(model, dataset), then visualise. The URLs under /models/<name>/ are reserved so these pages fill in without breaking links. Vote and comment on the model registry tracking issue; model manifests can be written now from templates/new_model/ and listed on Models wanted.

Model page Task What ships today Example (executed) DINOv3 and DINOv2 features for 3D and medical imaging dinov3 dense features dinov3_faster_rcnn.py, dinov3_features.py dinov2_features_kitti JEPA self-supervised pretraining on 3D medical volumes jepa pretraining jepa3d_pretrain.py jepa_hippocampus PointNet segmentation of medical and industrial point clouds pointnet segmentation make_point_dataset.py, pointnet_seg.py pointnet_hippocampus VAE anomaly detection on medical images vae anomaly detection vae_anomaly.py vae_anomaly_hippocampus Pretrained 3D medical image segmentation models: nnU-Net and friends medical segmentation models prepare_nnunet_dataset.py skill script on MSD spleen Dice, HD95, Chamfer and the other 3D evaluation metrics evaluation metrics 3d metrics3d.py metrics_liver_interobserver

The PyTorch scripts need pip install torch (CPU is enough for the examples); DINOv3 weights need the licence accepted on the Hub, DINOv2 does not.

docs.title: DINOv3 and DINOv2 features for 3D and medical imaging in Python
docs.text:
What ships today, and what is coming

Today: dinov3_features.py (patch features + PCA colouring, any image, DINOv2 or DINOv3 backbone through transformers) and dinov3_faster_rcnn.py (a frozen backbone under a Faster R-CNN head). No weights are shipped and there is no inference API: the scripts are reference implementations that read any pardesline dataset.

Coming: one-line model access. The same registry pattern as datasets, a model manifest (source, weights URI, licence, input type, task, memory needs, provenance) and pl.load_model(...) / pl.run(model, dataset). This page keeps its URL. Follow and vote on the model registry tracking issue; model manifests can be contributed now from templates/new_model/.

Reference scripts: dinov3_faster_rcnn.py, dinov3_features.py (shipped in the wheel under pardesline/skills/dinov3-dense-features/scripts/, served by the MCP tool get_skill).

Runnable example: examples/dinov2_features_kitti/run.py, executed on 2026-10-16; its outputs are committed next to it.

docs.title: DINOv3 dense features for medical and 3D work
The problem DINOv3 solved
docs.text:
Self-supervised ViTs (DINO, DINOv2) are trained with an image-level objective (L_DINO, teacher-student distillation of the class token) plus a masked patch objective (L_iBOT) and a spreading term (L_KoLeo). When training is scaled (more data, bigger model, longer schedules), global metrics keep improving while dense metrics peak around 200k iterations and then degrade: patch features lose local coherence, segmentation and depth probes fall, correspondence maps turn noisy. Two objectives pulling in opposite directions.

DINOv3 adds Gram anchoring:

L_Gram = || X_S X_S^T  -  X_G X_G^T ||_F^2
X_S : L2-normalised student patch features (P x d)
X_G : patch features from an earlier "Gram teacher" checkpoint (clean dense structure)
X X^T : the P x P matrix of patch-to-patch cosine similarities

It constrains the relations between patches, not the patches themselves: the student may move its features anywhere as long as patches that were similar stay similar. Applied late in training (and with the teacher run at higher resolution), it removes the degradation and unlocks scaling:

DINOv2 DINOv3 Data LVD-142M LVD-1689M (~1.7 B curated) Largest model ViT-g/14 (1.1 B) ViT-7B/16 (6.7 B) ADE20K segmentation, frozen backbone linear probe 63.0 mIoU (+6) COCO detection, frozen backbone - 66.1 mAP Instance retrieval / video tracking - +10.9 mAP / +6.7 J&F Distilled family few sizes ViT-S/B/L/H+ and ConvNeXt T-L (29 M-198 M)

Consequence for engineers: the fine-tuning stage that used to be needed before any correspondence or dense task is largely gone; a frozen backbone plus a small head is a legitimate production design.

docs.title: Using the features
docs.text:
# scripts/dinov3_features.py extracts patch tokens; the core is:
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "facebook/dinov3-vitl16-pretrain-lvd1689m"
)  # gated: accept the licence on the Hub
x = preprocess(image, size=512)  # multiples of 16; ImageNet mean/std; grayscale -> 3 channels
tokens = model(pixel_values=x).last_hidden_state  # (1, 1 + R + P, d): CLS, register tokens, P patches
patches = tokens[:, 1 + n_registers :]  # (1, 32*32, 1024) for 512 px / 16
fmap = patches.reshape(1, 32, 32, 1024)
  • Resolution: patch 16; 512 px gives a 32 x 32 map, 1024 px a 64 x 64 map (memory grows with P^2 in attention). For small lesions, tile or upsample features (bilinear or FeatUp) rather than upsampling the image blindly.
  • Register tokens (4) sit between CLS and patches in DINOv3; drop them for dense maps.
  • Visualise with PCA on the patch tokens (3 components to RGB): the first look that tells whether the modality transfers (myocardium / blood pool / pericardium separate on echo).
  • Normalise features (L2) before cosine similarity; for matching use mutual nearest neighbours + a ratio test.

docs.title: Heads on a frozen backbone
docs.text:
Task Head Notes Classification linear or small MLP on CLS (+ mean of patches) the baseline every claim is measured against Segmentation linear per patch, or a light decoder (UperNet / DPT style) on 4 intermediate layers 1x1 conv on upsampled tokens already beats many trained CNNs Detection ViTDet simple feature pyramid: from the single 1/16 token map build P2-P5 by deconv / identity / pooling, 256 channels, then a standard Faster R-CNN (RPN + RoIAlign + box head) or a DETR-style decoder the pericardial-effusion recipe: ViT-L/16 frozen (300 M params, 0 updates), ~25 M trainable, focal loss for the rare class, NMS 0.5 Dense correspondence / registration init cosine similarity between patch tokens of two views, RANSAC on the matches gives an initial pose for point-cloud-registration from images Retrieval / anomaly k-NN on CLS or patch tokens against a bank of normal images see vae-anomaly-detection for the reconstruction route

Training a head: AdamW 1e-4 (head only), batch 8-16, 20-50 epochs, strong photometric augmentation (gain, speckle noise, gamma for ultrasound), mild geometric augmentation (the backbone is frozen, geometry invariances come from it). Store features once (no backbone forward during epochs) when the dataset fits on disk: training then takes minutes.

docs.title: Medical transfer: where it works and where it breaks
docs.text:
• Works out of the box: B-mode ultrasound (effusion detection, chamber structure), chest X-ray, endoscopy frames, dermatology, fundus - 2D images with natural-image-like statistics.
  • Needs adaptation: histopathology (stain statistics; use a pathology foundation model or stain-normalise), OCT, mammography at full resolution (tile).
  • Does not apply directly: 3D volumes (CT/MRI). Options: run per slice and aggregate (2.5D), use the features as a prior for a 3D decoder, or use a 3D self-supervised backbone (jepa-pretraining). Do not feed Hounsfield units as RGB without windowing.
  • Validate on a modality-specific held-out set split by patient; report the linear-probe baseline so the head's contribution is visible.

docs.title: For 3D
docs.text: Dense, spatially coherent features at high resolution are the primitive for multi-view matching (two endoscopy frames, two photographs of a scan subject), for novel-view synthesis priors (feature splatting, gaussian-splatting), and for lifting 2D predictions onto a mesh (project the mesh into each view, sample the feature map, vote). The c3vd_endoscopy_splats and hf_3d_arena datasets give posed images and 3D outputs to try it on.

docs.title: Weights, licences, deployment
docs.text:
• DINOv3 weights are gated on the Hub under Meta's DINOv3 licence (accept the terms, use your token: huggingface-cli login); check the commercial clause for your product. DINOv2 is Apache-2.0.
  • Distilled models: ViT-S/16 (21 M) for edge, ConvNeXt variants for ONNX / TensorRT without attention kernels.
  • Export: the frozen backbone is a fixed graph; quantise to int8 with a calibration set of your modality, validate the head's metrics again.

Scripts: scripts/dinov3_features.py (extract, PCA-colour, save .npz of patch tokens), scripts/dinov3_faster_rcnn.py (frozen backbone + simple feature pyramid + torchvision Faster R-CNN, training and evaluation on a COCO- style box dataset). Both need torch, torchvision, transformers.

Source: skills/dinov3-dense-features/SKILL.md, published on 2026-10-14.

docs.text:
What ships today, and what is coming

Today: metrics3d.py: Dice, IoU, HD95, ASSD, surface Dice, volume error, Chamfer, F-score, pose error, on NumPy arrays with spacing. No weights are shipped and there is no inference API: the scripts are reference implementations that read any pardesline dataset.

Coming: one-line model access. The same registry pattern as datasets, a model manifest (source, weights URI, licence, input type, task, memory needs, provenance) and pl.load_model(...) / pl.run(model, dataset). This page keeps its URL. Follow and vote on the model registry tracking issue; model manifests can be contributed now from templates/new_model/.

Reference scripts: metrics3d.py (shipped in the wheel under pardesline/skills/evaluation-metrics-3d/scripts/, served by the MCP tool get_skill).

Runnable example: examples/metrics_liver_interobserver/run.py, executed on 2026-10-16; its outputs are committed next to it.

docs.title: Evaluation metrics for 3D vision and medical imaging
docs.text: scripts/metrics3d.py implements every metric below on NumPy arrays (label maps as (z, y, x) arrays with spacing, point sets as (N, 3)) and runs on a bundled dataset as a self-test.

docs.title: Segmentation (label maps)
docs.text:
Metric Definition Use / caveat Dice 2|A∩B| / (|A|+|B|) overlap of volumes; insensitive to boundary errors on large organs (liver Dice 0.95 can hide a 10 mm boundary error); report per class IoU (Jaccard) |A∩B| / |A∪B| IoU = Dice / (2 - Dice); stricter Hausdorff max(sup_a d(a,B), sup_b d(b,A)) on the surfaces, mm one stray voxel dominates it HD95 95th percentile of the two directed surface distances the robust version; always with the spacing applied ASSD mean of both directed surface distances boundary accuracy in mm Normalised surface Dice (NSD) fraction of surface points within tolerance tau of the other surface tau = 1-3 mm for organs, what challenges (TotalSegmentator, KiTS) use Volume error (V_pred - V_true) / V_true clinically meaningful (ejection fraction, tumour volume); sign matters

Rules: compute on the original spacing, never on resampled isotropic labels only; report the per-case distribution (median, IQR, worst case), not just the mean; an empty prediction on an empty reference is Dice 1 by convention only if you say so.

docs.title: Surfaces and point clouds
docs.text:
• Chamfer distance CD = mean_a min_b ||a-b|| + mean_b min_a ||a-b|| (some papers square the distances; say which). Units of the data.
  • F-score at threshold d: precision = fraction of predicted points within d of the reference, recall = the converse, F = 2PR/(P+R). Readable, bounded; pick d from the scanner noise (0.5-1 mm) or 1 % of the diagonal.
  • Point-to-mesh distance when the reference is a mesh: use the true distance to triangles, not to vertices (vertex-only overestimates on coarse meshes).
  • Hausdorff / HD95 as above; for partial overlap, restrict to the overlapping region or the number is meaningless.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
• Rigid: rotation error arccos((tr(R_est R_trueᵀ) - 1) / 2), translation error at the object centre ||T_est c - T_true c||.
  • Target registration error (TRE): mean distance between landmark pairs not used by the algorithm; fiducial registration error (FRE) on the ones used is optimistic and should not be reported alone.
  • Fitness / inlier RMSE (ICP): threshold-dependent, see point-cloud-registration.
  • Deformable: Jacobian determinant of the displacement field, det(J) <= 0 fraction = folding (must be ~0), its log standard deviation = smoothness; Dice of propagated labels; TRE.
  • Multimodal intensity registration (CT/MR): mutual information value is not comparable across pairs; use TRE on anatomical landmarks or Dice of propagated masks.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text: IoU between boxes (2D or 3D), AP = area under the precision-recall curve at IoU 0.5 (AP50) and averaged over 0.5:0.05:0.95 (COCO mAP). For medical lesions: sensitivity at a fixed false positives per scan (FROC, LUNA16 uses 0.125 to 8 FP/scan), because one missed nodule matters more than a loose box.

docs.title: Anomaly detection (reconstruction-based, VAE)
docs.text: Image-level AUROC on the anomaly score (reconstruction error or its percentile); pixel-level AUROC / AUPRC when masks exist (AUPRC is the honest one when anomalies cover 1 % of pixels); choose the operating threshold on a validation set by a target false-positive rate, never on the test set.

docs.title: Reconstruction and rendering
docs.text: PSNR 10 log10(MAX^2 / MSE) (dB), SSIM (structure, 0-1), LPIPS (learned perceptual, lower better) on held-out views; training views say nothing.

docs.title: Making a number credible
docs.text:
1. Split by patient / scene (ds.split(by="patient")), never by slice or frame.
  2. Report n, median and IQR (or mean and 95 % CI from bootstrap over cases).
  3. Paired comparison between methods on the same cases (Wilcoxon signed-rank).
  4. State the units, the spacing, the threshold d or tau, and whether the metric is on voxels or surfaces.
  5. Show the worst case, not only the best.
  6. "100 % label accuracy" on a scan generated from the atlas itself is a sanity check, not a result: say so.
from metrics3d import dice, hd95, surface_dice, chamfer, f_score, pose_error

Source: skills/evaluation-metrics-3d/SKILL.md, published on 2026-10-14.

docs.title: JEPA self-supervised pretraining on 3D medical volumes in Python
docs.text:
What ships today, and what is coming

Today: jepa3d_pretrain.py: a 3D ViT context encoder, a predictor and an EMA target encoder trained on masked blocks of any pardesline volume dataset. No weights are shipped and there is no inference API: the scripts are reference implementations that read any pardesline dataset.

Coming: one-line model access. The same registry pattern as datasets, a model manifest (source, weights URI, licence, input type, task, memory needs, provenance) and pl.load_model(...) / pl.run(model, dataset). This page keeps its URL. Follow and vote on the model registry tracking issue; model manifests can be contributed now from templates/new_model/.

Reference scripts: jepa3d_pretrain.py (shipped in the wheel under pardesline/skills/jepa-pretraining/scripts/, served by the MCP tool get_skill).

Runnable example: examples/jepa_hippocampus/run.py, executed on 2026-10-16; its outputs are committed next to it.

docs.title: JEPA: predicting in latent space instead of reconstructing pixels
The idea
docs.text:
An autoencoder (and MAE) learns z = f(x) by reconstructing x_hat = g(z) and paying ||x - x_hat||^2 on every pixel - including speckle, breathing motion, contrast timing and scanner noise that carry no semantics. Capacity goes to modelling noise.

JEPA removes the decoder. Mask part of the input; encode the visible context with s_theta; encode the hidden target with a second network s_bar (an exponential moving average of s_theta, no gradient); train a predictor q_phi to predict the target embeddings from the context embeddings plus the positions of the target patches:

L = || q_phi( s_theta(x_context), pos_target )  -  sg( s_bar(x_target) ) ||^2

The model predicts only what is predictable from context - anatomy, structure, texture statistics - and is free to ignore unpredictable detail. No pixel decoder, no reconstruction, no contrastive negatives.

Encoder-decoder / MAE JEPA Output pixels / signal embeddings Loss reconstruction (L2 / BCE) latent prediction (L2 / smooth L1) What it models everything, noise included the predictable structure Collapse risk none (decoder constrains) handled by EMA target + stop-gradient + predictor Compute decoder forward/backward on all patches encoder on context only (~25 %), predictor is light Transfer good with long schedules better linear-probe and low-shot transfer at a fraction of the epochs

docs.title: Why it fits medical data
docs.text:
• Cardiac MRI / CT: breathing, ECG gating, contrast phase, coil shading are nuisance; chamber geometry and wall texture are predictable from context.
  • 3D ultrasound: speckle is by construction unpredictable; anatomy is not.
  • ECG: baseline wander and electrode noise vs the P-QRS-T structure.
  • Labels are scarce; the pretrained encoder is fine-tuned (or probed) for segmentation, classification and anomaly detection with 10-100x fewer labels than from scratch.

docs.title: Architecture details that matter
docs.text:
• Tokenisation. 2D: ViT patches 16 x 16 at 224-448 px. Volumes: 3D patches (tubelets) of 16 x 16 x 16 or anisotropic 8 x 16 x 16 when the through-plane spacing is coarse; add learnable or sinusoidal 3D position embeddings; scale positions by voxel spacing when spacing varies across the dataset (pardesline volumes carry it in frame.affine). Signals: 1-D patches of 50-100 samples at 250-500 Hz, position = time.
  • Masking. I-JEPA samples 4 target blocks (15-20 % of tokens each, aspect 0.75-1.5) and one large context block (85-100 %) minus the targets; V-JEPA masks 3D tubelets with high ratios (~90 %). Masks must be large and semantic (blocks), not random pixels, or the task reduces to interpolation.
  • Target encoder. EMA of the context encoder, momentum from 0.996 to 1.0 over training; its outputs are layer-normalised per token; no gradient.
  • Predictor. A narrow ViT (depth 6-12, width 384) that takes context tokens plus mask tokens with the target positions; narrower than the encoder so the information must sit in the encoder.
  • Loss. L2 (or smooth L1) between predicted and target tokens, averaged over target tokens only.
  • Optimiser. AdamW, lr 1e-3 with warm-up 40 epochs then cosine, weight decay 0.04-0.4, batch 2 048 images (scale lr with batch), 300-800 epochs on ImageNet-1k scale; for 10k medical volumes, 100-300 epochs at batch 64 of 96^3 crops is a realistic budget (1-3 GPU-days on one 80 GB card with bf16).
  • Collapse diagnostics. Monitor the per-dimension standard deviation of target embeddings and the effective rank: a sudden drop means collapse (raise EMA momentum start, shorten warm-up, lower lr).

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
1. Linear probe / k-NN on the frozen encoder for classification (pathology present / absent, view classification).
  2. Fine-tuning for segmentation with a light decoder (UNETR-style) on 10 %, 50 %, 100 % of labels: the low-label regime is where pretraining shows; compare Dice / HD95 to from-scratch at equal compute.
  3. Anomaly detection: distance in latent space to a bank of normal cases (AUROC), complementary to vae-anomaly-detection.
  4. Always split pretraining and downstream sets by patient; pretraining on the downstream test patients is leakage even without labels.

docs.title: Datasets to pretrain on (bundled, lazy)
docs.text:
hf_openmind (114k head MRI, any study: hf://MIC-DKFZ/OpenMind/OpenMind/dsXXXXXX), hf_ct_rate_valid (chest CT, gated; 50k volumes in the full repo), totalsegmentator_ct (1 228 whole-body CT), amos22, ixi_brain_mri, tcia_lidc_idri (1 018 CT series), luna16; cardiac: msd_task02_heart; signals: not bundled yet (use PhysioNet PTB-XL with the same recipe).

import pardesline as pl

ds = pl.load("totalsegmentator_ct")  # 1 228 CTs, fetched on access
vol = ds[0].ct.to_sitk()  # resample to 1.5 mm isotropic, clip HU, crop 96^3 patches

scripts/jepa3d_pretrain.py is a complete reference: 3D ViT encoder, EMA target, block masking in 3D, predictor, loss, collapse monitor, a loader that reads any pardesline dataset volume role (resampled, windowed, cropped), and a linear-probe evaluation hook. Needs torch; runs on CPU at toy size for a smoke test.

Source: skills/jepa-pretraining/SKILL.md, published on 2026-10-14.

docs.title: Pretrained 3D medical image segmentation models: nnU-Net and friends in Python
docs.text:
What ships today, and what is coming

Today: prepare_nnunet_dataset.py: any pardesline dataset written in the nnU-Net v2 raw layout, plus the guide to the model families that win the public benchmarks. No weights are shipped and there is no inference API: the scripts are reference implementations that read any pardesline dataset.

Coming: one-line model access. The same registry pattern as datasets, a model manifest (source, weights URI, licence, input type, task, memory needs, provenance) and pl.load_model(...) / pl.run(model, dataset). This page keeps its URL. Follow and vote on the model registry tracking issue; model manifests can be contributed now from templates/new_model/.

Reference scripts: prepare_nnunet_dataset.py (shipped in the wheel under pardesline/skills/medical-segmentation-models/scripts/, served by the MCP tool get_skill).

docs.title: Which model (2026)
docs.text:
Need Choose Why A new organ / lesion task with 20-500 labelled volumes nnU-Net v2 (3d_fullres, + 3d_lowres cascade for large FOV) self-configures spacing, patch size, batch size, normalisation from the dataset fingerprint; still the strongest baseline on MSD, AMOS, KiTS 117 body structures on CT without training TotalSegmentator (its dataset totalsegmentator_ct is CC BY 4.0; the weights carry their own non-commercial terms, check before shipping) one command, nnU-Net inside Transformer backbone, large data Swin-UNETR / UNETR (MONAI), SegResNet gains appear above ~1 000 volumes or with self-supervised pretraining Interactive / few labels MedSAM, SAM-Med3D, nnInteractive prompt with boxes or clicks; validate per case Many sources, foundation-model style BiomedSegFM-type challenge models, STU-Net pretrain on pooled datasets (hf_biomedsegfm_3d_val shows the pooled format)

Every one of them is a voxel network: the label lives in the voxel grid (see 3d-representations).

docs.title: Data: from a pardesline dataset to a training set
docs.text:
import pardesline as pl

ds = pl.load("msd_task09_spleen").filter(split="Tr")  # 41 labelled CTs, licence attached
train, val = ds.split(by="id", fractions=(0.8, 0.2), seed=0)  # patient-level split, no leakage
ds.export("./spleen_std")  # NIfTI + sidecars + manifest if you want local files

scripts/prepare_nnunet_dataset.py writes the nnU-Net raw layout (imagesTr/CASE_0000.nii.gz, labelsTr/CASE.nii.gz, dataset.json) from any pardesline dataset with an image role and a labels role, including multi-channel inputs (MSD brain tumour: 4 modalities = _0000..._0003), DICOM series (materialised to NIfTI) and TotalSegmentator's one-mask-per-organ layout (merged into one label map with a class table).

Rules: - Split by patient (pairing key); never by slice. - Keep the licence: nnU-Net models trained on NC data (KiTS23, TotalSegmentator MRI, BiomedSegFM) inherit the restriction; say so in the model card. - Record spacing and orientation per case; nnU-Net resamples to the median spacing (or the 10th percentile along the low-res axis) and crops to the foreground.

docs.title: Preprocessing that matters
docs.text: Step CT MRI PET Resampling isotropic or dataset-median spacing, image linear / labels nearest same same Intensity clip to the 0.5-99.5 percentile of foreground HU, z-score with global mean/std (nnU-Net "CT" scheme) per-volume z-score (scanner-dependent intensities), optional N4 bias correction SUV normalisation Orientation reorient to a canonical frame (RAS or LPS) consistently; pardesline volumes are LPS same same Cropping to the non-zero / body region brain extraction optional Patches 128^3 (fullres) or anisotropic (e.g. 40 x 224 x 224) when spacing is anisotropic; oversample patches containing foreground (33 %)

docs.title: Training recipe (nnU-Net defaults, the ones worth knowing)
docs.text:
• Loss: Dice + cross-entropy, deep supervision at 3-4 decoder scales (weights 1, 1/2, 1/4...).
  • Optimizer: SGD momentum 0.99, Nesterov, lr 1e-2 with poly decay, 1 000 epochs x 250 iterations, batch 2; mixed precision.
  • Augmentation on the fly: rotation, scaling, elastic (light), Gaussian noise and blur, brightness / contrast, gamma, mirroring along anatomically valid axes only (never left-right if laterality matters: kidneys, lungs).
  • 5-fold cross-validation; ensemble folds at inference.
  • Budget: 1 fold of 3d_fullres ~ 1-2 GPU-days on a 24 GB card at 128^3; a "quick look" at 100 epochs tells whether the task is learnable.

docs.title: Inference
docs.text:
Sliding window with 50 % overlap and a Gaussian importance map (centre of the patch trusted more), test-time augmentation by flips, argmax, then post-processing: keep the largest connected component per class when the anatomy is a single object (spleen, liver), not for lesions or vessels. Resample the prediction back to the original grid with nearest-neighbour and write it with the original header. In pardesline:

pred = pl.load("pred_case07.nii.gz").as_labels({1: "spleen"})  # LabelMap in LPS mm
surf = pred.to_mesh(label=1)  # exact surface for review
pred.save("case07_pred.nii.gz")  # + sidecar with labels and provenance

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Per class and per case: Dice, HD95 (mm), NSD at 1-3 mm, volume error; median and IQR; worst cases shown. evaluation-metrics-3d/scripts/metrics3d.py implements them; metrics3d.py --dataset liver_tumor_patient01 prints the inter-observer agreement of three radiologists, the ceiling any model should be compared with.

docs.title: Common failures
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Dice fine, HD95 huge isolated false positives far away largest-component post-processing, lower-res cascade for context Collapses on small structures class imbalance foreground oversampling, Dice loss already helps, patch size covering the structure Works on one scanner only intensity shift per-volume normalisation (MRI), intensity augmentation, more centres Laterality swap mirroring augmentation on left/right classes disable left-right flips Looks good in 2D, striped in 3D 2D model on anisotropic data 3D model or 2.5D with neighbouring slices Train/val gap leakage by slice or by patient with several scans split by patient id

docs.title: Datasets to practise on
docs.text:
MSD tasks (msd_task01_braintumour ... msd_task10_colon), amos22 (15 organs CT/MRI), totalsegmentator_ct / totalsegmentator_mri, hf_kits23, verse19_spine, spider_lumbar_mri, hf_nsclc_radiomics, hf_biomedsegfm_3d_val (pooled npz), luna16 (detection), tcia_lidc_idri (DICOM + SEG).
